en: Maitreya said:
To Śatarūpā, Manu begot three daughters,
who were renowned as Ākūti, Devahūtī, and Prasūti.

The king, with the approval of Śatarūpā, gave Ākūti— who already had a brother— to Ruci, following the custom of the appointed daughter (*putrikā-dharma*). That lordly Prajāpati, Ruci, begot [offspring] upon her.
Possessing the splendor of Brahman, he produced a couple through supreme meditative concentration.
Of those two, the male was Viṣṇu himself, assuming the form of sacrifice;
she who was the female was Dakṣiṇā, the inseparable portion of prosperity.
Filled with joy, Svāyambhuva brought the son of his daughter, who possessed expansive luster, to his own home; Ruci accepted her as his sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and the Lord, the master of the Yajus formulas, married her as she desired him.
When Tuṣṭā was pleased, Toṣa attained satisfaction and begot twelve sons:
Toṣa, Pratoṣa, Santoṣa, Bhadra, Śānti, Iḍaspati,
Idhma, Kavi, Vibhu, Svahna, Sudeva, and Rocana— twelve in number.
In the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu, those gods were known as the Tuṣitas;
the sages were headed by Marīci, and Yajña was the lord of the hosts of gods.
The two sons of Manu, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, were endowed with great majesty.
O dear one, after that interval, Manu gave his daughter Devahūti to Kardama; her sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons followed in succession,
and their history has been heard by you mostly as I have related it.

The Lord Manu gave Prasūti to Dakṣa, the son of Brahmā; by her was produced the great and extensive creation spread throughout the three worlds. As for those nine daughters of Kardama who were mentioned as the wives of the Brahmarṣis—
Learn from me their progeny and descendants as they are being described.
The wife of Marīci, Kalā, daughter of Kardama,
gave birth to Kaśyapa and Pūrṇimāna, by whom the world was filled.
O scorcher of enemies, Pūrṇimā gave birth to Viraja and Viśvaga;
and from the washing of Hari’s feet, Devakulyā became the river that flows in the heavens.
Anasūyā, the wife of Atri, gave birth to three highly illustrious sons.
[He gave] Durvāsas, Soma, Ātman, Īśa, Brahmā, and Sambhava.
Vidura said:
"In the house of Atri were the best of the gods, who are the causes of maintenance, creation, and destruction."
"O Guru, tell me this: what did they wish to do?
Maitreya said:
"Urged by Brahmā to perform creation, Atri, the best among the knowers of Brahman,"
Accompanied by his wife, he went to Mount Ṛkṣa, the king of mountains, and remained there engaged in austerity.
In that place, within a forest of *aśoka* trees covered with clusters of blossoms and petals,
the waters of the Nirvindhyā river resounded on all sides as they flowed forth.
Having restrained his mind through breath control for a hundred years, the sage stood on one foot, free from dualities and subsisting only on air;
I take refuge in Him who is indeed the Lord of the universe.

Thinking, "May he grant me offspring equal to himself," the three lords of creation beheld the sage performing austerities with the fire of his breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) issuing from the crown of his head, which was consuming the three worlds.
The Apsarases, Munis, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas went to that hermitage, where his fame was being spread abroad; meanwhile,
the sage’s mind was illuminated by the thought of their arrival.
Rising on one foot, he beheld the preeminent among the gods;
bowing down like a staff upon the ground, he stood before them with his hands joined in reverence,
seeing them seated upon a bull, a swan, and Garuda, each marked by their respective emblems.
Having been graced by his compassionate glance and smiling countenance,
the sage closed his eyes, which were dazzled by that radiance; then,
with palms joined in reverence, he fixed his mind upon Him and offered this praise.

With gentle and well-spoken words, Atri spoke to Him who is most venerable to all the worlds: "In the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, by means of [the powers] being distributed..."
O Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Giriśa, you who assume bodies in each age through the qualities of Māyā— I bow down to you all. Which one among you has been summoned here by me?

"O Blessed One, how is it that you alone have been chosen by me here through various primary elements for the purpose of procreation, while you— how indeed have you come here from a distance even beyond the mind of embodied beings?"
"Speak! Be gracious! A great wonder has arisen here within me.
Maitreya said:
Having heard these words of his, those three bulls among the gods...
O Lord, having smiled, the gods replied to that sage with gentle words:
"The resolve you have formed must surely come to pass; it cannot be otherwise."
O Brahman, whatever you, whose resolve is virtuous, meditate upon, that indeed shall we do.
Furthermore, your sons, who are born from a portion of ourselves and are world-renowned, shall come into being; may all be well with you, and they shall spread your fame.

Having thus granted the boon of their desires, the lords of the gods departed after being duly honored by the couple as they looked on. Then Soma appeared as a portion of Brahmā, and Datta, the knower of yoga, as a portion of Viṣṇu.
Durvāsas was a portion of Śaṅkara; now learn of the offspring of Aṅgiras. Śraddhā, the wife of Aṅgiras, gave birth to four daughters:
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and likewise Anumati as the fourth.
He had two other sons who were renowned during the Svārociṣa Manvantara:
the venerable Utathya, who was manifestly the most devoted to Brahman, and Bṛhaspati;
and Pulastya begot Agastya upon his wife Havirbhū.
In another birth, he was Dahrāgni and Viśravas of great austerity.
Of him, the lord of the Yakṣas, the god Kubera, was born as the son of Iḍaviḍā;
likewise, Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa were born to another wife, as was Vibhīṣaṇa.
Gati, the virtuous wife of Pulaha, gave birth to three sons:
Karmaśreṣṭha, Varīyāṃs, and Sahiṣṇu, O high-minded one.
Kriyā, the wife of Kratu, also gave birth to the Vālakhilyas.
O scorcher of the enemy, sixty thousand sons were born to Vasiṣṭha through Ūrjā; blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
they were seven stainless celestial sages (brahmarṣis), headed by Citraketu.
Citraketu, Suroci, Viraja, Mitra, Ulbaṇa, Vasubhṛt, Yāna, Dyumān, Śakti, and others were born. Furthermore,
Cittī, the wife of Atharvan, obtained a son named Dhṛtavrata.
Learn from me about Dadhyañc Aśvaśiras, who belonged to the lineage of Bhṛgu. O fortunate one, the highly blessed Bhṛgu begot sons upon his wife Khyāti:
Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Śrī, who was entirely devoted to the Blessed Lord.
Meru gave Āyati and Niyati to his two sons;
from them were born Mṛkaṇḍa and Prāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya was the son of Mṛkaṇḍa, and from Prāṇa was born the sage Vedaśiras.
And Kavi Bhārgava, whose son was the divine Uśanas;
these sages, O Kṣattṛ, brought the worlds into being through their progeny.
This lineage of the grandson of Kardama has thus been described to you.
For one who hears it with faith, this supreme [narrative] instantly removes all sins.
Dakṣa, the son of Aja, married the daughter of Manu;
in her, he begot sixteen daughters of pure vision.
From among the thirteen daughters, the all-pervading Lord gave one to Dharma, one to Agni,
one to the Pitṛs, one to the Yuktas, and one to Bhava, the destroyer of worldly existence.
[These daughters were] Śraddhā, Maitrī, Dayā, Śānti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Kriyā, and Unnati.
Intellect, wisdom, forbearance, and modesty were the wives of Dharma;
Śraddhā bore him auspiciousness, Maitrī bore serenity, fearlessness, and compassion;
and Puṣṭi bore peace, happiness, joy, contentment, and pride.
Yoga gave birth to Kriyonnati, Darpam, Artha, and Buddhi;
Medhā gave birth to Smṛti, Titikṣā to Kṣema, and Hrīḥ to her son Praśraya.
Mūrti, the source of all virtues, gave birth to the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
At the birth of those two, this entire universe rejoiced with great tranquility;
the minds, the quarters of the sky, the winds, the rivers, and the mountains became serene.
Celestial musical instruments resounded and showers of flowers fell.
The sages, being satisfied, offered hymns of praise; the Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang;
the divine women danced, and there was supreme auspiciousness.
All the gods, headed by Brahmā, attended upon Him with prayers of adoration.
The gods said:
"He who, by his own power of illusion (*māyā*), has fashioned this universe within himself— as one perceives various forms in the sky for the sake of observation— "
By this means, today in the abode of Dharma, he who has assumed the form of a sage has manifested [himself] for the sake of the Supreme Person; salutations to Him.
He is the one who created these beings for the sake of the maintenance, transformation, and cessation [of the world].
O You whose true nature is to be inferred by us through Your goodness, look upon us— the hosts of gods— with a gaze of abundant compassion,
casting down Your stainless lotus, the abode of Śrī.
Thus, O dear one, having been praised by the hosts of gods who had obtained their vision, the two Blessed Ones departed for Gandhamādana after being honored. Indeed,
these two have come here as portions of the Blessed Lord Hari.
And for the sake of relieving the earth's burden, Kṛṣṇa begot two sons upon the daughters of Yadu and Kuru.
Furthermore, Svāhā, the wife of Agni who personifies the sacrificial oblation, gave birth to three sons:
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci, all of whom consume the offerings.
From them were produced forty-five fires; these, together with the fathers and grandfathers,
constitute the forty-nine [fires] by whose names the exponents of the Veda invoke [the deities] in the sacrificial rites.
In the sacrifice, the fire-offerings (iṣṭis) dedicated to Agni are presented;
those fires are the Agniṣvāttas, the Barhiṣads, and the Soma-drinking Pitṛs who consume clarified butter.
Among them, some possess fire and others do not; their wife is Dākṣāyaṇī, whose nature is the ancestral offering (svadhā).
From them, Svadhā bore two daughters: Vayunā and Dhāriṇī.
Both of them were expounders of the Veda and had reached the further shore of knowledge and realization.
Satī, however, was the wife of Bhava, and she was devoted to the god Bhava.

She did not obtain a son equal to herself in qualities and character; while her own father was unworthy and enraged at Bhava despite his innocence, she, though still immature, abandoned her body through yoga.
Vidura said:
Why did Dakṣa, who was devoted to his daughter and preeminent among those of virtuous character in this world,
show such hostility toward Satī, disregarding her as his own daughter?
Who hates that great deity of the world, the teacher of all moving and non-moving beings, who is free from enmity, whose form is peaceful, who delights in the Self, and who is the supreme Lord?
O Brāhmaṇa, tell me this regarding my son-in-law and my father-in-law.
But because of her hatred, Satī gave up her life-breaths, which are so difficult to abandon.
Maitreya said:
Long ago, the supreme sages assembled at the sacrifice of the creators of the universe.
Likewise, all the hosts of immortals with their followers, the sages, and the sacrificial fires—
seeing him who had entered there, shining like the sun with its radiance and dispelling the darkness from that great assembly, the seers were struck with wonder.
The members of the assembly rose from their respective seats along with the sacrificial fires,
except for Viriñca and Śarva, whose minds were captivated by that splendor;
Dakṣa was then duly honored by the presiding priests.
Having bowed to the unborn teacher of the world, he sat down by his command.
Seeing the Gracious One seated facing east, he, feeling slighted, could not endure it;
looking at him with a sidelong glance from his eyes as if burning him, he spoke.

"O Brahman-sages, together with the gods and the sacrificial fires, listen to me as I describe the conduct of the virtuous, spoken neither out of ignorance nor from malice. This shameless man, however, is a destroyer of the fame of the world-protectors."
"The path practiced by the virtuous has been defiled by that arrogant man, who—
acting like a saintly man— accepted the hand of my daughter before the fire and the Brahmins, just as Sāvitrī did."

Having taken the hand of the fawn-eyed girl, he whose eyes were like those of a monkey failed, even in speech, to offer the proper greeting or rise for her, who was worthy of such honor; for she was one whose religious rites had been abandoned, who was impure, proud, and a breaker of the bounds of propriety.
"Though unwilling, I gave this young girl away like a low-born woman uttering harsh words.
Now, surrounded by ghosts and hosts of spirits in terrible abodes of the dead,
I wander like a madman— naked, with disheveled hair, laughing and weeping."

Having performed his ritual bath with ashes from the funeral pyre, adorned with garlands of corpses and ornaments of human bone, he is known as Śiva, though he is in fact inauspicious; intoxicated by liquor, he is fond of those who are likewise intoxicated,
and he is the lord of the Pramathas, whose very nature consists of pure darkness.
"Alas! At the instigation of the Supreme Creator, I have given that virtuous woman to one who is the lord of madness, devoid of purity, and evil-hearted. Maitreya said:
Having thus reviled Giriśa, who remained unyielding,
Dakṣa then touched water and, filled with rage, proceeded to pronounce a curse.
"But this Bhava, in this sacrificial ground of the gods, [is attended] by Indra, Upendra, and the others..."
"May that lowest of the hosts of gods not receive his share along with the other deities!

O descendant of Kuru, as Dakṣa was being restrained by the chief members of the assembly, he hurled this curse at Giritra; then, departing from there with his anger fully aroused, he went to his own abode.
Having understood the curse, Nandīśvara, the foremost follower of Giriśa, corrupted by the bitterness of his wrath,
unleashed a terrible curse upon Dakṣa and those twice-born who had approved of it,
as well as upon that mortal who, toward the Lord who bears no enmity— bhagavaty apratidruhi ya etan martyam uddiśya [cursed].
The ignorant man, possessing a dualistic vision and turned away from reality, becomes hostile;
attached to homes where dharma is hypocritical, he strives for vulgar pleasures and expands the system of ritual action, his intellect corrupted by the mere literalism of Vedic discourse.

May that beast, who through a mind intent on the Supreme has forgotten his own true nature, become exceedingly desirous of women; may he soon become a goat-faced Dakṣa. May that dull-witted one, who perceives ignorance consisting of ritual action as true knowledge, remain a fool.
May those who follow this Śarva, who despises Him, wander here in the cycle of rebirth;
may those enemies of Hara, their minds churned by the churning-stick of the words of the Veda— which are like flowering trees with its abundant honey-scent— be utterly deluded.

"Let the twice-born, though possessing maintained knowledge, austerity, and vows, wander here as beggars, eating all things for their livelihood, delighting only in wealth, the body, and the senses. Having heard this curse being uttered by him regarding the community of the twice-born, [the sages spoke].
Bhṛgu discharged a curse, an invincible Brahman-staff:
"May those who observe the vows of Bhava and those who follow them become heretics, opponents of the true scriptures."
"Let those whose purity is lost, who are dull-witted, and who wear matted hair, ashes, and bones,
enter into the initiation of Śiva, wherein the deity is wine and where you revile both the Veda and the Brāhmaṇas."
Therefore, those who have resorted to heresy have abandoned this bridge, which is the support for men.
For this alone is the auspicious and eternal path for the worlds,
which the ancients followed and which Janārdana is the authority for.
"That is the supreme Brahman, pure and the eternal path of the virtuous;
abandon that heresy which you have followed, wherein the Lord of Beings is regarded as a mere deity.
Maitreya said:
While Bhṛgu was thus pronouncing his curse, the blessed Lord Bhava departed from there with his attendants, appearing somewhat dejected;
and those creators of the universe likewise continued their sacrificial session for a thousand years.
Having made arrangements there where the great archer Ṛṣabha had performed his sacrifice,
and having performed the final purificatory bath at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
they all then departed for their respective abodes with purified minds.
Maitreya said:
While the son-in-law and the father-in-law remained thus in constant enmity, a very long period of time passed by.

When Dakṣa was consecrated by the supreme Brahmā to the sovereignty over all the Prajāpatis, pride arose within him. Having performed the Vājapeya sacrifice and having surpassed those most devoted to Brahman, he became arrogant.

He commenced the supreme sacrifice named Bṛhaspatisava. At that time, all the Brahman-sages, celestial sages, ancestors, and deities were present, having performed the rites for auspiciousness, along with their wives and husbands.
Having overheard those words of the sky-dwellers as they conversed in the atmosphere,
the goddess Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, beheld the excellent wives of the secondary gods arriving from all directions for the great festival of her father’s sacrifice.

Seeing those women— traveling in celestial chariots, accompanied by their beloveds, wearing golden necklaces and fine garments, with restless eyes and polished earrings— in the vicinity of her own dwelling,
she spoke out of eagerness to the Lord of beings, the divine husband.
Satī said:
"O fair one, it is said that the great festival of the sacrifice of your father-in-law Prajāpati has now commenced.
We shall go there as well, for these gods are indeed proceeding there out of their desire for you."
"In that place, my sisters will surely go with their respective husbands, desiring to see their kinsmen;
and I, too, desire to go there with you to present the provisions brought by you.
"In that place, my sisters are indeed like mothers-in-law to me, and my maternal aunts are like mothers to me, as is my mother whose heart is moist with affection."

With a mind long filled with longing, I shall behold the banner of Śiva’s sacrifice being led forth by the great sages. This wonder, fashioned by Your own power of illusion (*māyā*) consisting of the three qualities (*guṇas*), appears within You;
nevertheless, I am but a woman ignorant of reality, and as such, I am miserable—O Bhava, grant me the destruction of worldly existence.
Behold these women, though they are not of celestial origin, traveling in groups with their beloveds as companions, beautifully adorned;
by their departure, the sky is graced with aerial chariots as white as swans and decorated with blue-throated peacocks.
O best of gods, how is it that the body of your daughter does not move, even after hearing of the festivities at her father’s house?
Even without being invited, they go to the assembly of their husband, their guru, and those who have provided them with a body, out of friendship.
O Immortal One, may you be gracious to me; indeed, it behooves you, who are compassionate, to fulfill this desire of mine.
For you, with your vast vision, have already designated me as half of yourself; therefore, please grant me this favor as I entreat you.
The sage said:
Thus addressed by his beloved, Giritra, who is dear to his friends, replied with a smile,
remembering those arrows of malicious speech which pierce the vitals and which someone had spoken in the presence of the creators of the universe.
The Blessed Lord said:

"O beautiful one, what you have said is indeed excellent. Even without being invited, kinsmen come to the aid of their kin, provided they have not been provoked by faults and are not overcome by the wrath born of the intoxication of power and self-conceit."

When the memory [of the Lord] is destroyed by these six qualities of the virtuous— learning, austerity, wealth, physical beauty, youth, and noble lineage— which are the opposite of the qualities of the wicked, those who are blinded by the evil sight of their own nourished pride become arrogant and do not perceive the abode of the Great Beings. One should not enter the homes of such people, whose minds are unstable, out of consideration for their own kinsmen.

He who does not feel as much pain from the arrows of his enemies, with their brows knitted and eyes full of indignation, as he feels when looked upon with crooked intent by his own people; he whose limbs are tormented and whose heart burns day and night, struck to the very marrow by the harsh words of those with crooked minds.
O fair-browed one, it is evident that in my opinion you are considered the most beloved among the daughters of Prajāpati, who have attained the highest status;

nevertheless, you shall not receive honor from your father, for who would suffer on account of me? With a heart burning with anxiety, his senses distressed by the prosperity of those who witness the intellect of men.
It is impossible for them to easily ascend to the supreme state, just as the demons hate Hari. O slender-waisted one, wise men properly perform mutual rising to greet, showing respect,
and salutation toward another as if toward the Supreme Person dwelling in the cave of the heart, and not toward one who merely identifies with the body.

The pure *sattva* denoted by the word Vasudeva is that in which the Person (the Supreme Soul) resides unobstructed. And within that *sattva*, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, who is beyond the senses (*adhokṣaja*), is indeed worshipped by me with my obeisance.
Therefore, you should not look upon him; neither your father, who gave you this body, nor Dakṣa, who is my enemy, nor those who follow his lead.
"O fair-thighed one, he who has insulted me with harsh words while I was engaged in the sacrifice of the Creator of the Universe— though I am innocent—
if you shall depart, disregarding my word, no good will come of it for you. For when one who is highly esteemed suffers defeat at the hands of his own kin, that very moment leads to death."
Maitreya said:
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara fell silent, reflecting upon the destruction of his wife's body in both worlds.
Desiring to see her friend, she became apprehensive; as she was about to emerge and yet enter again, she became divided in two.
Distressed at heart by the frustration of her desire to see her friend, weeping out of affection and overwhelmed by a flood of tears,
Satī— her body trembling with rage— glared at Bhava as if she would consume him, who has no equal among men. Then, sighing deeply, she left him, her heart burning with grief and anger.
He whose mind was deluded by women went to his parents' home, he who, beloved by the virtuous, had given half of himself out of love;
thousands of attendants of the Three-eyed Lord followed that chaste woman as she moved with swift strides—
Maṇiman, Madgu, and others, along with their yakṣa followers, preceded by the lordly bull, moving with speed and free from distress.

Adorning the lordly bull with female parrots, balls, mirrors, lotuses, white parasols, fans, garlands, and other ornaments, they proceeded while singing songs and playing kettledrums, conchs, and flutes;
they went toward that place where the sacrificial slaughter was intense with the sound of Vedic chanting, frequented by brahminical sages and gods from all sides.
He entered the sacrificial ground where vessels had been prepared from clay, wood, iron, gold, darbha grass, and skins.
When she arrived there, no one paid her any heed; the people, out of fear of the performer of the sacrifice, treated her with contempt.
Only her sisters and her mother embraced her with joy, their throats choked with tears of love.

She did not accept the respectful hospitality, the excellent seat, and the inquiries after her welfare offered by her maternal aunt, her mother, and her maternal aunts, as she had not been greeted with approval by her father.
She observed that the sacrifice was devoid of a portion for Rudra, and that her powerful father had shown disrespect toward the Lord.

Disregarded in the assembly of the sacrifice, the Sovereign Lady became enraged as if she would burn the worlds with her wrath. Restraining the hosts of spirits who had arisen by her own splendor, the Goddess rebuked the hater of Śiva— who was arrogant from the fatigue of his journey along the path of smoke— with words faltering from indignation, while the world listened.
The Goddess said:

In this world, there is no one dearer or less dear to Him who loves all embodied beings as His own Self; for He is the Self of all, free from enmity toward anyone. Who other than You would act with hostility toward Him?

O twice-born one, some virtuous people indeed perceive the faults of others amidst their virtues, but none such as you; the most exalted ones, who are intent on magnifying even the slightest virtues, have attributed sin to those very qualities in your case. It is not surprising that there is constant reviling of the great by the wicked, who speak of themselves as if they were corpses.
O Great Person, it is truly auspicious that the splendor of those whose own brilliance has been eclipsed by the dust of Your feet is surpassed by that very thing:
the two-syllable name uttered from the mountain, which instantly destroys the sins of men through even a single instance of association.
Alas, You—who are the opposite of auspiciousness—hate Him whose fame is purifying and whose command is inviolable, even though He is the source of all well-being.
To him whose lotus feet are served by the bee-like minds of the great— who seek the intoxicating nectar of Brahman—
and who showers blessings upon those in the world who petition him, you bear malice toward that friend of the universe.
Or rather, do not others besides you, such as Brahmā and the rest, know that he who is called Śiva is inauspicious, having scattered his matted locks in the cremation ground?

Those who dwell with Piśācas wearing his garlands, ashes, and human skulls—those who, when the Lord, the protector of Dharma, was being reviled by unbridled men who stopped their ears while he was incapable of acting, did not themselves stop their ears—they would have had their foul and wicked tongues forcibly cut out by that powerful Lord; yet if he had done so, they would have given up even their lives. That indeed is true Dharma.

"Therefore, I shall no longer maintain this body born of you, O Blue-throated One, for it is despised by you. For they declare that purification comes from vomiting what has been eaten out of delusion, or from the extraction of what is loathsome.
"The mind of a great sage who delights in his own world does not follow the doctrines of the Vedas."

Just as the destinies of gods and humans are distinct according to their own respective duties, one who remains established in his own duty should not disparage another; and just as the Veda, having distinguished between the two types of rites— those characterized by engagement (*pravṛtta*) and those by withdrawal (*nivṛtta*)— rests upon both, so too these two, though seemingly contradictory when performed by a single agent simultaneously, do not conflict within the Supreme Brahman.

O Father, may the paths you have trodden—not frequented by those who follow the path of smoke in the sacrificial halls, nor praised by living beings satiated by their food, but rather followed by the Avadhūtas whose outward signs are unmanifest—not be ours.
O Hari, enough, enough with this wretched birth, this body born of sin; let us not commit further offenses with it.
I felt shame due to association with wicked people; fie on that birth which committed an offense against the great!

When the Lord Śiva, the bull-bannered one, spoke of you as "the daughter of Dakṣa" with a deeply troubled mind, devoid of jesting and smiles, I shall immediately cast off this corpse born from your body.
Maitreya said:
O slayer of enemies, having thus addressed Dakṣa during the sacrifice, he sat down upon the ground facing north with his speech stilled;
having touched water and being clothed in yellow silk garments, he closed his eyes and entered the path of yoga.
Having made the two breaths equal and mastered her posture, she raised [the vital energy] from the navel-wheel with effort;
slowly placing it in the heart, the faultless woman brought it from the chest to the throat and then to the space between the eyebrows.
Thus, out of reverence, she repeatedly placed her own body upon the lap of the Great One, who is greater than the great.
Desiring to cast off her body out of anger toward Dakṣa, the wise Satī maintained within her limbs the yogic concentration on air and fire.
Then, meditating solely upon the nectar of the lotus feet of her husband, the teacher of the world, and perceiving nothing else,
her body— its impurities destroyed— was instantly consumed by the fire born of her meditative absorption.
As they beheld that great wonder in the sky and upon the earth, a tremendous outcry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
"Ah! By what means has his beloved goddess, the deity Satī, been provoked to anger so that she has abandoned her life?
"Behold the great lack of self-restraint of this Prajāpati, whose progeny consist of both the moving and the unmoving!"
That he, whose son was a virtuous and wise woman who deserved constant respect, yet abandoned his life out of resentment—
this man of intolerant heart and betrayer of Brahmanas shall incur great infamy in the world, since,
being a hater of men, he did not prevent his own daughter from seeking death for the sake of his offense.
While the people were speaking thus, Satī, having witnessed that wonderful renunciation of her body, [departed].
Then Dakṣa’s attendants rose up with weapons raised to kill her.
Observing the force of those as they were rushing forward, the venerable Bhṛgu—

With the *yajus* mantra that destroys the destroyers of sacrifice, he offered oblations into the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire. While the *adhvaryu* priest was offering the libations, the gods known as the *Ṛbhus*, who had attained the status of Soma by means of their austerity, rose up by the thousands with great power.
Struck by those firebrand-weapons, all the Pramathas along with the Guhyakas fled in all directions, overwhelmed by the blazing power of Brahman.
Maitreya said:
Having learned from Nārada that Bhava was the cause of the destruction of Prajāpati, whose sacrifice had been rendered fruitless,
and that his own army of attendants had been put to flight by the gods at that sacrifice, he conceived boundless wrath.
Enraged, with the corners of his lips bitten by his teeth, the one with matted hair (Śiva) [seized] his matted locks, which possessed the fierce luster of lightning and the flames of fire.

Having cut it off, Rudra suddenly rose up laughing and, with a deep roar, cast it upon the earth. Then [the demon] appeared, possessing a massive body that touched the heavens, with a thousand arms, the luster of a dark cloud, eyes like three suns,
formidable tusks, hair like blazing fire, wearing a garland of skulls, and brandishing various uplifted weapons.
To him who was speaking thus with palms joined in reverence, "What shall I do?", the Blessed Lord, the Master of Beings, said:
"O Rudra, you are a portion of my own power; as my foremost leader among my warriors, destroy Dakṣa along with his sacrifice.
Thus commanded by the enraged Manyu, he circumambulated the omnipresent God of gods.
O dear one, he then considered himself capable of enduring the power of the great ones through his own unimpeded and mighty speed;
yet, pursued by the attendants of Rudra who were roaring loudly, he let out a most terrifying cry and,
raising his trident— the destroyer of even the Destroyer of the Universe— he fled with his feet jingling with the sound of his ornaments.
Then the officiating priests, the patron of the sacrifice, and the members of the assembly, observing the dust in the northern quarter, pondered:
"What is this darkness? From where has this dust arisen? O twice-born ones, the brahmins and their wives reflected thus:
"The winds do not blow, nor are there any robbers; for the king Prācīnabarhis, who wields a terrible rod of punishment, is still alive."
"The cows are not being driven home; whence comes this dust? Is the world now preparing for dissolution?

Thus spoke the women, including Prasūti, their hearts filled with anxiety: "This is surely the ripening of that very sin, since the Lord of Creatures has cast his eye upon his own daughter Satī while her sisters were looking on, though she was innocent."
But at the time of the end, he whose mass of matted hair was disheveled, who pinned the lordly elephants of the quarters to his trident’s points,
and who danced with outstretched arms like banners of raised weapons, shattering the directions with his loud, thundering laughter—
him, of unbearable splendor, overflowing with wrath, and difficult to behold because of his furrowed brow, [Śiva] could not endure.
"Will there be well-being for the Creator who, with his terrifying fangs, has cast down the host of stars? What is the use of provoking him?
While the people spoke thus repeatedly to the high-souled Dakṣa with eyes full of agitation, thousands of most terrible and fearsome portents arose all around, both in heaven and upon the earth.

Meanwhile, Vidura was besieged by the followers of Rudra—great sacrificers with various weapons, who were dwarfish yet held them aloft; they were tawny and reddish-brown, with faces like the bellies of sea-monsters, as they rushed about.
Some broke the sacrificial hall, while others destroyed the wife’s quarters.
They demolished the hall of the Āgnīdhra priest, his dwelling, and the kitchen;
they broke the sacrificial vessels, while some extinguished the sacred fires. Some urinated into the ritual pits, and others shattered the girdles of the altar.
Some harassed the sages, others threatened their wives,
and still others seized the gods who had fled and were nearby.
Maṇimān bound Bhṛgu, and Vīrabhadra bound Prajāpati.

Caṇḍeśa seized the god Pūṣan, and Nandīśvara seized Bhaga. Seeing this, all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the members of the assembly (*sadasya*), and the celestial inhabitants were violently oppressed by them; being tormented in many ways, they fled with the pressing-stones.
While Bhrigu was offering oblations with a sacrificial ladle in his hand, the Lord Bhava plucked out his beard in the assembly,
revealing his own beard as he laughed. Then,
the Lord, in his wrath, cast Bhaga to the ground and struck out his eyes.
He who, remaining ever-steadfast, uprooted with his eye the one who cursed him; indeed, he who,
like Balarāma, knocked out the teeth of Pūṣan,
and who laughed while showing his own teeth when the Great One was being cursed.
Striking the chest of Dakṣa with his sharp-edged weapon,
Tryambaka was then unable to sever it even while attempting to uproot it;
likewise, Hara could not pierce the skin with his weapons and missiles.
Filled with supreme wonder, Paśupati meditated for a long time;
having seen that yogic power of subduing animals at the sacrifice, he, their lord,
wondered from whose body the sacrificer had taken the head of the sacrificial beast.
At that time, as they watched his deed, there was praise for him from the *bhūtas*,
*pretas*, and *piśācas*, while others expressed the opposite;
then, filled with indignation, he offered that head as an oblation into the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*).
Having burned that sacrificial ground of the gods, he departed for the abode of the Guhyakas.
Maitreya said:
Then all the hosts of gods were defeated by the armies of Rudra.
With their entire limbs severed and mangled by spears, sharp-edged axes, swords, maces, iron clubs, and hammers, the priests and members of the assembly, overwhelmed with fear,
offered salutations to Svayambhū and reported this in its entirety.
Having perceived this beforehand, the Lord born from the lotus and Nārāyaṇa,
the soul of the universe, did not attend anyone's sacrifice.
Hearing that, the all-pervading Lord said to the one who had committed an offense against the more powerful:
In that regard, she may not generally lead to the welfare of those who merely desire prosperity;
nevertheless, since you have committed an offense by excluding him from his share of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*),
you must propitiate him with a purified mind— he who is easily appeased and whose lotus feet are held in reverence.

"Desiring the life of the sacrifice, you— along with the world and its guardians— must quickly seek forgiveness from that God who is separated from his beloved and pierced in the heart by harsh words;
for neither I, nor the sacrifice, nor you, nor others who possess bodies, nor even the sages, are the ultimate reality."
"Who would dare devise a means against him who is self-dependent and whose strength and prowess are known only to himself?
Having thus instructed the gods, Brahmā, accompanied by them, by the Pitṛs, and by the lords of progeny,
went to Kailāsa, the best of mountains and the beloved abode of the Lord, the enemy of Tripura, from his own celestial throne.
It was frequented by non-humans who had attained perfection through birth, herbs, austerity, mantras, and yoga; it was always surrounded by *kinnaras*, *gandharvas*, and *apsarases*;
and it possessed peaks composed of various jewels and variegated with diverse minerals.
It was filled with various trees, creepers, and shrubs, inhabited by diverse herds of wild animals,
and possessed various pure springs, caves,
and mountain peaks; it was the place where the wives of the Siddhas sported in pleasure with their lovers.
It resounded with the cries of peacocks and was filled with the humming of bees blinded by intoxication; it was further filled with the warbling of birds whose throats were reddened by bathing,
and which seemed to call out to the twice-born with their upraised, wish-fulfilling trees.
It seemed as if it were walking with its elephants and speaking with its waterfalls;
it was adorned with *mandāra*, *pārijāta*, and *sarala* trees,
as well as with *tamāla*, *śāla*, *tāla*, *kovidāra*, *āsana*, and *arjuna* trees.
With mango trees, kadamba, and nīpa; with nāga, punnāga, and campaka; with pāṭala, aśoka, bakula, kunda, and kurabaka;
and with golden-hued śatapatra, excellent reṇuka, and jāti flowers.
It was adorned with *kubjaka*, *mallikā*, and *mādhavī* vines;
with *panasa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, and *hiṅgu* trees;
with *bhūrja* trees, medicinal herbs, *pūga*, *rājapūga*, and *jambu* trees.
It was adorned with date palms, *āmrātaka*, mangoes, and other trees such as *priyāla*, *madhuka*, and *iṅguda*,
as well as various species of trees and bamboo reeds;
and it was enriched by groves of white water lilies, blue lotuses, *kahlāra* lilies, and hundred-petaled lotuses.
It was graced by flocks of birds warbling melodiously among the lotus ponds,
and by deer, monkeys, boars, lions, bears, porcupines,
gavayas, śarabhas, tigers, ruru deer, buffaloes, and other such creatures.
It was frequented by wolves and jackals that were panting with their mouths open,
and it possessed the beauty of lotus-filled sandbanks concealed within groves of plantain trees;
it was further graced by the exceedingly meritorious waters of the river Nandā, which had overflowed from Satyabhāmā’s ritual bathing.
Beholding the mountain of the Lord of Beings, the gods were filled with wonder;
there they beheld the beautiful city named Alakā and also the Saugandhika forest, where that species of lotus grows.
Outside the city are the two rivers, the Nandā and the Alakanandā,

which are exceedingly purifying due to the dust from the lotus feet of Him whose feet are the source of all holy places (tīrtha-pāda). O Vidura, the celestial women descend from their own celestial chariots to these rivers.

Exhausted by passion, the men sport there, plunging into the water and splashing one another; even though they are not thirsty, the male elephants drink the water that has become tawny with the fresh saffron washed from the bodies of the females as they bathe, while the females let them drink.

Abandoning that city of the Lord of Yakṣas, which was crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots made of silver, gold, and great jewels, and frequented by the wives of the Puṇyajanas— resembling the sky filled with clouds and lightning— he went to that Saugandhika forest.
It was delightful with trees that yielded all desires, adorned with variegated garlands, fruits, and foliage;
it was graced by the songs of flocks of sweet-voiced birds and by bees;
it was most dear to the swarms of *kalahaṃsa* geese, and its ponds possessed stalks of lotuses as hard as steel.
With breezes from the yellow sandalwood trees rubbed by herds of wild elephants,
he repeatedly agitated the minds of the wives of the Puṇyajanās;
there were ponds with staircases made of vaidūrya gems, garlanded with blue lotuses.
Seeing that [place] had been reached by the Kiṃpuruṣas, they beheld from afar a banyan tree.
It was a hundred *yojanas* in height, with its branches extending for three-quarters of that measure;
it provided shade like a surrounding mountain, was devoid of nests, and was free from heat.
In that place consisting of great yoga, the refuge of those seeking liberation, the gods beheld Śiva seated there, having abandoned his wrath like Death himself,
his form perfectly tranquil along with Sanandana and other great perfected beings who were peaceful.
He was being attended by his friend and lord of the Guhyakas and Rakshasas;
that Supreme Lord, who had established himself on the path of knowledge, austerity, and yoga,
moved about as a friend to all, out of affection for the welfare of the world.
He bore the emblems desired by ascetics— ashes, staff, matted hair, and deerskin—
and with his body, which possessed the luster of twilight clouds, he wore a crescent moon;
he sat upon a seat made of darbha grass as the eternal Brahman.
To Nārada, who was questioning Him as He spoke, while the virtuous ones were listening,
He sat with His left lotus-foot placed upon His right thigh and His arm resting on His knee,
holding a rosary of beads in His forearm in the gesture of philosophical inquiry (*tarka-mudrā*).

The sages, together with the guardians of the worlds, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down before Giriśa— the first Manu of all Manus— who was resting upon and fully absorbed in that samādhi of Brahman-extinction, having attained the state of yoga. He, whose feet were worshipped by the lords of gods and demons, perceived that the Self-born One had arrived.
Having risen, that most worthy one paid homage with his head, just as Viṣṇu does to Kaśyapa;

likewise, the other hosts of Siddhas and great ṛṣis from all sides followed suit. To Nīlalohita, who had been saluted by them, the Self-born One (Brahmā), as if smiling, spoke after he himself had offered his prostration to the Moon-crested Lord.
Brahmā said:
O Lord, I bow to You, the source and seed of the entire universe,
who are the eternal Brahman, transcending both Śakti and Śiva.
O Blessed One, you alone, through these two forms of Śiva and Śakti,

create, protect, and consume the universe while sporting, just as a spider [weaves and devours] its web. You alone have fashioned the sacrifice with skillful thread for the attainment of dharma and artha.
By you alone have the bridges been established in the world, which the *brāhmaṇas* of firm vows hold in faith. You manifest your own realm or the supreme heaven for the performer of auspicious deeds;
yet for those of inauspicious deeds, there is the terrible darkness—the reverse of that very same state—for what reason? To whom does it belong?

Indeed, anger does not generally overcome those virtuous ones who have surrendered their souls at Your feet, who perceive You in all beings, and who desire to see all beings as non-different from themselves; rather,
it is those of separate intellect, whose vision is fixed on ritual action, who are evil-minded, and whose hearts are constantly tormented by the success of others.
Those who pierce others with harsh words, wounding their vital spots—do not strike them, for they are like those slain by fate; such as you are not like that.

O Lotus-navelled One, when those whose intellects are touched by Your insurmountable māyā perceive things diversely, the virtuous show compassion toward them out of pity; they do not take action against what has been brought about by the power of destiny.

But you, O Lord, whose intellect is untouched by the insurmountable illusion of the Supreme Person and who perceives all things, ought to show favor here toward those whose minds are destroyed by that [illusion] and whose hearts are intent on their own actions. O Master, perform the restoration of the sacrifice of Manu Prajāpati, which was interrupted and left unfinished by you.
"Where the performers of the sacrifice, though entitled to shares, do not give you your portion, by which means the sacrifice is led astray—
may this sacrificer live, may Bhaga regain his eyes,
and may Bhrigu’s beard and Pūṣan’s teeth grow back as they were before!"
"O Manyu, may those gods whose limbs were broken by the weapons and stones of the priests,
and who have been favored by you, quickly become free from affliction. O Rudra, let this which remains of the sacrifice be your portion."
"O Rudra, slayer of the sacrifice, may your sacrifice be fulfilled today by means of your portion.
Maitreya said:
When Bhava was thus entreated by Aja and became well-pleased, [he spoke].
"O mighty-armed one, it has been said: 'Laughing, he replied, "Let it be heard.
Mahādeva said:
'O Lord of Creatures, I do not describe nor even consider the sin of children.'"
I have inflicted this punishment upon those who were overcome by the illusory power of the gods.
Let the head of Prajāpati, whose own head has been burnt away, become the head of Aja (Brahmā) with its horse-like face.
And let Bhaga behold his own portion of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the eye of Mitra.
"May Pūṣan eat the flour with the teeth of the sacrificer;
may the gods, whose limbs were restored, give me the remains of the offering.
May we have arms made by the two Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan."
"Let there be other Adhvaryu priests, and let Bhṛgu have a beard like that of a goat.
Maitreya said:
"Then all living beings, having heard what was spoken by Mīḍhuṣṭama..."

With their minds fully satisfied, O dear one, they exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! Then, having taken leave of the Bountiful One (Indra), those who were the lords of sacrifice along with the ṛṣis returned once more to that sacrificial ground of the gods, accompanied by the Bountiful One and the wise priests.
Having performed in its entirety that which Lord Bhava had commanded,
they joined the head of the sacrificial animal to the body of Dakṣa;
as the head was being joined, Dakṣa was glared at by Rudra.
Like one who has just awakened from sleep, he immediately rose and beheld Mṛḍa before him;
at that moment, Prajāpati, whose soul had been turbid with hatred for the bull-bannered god,
became as pure as an autumnal lake upon seeing Śiva.
Having set his mind upon praising Bhava, he was unable to do so due to his deep affection;
remembering his deceased daughter with intense longing, his eyes filled with tears,
the wise king steadied his mind with great difficulty, though overwhelmed by love.
With a sincere disposition, Prajāpati Dakṣa praised the Lord;
Dakṣa said:
"Oh, how great a favor has been bestowed upon me by you!"
The punishment you have inflicted upon me was indeed deserved,
yet there should be no contempt from you toward those who are merely nominal Brahmins, O Blessed One; for how could there be such disregard for You, O Hari, or for those who are firm in their vows?
O Supreme One, You first created the Brahmins— bearers of knowledge, austerity, and vows— from Your mouth in order to protect the true nature of Brahman and the Self;
therefore, You protect the Brahmins in all calamities.
O All-pervading Lord, like a herdsman with a raised staff over his cattle,
You disregarded me and struck me in the assembly with the arrows of Your harsh words, while my vision was obscured by ignorance regarding Your true nature.
May that Blessed One, out of His compassionate gaze, be pleased by my own deed— even though I have fallen low by censuring the most worthy. Maitreya said:

Having thus asked forgiveness from the one who pours oblations (the Fire-god), and being authorized by Brahmā, O best of the twice-born, he performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice with three potsherds for the continuity of the ritual, together with his preceptors, officiating priests, and others.
O Lord of the People, for the sake of purification from contact with the hero, they offered the *puroḍāśa* oblation; while the Adhvaryu priest held the sacrificial offering,
the sacrificer meditated with a pure mind, and thus Hari appeared.
Then, as His own radiance illuminated the ten directions,
He was brought forward by Tārkṣya, whose vigor was aroused by hymns of praise;
He was dark-complexioned, girt with a golden waistband, and adorned with a crown of sun-like splendor.
His face was adorned with earrings and dark locks of hair like bees; with his golden arms—
busily holding a conch, lotus, discus, arrow, bow, mace, sword, and shield—
he resembled a *karṇikāra* tree.
With his bride resting upon his chest, adorned with forest garlands, he delights the entire universe with the grace of his smiles and glances; meanwhile,
royal swans serve as fly-whisks as they circle beside him.
Shining above him with a white parasol like the moon,
Brahmā, Indra, Śiva, and the other leaders among the hosts of gods all rose suddenly and bowed down upon seeing him approach.
Their luster eclipsed by his splendor, their tongues failing, and filled with awe,
they stood before Adhokṣaja with their palms joined in reverence upon their heads—
even Brahmā and the others, whose own powers are limited, yet who are unable to fathom his majesty.
According to their understanding, they praised Him whose form was the embodiment of grace—
the Lord of Sacrifice, the supreme teacher of the creators of the universe— whom Dakṣa had honored by providing him with the finest seats and offerings.
Surrounded by his joyful followers, Sunanda, Nanda, and others,
Dakṣa approached him with devotion, palms joined in reverence, chanting praises.
Dakṣa said:

In His own abode, He remains as pure consciousness alone— free from fear, singular, and having negated all states of the intellect by means of Māyā itself; yet, through that very Māyā, He assumes the state of the Person (puruṣatva) within it.
"You sit here as if you were impure, though you are independent of others.
The priests said:
"O Anañjana, we do not know the truth of you because of Rudra’s curse."

O Blessed One, we understand that this threefold sacrifice known as the *adhvara*, characterized by ritual duty (*dharma*), is for the sake of that [Supreme Reality] whose manifestations are established as the deities; yet our minds are obstructed regarding the action itself.
The members of the assembly said:

On the path of birth, which is without refuge, a difficult wilderness of great suffering, infested by the fierce beasts of death, and where one thirsts for the deer-like objects of the senses while bearing the heavy burden of the body’s own frailty—

O Giver of Refuge, when will the caravan of the ignorant— afflicted by desires— reach Your feet, which are like a tree providing shelter in the pit of dualities, fearful with the wild beasts of the wicked, and ablaze with the forest fire of sorrow?
Rudra said:

O Giver of Boons, if the world of ignorance should cast me away— me whose mind is fixed upon Your excellent feet, which are worthy of being honored with devotion even by sages who are unattached to all worldly aims for the sake of their own blessings; [then let it be so].
He mutters [the mantra], yet he does not count it, for he is sustained by your supreme grace.
Bhṛgu said:
Those whose self-knowledge has been stolen away by your profound *māyā*...
Even now, Brahmā and the other embodied beings, sleeping in darkness, do not know Your true nature which rests within themselves; may You,
the kinsman of those who bow before You, be gracious toward them.
Brahmā said:
This is not Your true nature as long as a person perceives it through the grasping of distinctions between objects;
You are considered to be the substratum of knowledge, the object, and the qualities, yet distinct from that which consists of illusion.
Indra said:
O Acyuta, this form of Yours, which brings about the manifestation of the universe and bestows bliss upon the mind and the eyes,
is endowed with eight mighty arms bearing uplifted weapons for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
The wives said:
"This sacrifice of yours, intended for Your worship, was destroyed today by Paśupati out of anger toward Dakṣa; by whom was it created?
O Soul of Sacrifice, purify us with Your lotus-hued glance this sacrifice whose sacrificial fires have been extinguished and which resembles a bed of corpses."
The sages said:
O Blessed One, Your conduct is incomprehensible, for though You perform actions by Yourself, You are not tainted by them.
Since they approached the Sovereign for the sake of prosperity, You do not regard Her as one who must wait upon You, even though She follows You of Her own accord.
The Siddhas said:

Our mind-elephant, scorched by the forest fire of suffering, having plunged into the river of the nectar cleansed by Your stories while afflicted by thirst, no longer remembers the forest and does not emerge, like one who has attained the state of Brahman.
The sacrificer’s wife said:
"Welcome to you! Be gracious, O Lord; salutations unto you, O Abode of Śrī. Protect us with your beloved consort Śrī.
Without you, O Supreme Lord, the sacrifice does not shine with its limbs, like a headless man who is merely a torso."
The world-protectors said:

"Have we not seen You with our eyes, which were once seized by the unreal—that inner Seer by whom the universe is perceived? O Infinite One, this is indeed Your own *māyā*, by which You, the Sixth, appear through the five elements."
The masters of yoga said:
"O Lord, there is no one dearer to You than this [person], for one who perceives nothing separate from the Self cannot see anything other than You, the Soul of the universe.
Nevertheless, O affectionate One, favor those who approach You with devotion, their sole occupation being You."

Salutations to Him who, by His own Māyā consisting of the qualities that are diversely differentiated according to destiny, effects the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe; who, by His own inherent nature, removes the delusion of those whose minds perceive duality created by that Māyā; and who is the Self beyond the qualities of material nature.
Brahmā said:

Salutations to You, the refuge of all beings and the source of dharma and the other goals of life; salutations to the one who is beyond the material qualities (nirguṇa), whose ultimate limit neither I nor others know.
Agni said:
"O Lord of the excellent sacrifice, by whose splendor my own luster is well-kindled, I carry the oblation sprinkled with clarified butter;
to that fivefold sacrificial rite, which is well-offered with the five *yajus* mantras, I bow down.
The gods said:
In the past, at the end of a kalpa, having withdrawn your own created universe into your belly,
you alone remain today as that Supreme Person upon the serpent-king’s couch in the waters, while the perfected ones contemplate the path of the supreme self within their hearts.
"You are that very one who moves along the path before our eyes; you protect us, your servants.
The Gandharvas said:
"O Lord, these Marīci and others, as well as the hosts of gods led by Brahmā and Indra, with Rudra at their head, are all but portions of Your own portions."
O All-pervading Lord, we offer our eternal obeisances unto You, for whom this entire universe is but a plaything.
The Vidyādharas said:
Through Your illusory power (māyā), having assumed a physical body for a specific purpose in this world...

Having formed the false notion of "I" and "mine," the evil-minded one, though cast down by his own deviant paths and longing for unreal sense objects, may cast off that self-delusion by serving the nectar of your stories.
The brāhmaṇas said:
You are the sacrifice, you are the oblation, and you are the fire itself; for you are the mantra, as well as the sacrificial fuel, the darbha grass, and the vessels.
You are the members of the assembly, the officiating priests, the husband and wife, the deity, the agnihotra offering, the svadhā, the soma, the clarified butter, and the sacrificial animal.

In ancient times, O You whose body is the three Vedas and who are the sacrifice itself, while being praised by yogis, You playfully lifted up the earth from the netherworld with Your tusk— just as a lordly elephant uproots a lotus pond—
while roaring aloud; be gracious to us, whose virtuous deeds have fallen away and who now long for a vision of You.
"O Lord of Sacrifice, when Your name is being glorified by men, the obstacles to sacrifice perish; salutations unto You!
Maitreya said:
Thus did the wise Dakṣa [praise] the sacrifice, O gentle one, which had been defiled by Rudra.
While Hṛṣīkeśa, the source of all sacrifice, was being glorified, the Blessed Lord— the soul of all and the enjoyer of all shares— concluded the sacrifice by means of his own portion; then,
O sinless one, as if feeling affectionate, he addressed Dakṣa.
The Blessed Lord said: I, Brahmā, and Śiva are the supreme cause of the universe;
I am the Self, the Lord, the witness, self-perceiving and devoid of all attributes.
O twice-born one, having entered my own *māyā* composed of the *guṇas*, I— being that very Self— assuming names appropriate to my actions, create, protect, and withdraw the universe;
yet in that non-dual, absolute Supreme Self, there is no such differentiation.
An ignorant person perceives Brahmā, Rudra, and all beings as distinct entities; however,
one who is devoted to Me does not entertain the notion of "otherness" toward any beings, just as a man never regards his own limbs— the head, hands, and so forth— as belonging to another.
"O Brahmin, he who does not perceive any difference between these three— which possess a single nature and are the self of all beings— attains peace. Maitreya said:
Thus instructed by the Blessed One, the Lord of Progenitors (Brahmā) worshipped Hari with his own sacrifice and offered oblations to the gods on both sides;
and with a concentrated mind, he propitiated Rudra with his own allotted portion.

Having concluded the ritual with the *udavasāna* ceremony, he dismissed both the Soma-drinkers and the others; then, together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), he performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
Even for him, whose success was attained through his own power, [the Lord acted] by His own majesty.
Having bestowed their resolve upon Dharma alone, those gods departed for heaven. Thus, Satī, having abandoned her former body, was born from Menā in the domain of Himavat; so we have heard.
Ambikā again chose that very same beloved as her husband—
he who was her sole refuge and whose devotion was directed toward no other— just as Śakti chooses the Puruṣa when she has been asleep.
This is the deed of the Blessed Lord Śambhu, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.

O descendant of Kuru, I have heard from my disciple Uddhava, who was himself a student of Bṛhaspati, this supreme purifier concerning the activities of the Lord; it brings fame, lengthens life, and washes away the multitude of sins. Any man who, having heard it constantly, recites it with a spirit of devotion, shakes off all evil.
Maitreya said:
Sanaka and the others, as well as Nārada, Ṛbhu, Haṃsa, Aruṇi, and Yati—
these sons of Brahmā, being perpetual celibates, did not dwell in household life.
O slayer of enemies, Mṛṣā-dharma had two wives, Dambha and Māyā;
they gave birth to a pair of children whom Nirṛti, being childless himself, adopted. From those two, O great-minded one, were born Lobha (Greed) and Nikṛti (Deceit).
From those two were born Wrath and Violence, whose sister was Harsh Speech, who is Kali.
O best of men, Kali begot Fear and Death upon Harsh Speech. And from those two a pair was born: Torture and Hell.
O sinless one, I have described to you in brief the secondary creation (*pratisarga*).
By hearing this meritorious account three times, a person shakes off the impurity of his own soul.
Now, O best of the Kurus, I shall proclaim the lineage (*vaṃśa*) of him whose fame is holy.
Of Svāyambhuva Manu, who was born from a portion of a portion of Hari,
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were the two sons of Śatarūpā;
by a portion of Vāsudeva, they remained for the protection of the world.
Uttānapāda had two wives, Sunīti and Suruci; of these two, Suruci was the husband’s favorite, not the other, because their son was Dhruva.
Once, having placed Suruci’s son upon his lap, he was fondling him.
The king welcomed Dhruva as he was desirous of ascending to the highest state; however, Suruci,
filled with excessive pride, spoke with envy while the king was listening, regarding Dhruva, the son of her co-wife, who was likewise intent on that same task.
"My child, you ought not to ascend the throne of the king,
since you, though born of a prince, were not conceived by me in my own womb. Alas, you are but a child, one produced from the womb of another woman."
"Surely you know whose desire it is for that which is difficult to attain;
having propitiated the Supreme Person through austerity, by His very grace, you may accomplish your purpose in my womb, if you desire the throne of a king."
Maitreya said:

Pierced by the harsh words of his stepmother, he hissed in rage like a snake struck by a staff; leaving his father—who looked on with indifference and whose speech had failed—he went weeping to his mother’s side.
Taking the child, who was sighing with his lower lip quivering, onto her lap,
Sunīti heard from the mouths of the citizens what had been said by her co-wife; hearing it, she was deeply distressed and,
casting aside her fortitude, that young woman lamented like a forest creeper consumed by a wildfire of grief.
Remembering the words of her co-wife, she bore a stream of tears with eyes possessing the beauty of a lotus;
sighing deeply and seeing no end to her suffering, the young woman said to the boy:
"O dear one, do not consider me to be inauspicious toward others, for a person reaps that which they inflict as suffering upon another."

"What Suruci has said is true: that you were conceived in the womb of me, an unfortunate woman, and that you now feel ashamed even to offer me your breast-milk. That the Lord of Sacrifice (Indra) would not deign to take me as his wife—O dear one, be free from resentment toward those truthful words spoken by my mother."

Worship the lotus feet of Adhokṣaja if you desire to attain a station as exalted as his. By serving whose lotus feet— the source from which the qualities for the manifestation of the universe are acquired—
the Unborn (Brahmā) indeed attained the supreme status of Pārameṣṭhya, which is honored by those who have conquered their own breaths and selves.

Likewise, O child, you should take refuge in that very Lord Manu, your venerable grandfather, who— by means of sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees and with one-pointed resolve— attained that earthly happiness, celestial bliss, and even liberation which are difficult to obtain from any other source;
he whose path of lotus feet is sought by those desiring release, and who is affectionate toward his servants.
Fixing your mind, which has been cultivated by your own duty, on the Supreme Person with undivided devotion, worship Him;
for other than that lotus-eyed One, the cutter of your suffering, I seek no one else, O dear one— He who is sought even by Śrī, who holds a lotus in her hand, while He is being sought by others.
Maitreya said:
Having heard these words of his mother, which were full of meaningful purpose,
he restrained himself by his own mind and departed from his father’s city.
Having heard that and understood what he intended to do, Nārada touched him on the head with his sin-destroying hand and, filled with wonder, said:
"Oh, the splendor of the Kṣatriyas who cannot endure an insult to their honor!"
"Even though he is but a child, he holds in his heart the improper words of one who is distressed.
Nārada said:
"O son, even now you have neither experienced contempt nor honor."
We observe that even though the boy was engaged in play and other such diversions,
there were no causes for dissatisfaction,
for among men, differences arise from their own past actions only through the power of delusion.
Therefore, my dear, a wise person should be satisfied with just that much—
the path of the Lord as it has been attained by destiny— once he has perceived it;
yet, you now desire to attain it through the yoga taught by your mother.

He whose grace is considered by me to be difficult for men to attain— even sages seeking his path with great detachment through births of long duration do not find it, despite their intense yoga and meditative absorption.
"Therefore, let this fruitless persistence of yours cease;
you shall strive when the time for your ultimate welfare has arrived. Whatever is ordained by destiny for each person, by that alone they experience pleasure and pain."

Satisfying the self, the embodied soul reaches the further shore of darkness. One should seek joy from those superior in qualities, compassion from those inferior in qualities, and friendship from equals; thus one is not overcome by sufferings.
Dhruva said:
This very peace, which is difficult for those like us to perceive, has been shown out of compassion by the Blessed Lord for the sake of men whose minds are afflicted by pleasure and pain.
Nevertheless, although I am undisciplined and have resorted to the terrible ways of a warrior, and although my heart has not been pierced by the arrow-like harsh words of Suruci,
may the path of the virtuous, which is the most excellent in the three worlds, take hold of me as I desire to conquer.
"O Brahmin, please tell us of that which has not been taught by our ancestors nor by others.
Surely you are a son of the Supreme Lord Parameṣṭhin;
like the sun, you wander about playing the lute for the welfare of the world."
Maitreya said:
Having heard what was thus spoken, the blessed Nārada then,
being pleased, replied with virtuous words out of compassion for that boy.
Nārada said:
"The path pointed out by your mother is indeed the way to your ultimate welfare. Devote yourself with a surrendered soul to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva."

O dear one, if one desires for oneself that supreme good known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, the sole cause for that is indeed the service of the feet of Hari. Therefore, go to the pure bank of the Yamunā; may prosperity be yours.
In that holy Madhuvana, where Hari is eternally present,
having bathed at each of the three daily libations in the auspicious waters of the Kālindī and having performed the appropriate rites, he dwelt there,
having prepared a seat for himself.

Having gradually cast off the impurities of the vital breath, the senses, and the mind by means of the threefold *prāṇāyāma*, one should meditate with the mind upon the Guru who is the Supreme Teacher—
He who is eternally inclined toward grace, with a serene face and eyes.
With a beautiful nose, lovely eyebrows, and charming cheeks, he was as handsome as a celestial being;
youthful with graceful limbs, his lips and eyes were copper-hued;
he was the refuge for those who bow to him, the source of human happiness, the protector, and an ocean of compassion.
[He saw] the Person marked with the Śrīvatsa, dark as a rain cloud, wearing a forest garland,
with four arms clearly manifesting the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
he was adorned with a crown, earrings, armlets, and bracelets.
With a neck adorned by the Kaustubha gem, wearing yellow silken garments,
encircled by a girdle of bells, and with shimmering golden anklets,
he was most beautiful to behold, peaceful, and a source of delight to the mind and eyes.

One should meditate upon Him who stands within the self, occupying the station of the pericarp of the heart-lotus of those who worship Him with His feet— which shine with rows of jewel-like nails— and who gazes with affectionate looks while smiling.
With a mind restrained and focused on a single object, as he thus meditated upon the auspicious form of the Lord, the bull among givers of boons,
his mind was quickly filled with supreme bliss and did not turn back.
O son of a king, hear from me the supreme secret mantra for silent recitation (*japa*),
by reciting which for seven nights a person beholds the sky-dwellers (*khecaras*).
*Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*.
With this mantra, the wise man, who understands the distinctions of place and time, should perform worship of the Lord with various materials consisting of substances,
using pure waters, garlands, and forest-grown roots, fruits, and the like.
One should worship the Lord with auspicious sprouts, cloths, and with *tulasī*, His beloved.
Having obtained a material image, one may worship it in earth, water, or other such elements.
With a purified self, silent, peaceful, restrained in speech, and eating limited forest-gathered food, one should perform the worship.

The Lord of excellent renown will perform deeds through His own incarnations by means of His inconceivable innate *māyā*; one should meditate upon that which is heart-pleasing. Whatever modes of service to the Blessed One were previously practiced—
One should employ those [mantras] with the very heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra) for the sake of Him whose form is the mantra.
Thus, being served by means of body, mind, and speech through the service of a devoted person, the Blessed One— whose mind is already present within— that devotee...
For those men who are free from deceit and who worship Him perfectly, He increases their devotion and bestows the desired spiritual welfare that embodied beings seek through dharma and other means;
yet, becoming detached from the pleasures of the senses, they attain this through abundant *bhakti-yoga*.
"One should worship Him with uninterrupted devotion for the sake of certain liberation.
Having been told this, the prince circumambulated and bowed down to him,
and then departed for the holy Madhuvana, which was graced by the footprints of Hari.
When he had departed for the forest of asceticism, the sage entered the inner apartments;
having been offered hospitality by the king, he sat comfortably and spoke to him.
Nārada said:

"O King, why do you meditate so long with a parched face? Is it that your desire, or your duty joined with material prosperity, has not been fulfilled? The King replied: bhagavan kāmam ārādhye na prāpto 'haṃ mahodayam / tasyānuśocann āse 'haṃ yathā duhitaraṃ tava // 1 // "O Blessed One, though I propitiated Kāma, I did not attain great success; grieving for him, I sit here as I would for your daughter. śrī-śuka uvāca evam ukto bhagavān nāradaḥ pratyuvāca— "O King, what are you reflecting upon so long with a parched face? Or is it that your desire, or your duty joined with material prosperity, has not been fulfilled? The King said: bhagavan kāmam ārādhye na prāpto 'haṃ mahodayam / tasyānuśocann āse 'haṃ yathā duhitaraṃ tava // 1 // "O Blessed One, though I propitiated Kāma, I did not attain great success; grieving for him, I sit here as I would for your daughter. śrī-nārada uvāca aho bata vṛthā-rājan kṛtavān asi cintitam / yo 'nutapyasi kāmena yoṣin-mūlena bhūyasā // 2 // "Alas! O King, you have indeed thought in vain, you who now repent because of this desire rooted in a woman, which will lead to further suffering. śrī-rājovāca bhagavan kim idaṃ nāma pumāṃsaṃ strī-kṛtāṃ vyathām / prāpayaty uta vā manye strī svabhāvo 'yam īdṛśaḥ // 3 // The King said: "O Blessed One, what is this? Does a woman cause such agony to a man, or do I think this is simply the nature of women? śrī-nārada uvāca satyam etad bhavān āha strī-svabhāvo yathā tvayā / vyākhyātaḥ puruṣo 'py evaṃ yoṣid-vyasanam ṛcchati // 4 // Nārada said: "What you have said regarding the nature of women is true; likewise, a man also falls into the distress caused by a woman. śrī-rājovāca bhagavan yan mayā pṛṣṭas tat samyak pratibodhitaḥ / idānīṃ śrotum icchāmi strī-puṃsoḥ saṅgamaṃ katham // 5 // The King said: "O Blessed One, I have been properly enlightened by what I asked; now I wish to hear how the union of woman and man occurs. śrī-nārada uvāca strī-puṃsor darśanāl liṅga-spṛṣṭyā saṅkalpataḥ smṛteḥ / sambhāṣaṇāt saṅgama-cchāyā-samāsanāt // 6 // Nārada said: "From the sight of each other, from the touch of their organs, from intention, from remembrance, from conversation, and from sitting together in the shade... kandarpa-darpita-yoṣit-puṃsayoḥ saṅgamo bhavet / tato retaḥ-prakṣaraṇaṃ garbhaḥ syāt tatra cātmanaḥ // 7 // ...the union of the man and woman, inflamed by passion, occurs; from that comes the emission of semen, and therein the self enters as the embryo. śrī-rājovāca bhagavan katham ātmānaṃ retasā saha yojayet / kathaṃ ca garbhe bhavati śrotum icchāmi tattvataḥ // 8 // The King

"O Brahmin, my young son, a great sage of only five years, has been exiled along with his mother by my pitiless and woman-obsessed self. O Brahmin, let not the wolves devour that helpless child in the forest."

"Alas! Behold my own wickedness, I who am conquered by a woman; for I, the most wretched of men, did not welcome him when he sought to climb onto my lap out of love, while he was exhausted, lying down, hungry, and with his lotus-face faded."
Nārada said:
"O lord of the people, do not grieve for your son, who is protected by the gods;
you have been overcome by grief because you do not recognize his power, which has spread its fame throughout the world."
"O King, having performed a most difficult task even for the guardians of the world,
the Lord will soon arrive, spreading your fame far and wide.
Maitreya said:
Having heard these words spoken by the celestial sage,
the lord of the earth disregarded royal fortune and thought only of his son.
Having been consecrated there, he purified himself and fasted through that night.
With a concentrated mind, he attended upon the Supreme Person according to the instruction of the sage; eating wood-apples and jujubes every three nights,
he spent a month worshipping Hari in accordance with his own means of subsistence.
In the same manner, during the second month, the child, having prepared food from withered grass, leaves, and other such materials, worshipped the Lord every sixth day.
Then he brought the third month, offering on every ninth day.
Subsisting on water, he approached the Lord of Excellent Renown through meditative absorption;
indeed, during the fourth month as well, on every twelfth day,
subsisting only on air and having mastered his breath, he held the Lord in his meditation.
When the fifth month had arrived, the prince, having mastered his breath,
stood motionless like a pillar, meditating on Brahman with one foot lifted,
having withdrawn his mind from all sides along with the elements, senses, and the seat of the heart.
Meditating on the form of the Blessed One, he perceived nothing else whatsoever;
as he maintained his focus upon Brahman— the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, and the substratum of Mahat and the other principles— the three worlds trembled.
When that child of the earth stood on one foot, the earth, pressed by his big toe,
sank down at that spot like a boat occupied by a lordly elephant, tilting from side to side at every step.
While he was thus meditating upon the universe as his own self, having closed the door of the breath with an undistracted mind, [the earth began to sink].
The worlds, along with their guardians, were severely oppressed by the lack of breath and went for refuge to Hari.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, we do not know how this obstruction of the vital breath of all moving and non-moving beings—who are the abode of every living creature—has come to pass."
"Grant us liberation from this evil; we have come to You for refuge, O Worthy Refuge.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Do not fear. I shall cause the boy to turn back from his penance that is so difficult to overcome. Return now to your own abode."
"For it was because of you that the cessation of breath occurred for the son of Uttānapāda, whose mind was absorbed in me.
Maitreya said:
"Thus, their fear being dispelled, they bowed down to the Wide-striding One and departed for the celestial realm."
Then, by means of Garuḍa, the thousand-headed one went to the forest of Madhu with the desire to see his servant.
Indeed, through his intellect sharpened by the ripening of yoga, he perceived that flash of lightning-like radiance within the bud of his heart-lotus;
having noticed that it had suddenly vanished, he beheld it standing outside, in that very same state.
Upon seeing him, his awe was dispelled; bowing his body like a staff, he prostrated himself upon the ground.
Beholding Him with his eyes as if drinking Him in, kissing Him with his mouth as if a child, and embracing Him with his arms as it were, he remained there.
Knowing that the boy, who did not yet understand, desired to speak, Hari, who dwells in the hearts of all, [spoke].

With compassion, He touched the cheek of the boy— who stood with palms joined in reverence— with His conch-shell made of *brahman*. At that very moment, having realized the definitive truth regarding the Supreme Self, Dhruva, whose fame was vast and who possessed firm resolve, spoke divine words with devotion, reciting them without haste.
Dhruva said:
He who, having entered within, awakens this speech of mine which was dormant by His own power, is the possessor of all potencies.

And [I offer] the other vital breaths—the hands, feet, ears, skin, and so forth—to You, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person; salutations to You! O Blessed One, You alone are this universe by Your own power.

Having created the entire universe beginning with the mahat-tattva by means of His own power called Māyā consisting of the three modes, the Supreme Person enters it and shines forth as if manifold within those unreal modes,
just as fire appears diverse within various pieces of wood.
O Lord, one who has taken refuge in you perceives this entire universe through the wisdom granted by you, like one awakened from sleep;
for such a person, the root of your feet is the ultimate refuge leading to liberation.
O friend of the distressed, how can You be forgotten by one who knows what has been done for them?
Surely those whose intellects are stolen away by Your illusory power (māyā) worship You— the means of liberation from birth and death— for the sake of some other purpose.
They worship the wish-fulfilling tree as if it were a corpse to be consumed,
for they desire even in hell that touch which arises from Your lotus feet, O Embodied One— the very bliss that belongs to those who bear Your form.
