O Lord, let that [desire] not arise even for Brahman in his own glory, whether through meditation or from hearing stories of worldly existence; rather,
let it arise for those falling from their celestial chariots, shaken by the sword of Death.
O Infinite One, may I have constant association with those great souls of pure intent who repeatedly offer devotion unto You,
by which I may easily cross this vast and turbulent ocean of worldly existence.

"I shall lead you away, intoxicated by drinking the nectar of the stories of Your qualities. O Lord, those who are utterly devoted to You do not remember even their own dear mortal selves, nor these things: sons, friends, home, wealth, and wives."
But those who have formed attachments to those whose hearts are greedy for the fragrance of your lotus feet, O Lotus-navelled One—
whether they be animals, trees, birds, reptiles, gods, or demons— [attain Your state].

O Unborn One, I know Your most massive form, which consists of many elements beginning with the Mahat, and which— distinguished as both existent and non-existent— is perceived by mortals and others; beyond this, O Supreme One, I know nothing where no dispute exists.

At the end of the kalpa, that Supreme Person, whose own vision is His own witness, reclines with Ananta as His companion, holding this entire universe within His belly; from the golden world-lotus born from the ocean at His navel—
I bow down to that effulgent Lord within the womb.
You are the Self, eternally liberated, pure, and awakened; you are the immutable, the primordial Person, the Blessed One, the sovereign of the three worlds.
O observer, you sit apart from that state which remains undivided through your own unbroken vision;
for it is in that state that those of opposing courses incessantly fall.

I take refuge in that Brahman— the source of the universe, one, infinite, primordial, consisting of pure bliss, and immutable— by whom knowledge and the various powers have been manifested in succession.
O Blessed One, for those whose blessings are rooted in truth, Your lotus feet are indeed the source of their blessing; likewise, for one who worships You, the embodiment of the goals of human life,
the Blessed One thus protects even the most wretched, O Noble Lord.
"Like a cow anxious for her calf, He is compassionate toward us.
Maitreya said:
"Then, having been thus praised by that wise one with pure intentions,"
The Blessed One, affectionate toward His servants, greeted him and spoke thus.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O prince, I know the resolve within your heart."
"I bestow that upon you, O observer of noble vows; may it be well with you—even though it is difficult to attain.
It is not presided over by others, O blessed one, and it is radiant and eternal, wherein the wheel of luminaries—the planets, constellations, and stars—is established."
Beyond that lies the stationary realm of those who dwell in the subsequent kalpa, situated like the wheel of cows in the sacrificial enclosure (medhyā). There,
Dharma, Agni, Kaśyapa, Śukra, and the forest-dwelling sages wander about,
keeping it to their right, together with the stars.

When he had set out for the forest after his father had given him a cow, he— whose senses remained unimpaired— protected it for thirty-six thousand years, being devoted to righteousness; meanwhile, your elder brother, whose mind was fixed on hunting, perished.
Searching for you in the forest, your mother will enter a forest fire.
Having worshipped me— the heart of sacrifice— with sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
and having enjoyed the fulfillment of her desires here on earth, she will remember me at the end.
"Then you shall go to My abode, which is honored by all the worlds;
situated above the sages, once gone there, one does not return.
Maitreya said:

Thus honored, the Blessed Lord, whose banner bears Garuḍa, having pointed out his own abode to the boy while he looked on, departed for his own realm. He too [attained] that which was born of his resolve and brought about through service to the feet of Viṣṇu.
Having attained the cessation of his mental constructs, he returned to the city not feeling particularly joyful.
Vidura said:
"That supreme state of Hari, the master of illusion, which is so difficult to attain, was earned by him through the worship of His feet."
Having attained [all this] yet feeling as if his purpose were unfulfilled in that single lifetime, how did he, the knower of all things, regard himself?
Maitreya said:
"But he, pierced in the heart by the word-arrows of his mother’s co-wife, remembered them."
They did not desire liberation from the Lord of Liberation; therefore, Dhruva experienced distress.
Dhruva said:
"That state which Sananda and others, who have drawn up their vital energy (*ūrdhva-retas*), know through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) over many births—"
"Having approached the shade of his feet for six months, I have departed with a divided mind.
Alas! Behold the lack of self-knowledge in me, a man of wretched fortune;
having gone to the foot of the one who cuts asunder worldly existence, I pray for that which is finite."
My intelligence was corrupted by the gods who fell [from their status] out of intolerance; I,
the most wretched of men, did not grasp the truth of Nārada’s words,
having resorted to divine illusion like one who is fast asleep with impaired vision.

I performed austerities even though there was no second person [to benefit], for the pain in the hearts of brothers and rivals; this which I have prayed for has been rendered futile, like medical treatment for one whose life has departed, after I had propitiated the Soul of the Universe— who is difficult to propitiate— through my penance.
Deprived of good fortune, I have begged from Bhava— who cuts asunder worldly existence— the very thing that causes bondage.
Alas, out of folly, I have asked for pride from the Lord who bestows sovereign self-rule,
like a pauper with exhausted merit begging for mere chaff.

Maitreya said: O dear one, those people like you who serve the lotus feet of Mukunda do not desire anything for themselves other than service to Him, for their mental fulfillment has been attained by His mere will.
Having heard that his son was returning as he had departed after passing away, the king could not believe it; for how could there be good fortune for one such as he?
Yet, placing faith in the words of the celestial sage, he was overwhelmed by a surge of joy.
Extremely pleased with the messenger who brought the news, he gave him a great deal of wealth as a reward;
then, mounting a chariot drawn by excellent horses and adorned with gold,
he was escorted by brahmins, family elders, ministers, and kinsmen.
Amidst the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, the chanting of the Vedas, and the music of flutes,
he quickly departed from the city, eager to behold his sons;
his two queens, Sunīti and Suruci, were adorned with golden ornaments.
Having ascended the palanquin together with Uttama, they both proceeded toward him.
Seeing him approaching from the vicinity of the grove,
the king quickly descended from his chariot and, overwhelmed with love, hastened to meet him.
With his mind filled with long-standing longing and sighing deeply, he embraced his son with both arms; then,
smelling him repeatedly on the head, he drenched him with the cool waters of his tears— [tears] that destroyed all the bonds of sin through contact with the feet of Viṣvaksena.
His intense desire having been fulfilled, he bathed his son;
then, having saluted his father’s feet and being blessed with benedictions,
that leader of virtuous men bowed his head to his two mothers, being treated with great honor.
Suruci raised up the child who had prostrated at her feet,
embraced him, and said with a voice faltering with tears, "Live!"—
he for whom the Blessed Lord Hari was pleased by his virtues such as friendliness and the like.
All living beings bow down to him of their own accord, like waters flowing toward a low-lying place.
Both Uttama and Dhruva, overwhelmed by mutual love,
stood with their hair standing on end from the touch of each other's limbs, repeatedly shedding streams of tears.
Sunīti, his mother, embraced her son who was dearer to her than her own life; finding solace through the touch of his limbs, she cast off her mental anguish,
and milk flowed from her breasts along with the auspicious tears born from her eyes.

Then, O hero, as the two were being consecrated, the people repeatedly praised that queen, saying: "By good fortune, O mother of heroes, your son—who had long been lost—has been recovered; he shall be the dispeller of your distress and the protector of the realm."
"The Lord, the remover of the distress of those who bow before Him, has surely been worshiped by you;
for by meditating upon Him, the wise have conquered death, which is so difficult to overcome. O King, [the sage saw] Dhruva with his brothers being thus cherished by the people.
Having mounted his female elephant, he entered the city joyfully while being praised;
there, at various points, were archways with shimmering sea-monster motifs,
along with clusters of plantain trunks and young betel-nut trees of the same kind.
At every door, it was adorned with water-jars accompanied by lamps, hung with mango sprouts, garments, garlands,
and strings of pearls; and it was surrounded by walls and gate-towers covered in gold.
It was adorned on all sides by the splendor of the peaks of magnificent palaces;
its courtyards, streets, balconies, and roads were polished and anointed with sandalwood paste;
and it was filled with parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, fruits, grains, and sacrificial offerings.
As Dhruva was seen on his path here and there, the women of the city brought him white mustard seeds, unbroken rice grains, curd, water, dūrvā grass, flowers, and fruits,
while offering auspicious blessings out of maternal affection.
Listening to those charming songs, he entered his father’s palace; in that most excellent residence, which was filled with a multitude of great jewels,
he dwelt like a god in heaven, being cherished exceedingly by his father.
The beds were like the foam of milk, made of ivory with golden coverings;
there were highly precious seats where the furnishings were made of gold.
There, against walls of crystal and great emeralds, [the women reclined].
The jewel-lamps shine forth, joined with the gems that are women;
and there are delightful gardens filled with various celestial trees,
where pairs of warbling birds and intoxicated bees are singing.
The ponds, with their steps made of vaidūrya gems, were filled with lotuses, blue water-lilies, and white lilies, and were frequented by flocks of swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, cakravāka birds,
and cranes; such was the power of that son of the royal sage Uttānapāda.

Having heard and seen that most wonderful marvel, the king attained the highest astonishment; and beholding him to be of mature age, esteemed by his subjects, and beloved by his people, he appointed Dhruva as the lord of the earth.
And perceiving himself to be advanced in years, the lord of the people,
becoming detached, set out for the forest while reflecting upon his own future destination.
Maitreya said:
Dhruva married Bhramī, the daughter of Prajāpati Śiśumāra; their two sons were Kalpa and Vatsara. Furthermore, the mighty Dhruva begot a son upon his wife Ilā, the daughter of Vāyu.

She gave birth to a son named Utkala and a jewel among women. But Uttama, having not yet been married, was killed by the powerful Puṇyajana on the mountain while out hunting; his mother followed him in death.
Having heard of the slaughter of his brothers, Dhruva was overcome with anger, indignation, and grief;
mounting his victorious chariot, he went to the abode of the Puṇyajanas.
Having traveled toward the northern direction frequented by the attendants of Rudra, the king [proceeded].
In a valley of the Himalayas, he beheld a city teeming with Guhyakas;
the long-armed one blew his conch shell, making the sky and all directions resound,
at which the Upadevis, their eyes agitated, were greatly terrified, O Vidura.
Then, emerging from there, the powerful great warriors of the secondary gods (upadevas),
unable to endure that roar, rushed forward with their weapons raised.
As they were charging, the hero, a great car-warrior (mahāratha) wielding a formidable bow, [confronted them].
He struck each one of them, all at once, with three arrows each. Indeed,
with those arrows lodged in their foreheads, they all considered themselves defeated and praised that deed of his.
Unable to endure him, like serpents provoked by the touch of a foot,
they pierced him simultaneously with arrows, desiring to double their previous effort;
then, with iron clubs, swords, spears, tridents, and axes—

Enraged and desiring to counter that [attack], thirteen myriads showered him— along with his chariot and charioteer— with spears, double-edged swords, *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles, and arrows of variegated feathers.
At that time, the son of Uttānapāda was not seen at all, being completely covered by the heavy rain of weapons, like a mountain shrouded by a downpour.
Then, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the Siddhas watching from the heavens.
"This man has been slain; the sun has sunk into the ocean of the Yakṣas," so they cried as the Yātudhānas shouted for victory in the battle.
Then his chariot rose up like the sun emerging from the mist.
Making his divine bow resound and bringing distress to his enemies,
he scattered their flood of missiles with his arrows, just as the wind disperses a mass of clouds.
Those arrows released from his bow pierced the armor of the rākṣasas.
Sharp arrows entered their bodies like thunderbolts striking mountains.
As they were being cut down by broad-headed shafts, there lay heads adorned with beautiful earrings, thighs resembling golden palm trees, and arms graced with shimmering bracelets.
Strewn with necklaces, armlets, crowns, and highly precious turbans,
those battlefields, captivating to the minds of heroes, shone resplendent.
The remaining hosts of Rākṣasas, who had survived the slaughter on the field of battle by the arrows of the best of Kṣatriyas, [fled].
With their limbs mostly mangled, they fled like herds of elephants sporting with a lion-king.

At that time, that best of men, not seeing any assailant in the great battle, desired to see the city; yet he did not enter the city of his enemies, for a person does not know the intentions of those who employ deceitful means.
Speaking thus to his charioteer, Citraratha— vigilant and apprehensive of an encounter with his enemies—
heard a sound like that of the ocean stirred by the wind, and dust was seen in all directions.
In an instant, the sky was completely shrouded on every side by a dense mass of clouds.
O sinless one, with lightning flashing in all directions and with thunder terrifying them,
they rained down floods of blood, flesh, pus, excrement, urine, and fat;
and from the sky, headless trunks fell before him.
Then a mountain appeared in the sky, and from all directions there fell maces,
iron clubs, swords, and pestles, along with showers of stones;
and serpents hissed like thunderbolts, vomiting fire from their eyes in rage.
Intoxicated elephants, lions, and tigers rushed forward in herds;
the ocean, with its terrifying waves, inundating the earth on all sides,
approached like a great, formidable lake at the end of a kalpa.

In this manner, the Asuras, possessing fierce speed, created many such terrifying things for the ill-minded through their demoniacal *māyā*. That *māyā*, which was exceedingly difficult to overcome, had been employed by the Asuras against Dhruva.
Having heard him, the sages who had assembled there wished him peace.
The sages said:
"O son of Uttānapāda, the Blessed One, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, [is with you]."
May the Lord, who removes the suffering of those who bow before him, destroy our enemies— he whose name, when truly uttered or heard,
enables the world to easily cross over death, O dear one, which is otherwise so difficult to traverse.
Maitreya said:
Having heard the sages speak thus, Dhruva,
after touching water for purification, fixed upon his bow that weapon which had been fashioned by Nārāyaṇa.
O Vidura, as this [battle] was being joined, the illusions created by Guhyaka vanished instantly, just as afflictions perish upon the arising of knowledge; meanwhile,
as he fixed his divine arrow to the bow, golden-feathered shafts with the plumage of swans [fell from the sky].
Issuing forth, they entered the enemy force like peacocks with terrifying cries entering a forest; harassed on all sides in that battle by those sharp-edged arrows,
the Yakṣas rushed at him in anger with their weapons raised, like serpents with upraised hoods attacking Garuḍa.

Seeing those Guhyakas being slaughtered in great numbers by Citraratha with his arrows— men whose arms, thighs, necks, and bellies were severed in battle— he sent them to the supreme world, the solar orb, which the perpetual celibates enter after piercing through it; for they were indeed innocent.
The Grandfather Manu, having approached with the sages, spoke out of compassion to the son of Uttānapāda.
Manu said:
"Enough, my child, with this excessive anger, which is a gateway to darkness and a source of evil."
"O dear one, you have slain these sinless Puṇyajanas; this deed, which is condemned by the virtuous, is not worthy of our family,
for you have undertaken the slaughter of demigods who have committed no offense."

"O dear one, beloved of your brother, it is surely not the path of the virtuous who follow Hṛṣīkeśa that many were slain through the transgression of one, by you who were tormented by the thought of killing your brother."

Since you have worshipped Hari— the abode of all beings— by regarding yourself as an external object and treating living beings like cattle, you have attained that supreme station of Viṣṇu, which is otherwise so difficult to reach.
Being meditated upon by Hari and honored even by His devotees, how could you have committed a blameworthy act while instructing others in the vow of the virtuous,
through your forbearance, compassion, and friendliness toward all living beings?
And through equanimity, the Lord, the Self of all, becomes fully pleased;
when the Lord is fully pleased,
the person, liberated from the material modes and released from the cycle of individual existence, attains the Brahman that is liberation.
Indeed, woman and man are composed of the five elements;
from the union of those two, woman and man, birth occurs here.
In this very manner proceed creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
O King, O bull among men, due to the agitation of the modes by the illusory energy of the Supreme Self,
that Lord of pure nature acted as the mere instrumental cause therein;
within Him this entire universe, both manifest and unmanifest, revolves like iron in a magnet.

Indeed, this Blessed One, whose power is distributed through the flow of the modes by the energy of time, though he is a non-doer, acts; though he is without ego, he destroys; for the activity of the All-pervading Lord is truly difficult to conceive. He is the infinite one who brings an end, time itself, without beginning yet the creator of the beginning, and imperishable.
Creating beings through beings and destroying the Ender through death,
for that Death who enters all creatures equally, there is neither a partisan nor an opponent;
powerless, the hosts of living beings follow him as he runs, just as particles of dust follow the wind.

The omnipresent Lord, who is himself free from both the decrease and the increase of a living being's lifespan, ordains the circumstances of one who is well-off or ill-fated. O King, some call this "karma," while others call it "svabhāva" (inherent nature).
Some say it is time, others say it is destiny, and still others say it is the desire of the person;
yet none truly know the intended purpose of the Unmanifest, the Immeasurable, from whom the emergence of diverse powers occurs, nor indeed their own origin, O dear one.
"O dear son, these followers of Dhanada are not the slayers of your brother;
for in the matter of creation and destruction, O child, destiny alone is the cause.
He alone creates the universe, and He alone protects and destroys it."
Moreover, because he is free from egoism, this Self of beings, the Lord of beings, and the source of all beings, is not tainted by the qualities or their activities;
joined with his own power, *māyā*, he creates, consumes, and protects.
O dear one, with your whole being, take refuge in Him alone— the Lord who is both death and immortality, the ultimate goal of the universe—
to whom the creators of the world offer tribute, just as oxen are led by their noses bound with a rope;
He who, at the age of five, abandoned his mother because his vital organs were pierced by the words of her co-wife.

Having gone to the forest, he worshipped the inner sense through austerity and attained the supreme station at the head of the three worlds. Seek that very Self— the one, imperishable, devoid of qualities—
who is free from material form and upon whom this world appears as an unreal duality, while you yourself perceive Him through self-realization.

By cultivating supreme devotion toward the Lord—the inner self, who is infinite, pure bliss, and endowed with all potencies—you will gradually sever the knot of ignorance consisting of the deeply rooted notions of "I" and "mine.
Restrain your anger; may it be well with you, for such wrath is the greatest obstacle to spiritual welfare.
O King, just as one who has abundant medical knowledge does not suffer from disease,
so a wise man should not fall under the sway of that by which people are greatly terrified, if he desires his own fearlessness.
O child, you have committed an offense against Dhanada, the brother of Giriśa,
by killing the Puṇyajanas out of resentment because they were the slayers of your brother; appease him quickly with prostrations and humble words.
"As long as the splendor of the great does not overwhelm our lineage," having thus instructed his grandson Dhruva, Manu, the son of Svāyambhuva,
being saluted by him, departed for his own city along with the sages.
Maitreya said:
When the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) perceived that Dhruva had desisted from his slaughter and was free from anger,
he approached him while being praised by Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, and Kinnaras, and spoke to him as he stood with palms joined in reverence.
The Giver of Wealth said:
"O blameless scion of the Kṣatriyas, I am well-pleased with you,
since by the command of your grandfather you have abandoned this enmity so difficult to relinquish."
You did not kill the Yakṣas, nor did the Yakṣas kill your brother;
for Time alone is the lord over the birth and destruction of all beings. Indeed, the notion that "I" or "you" exist is a meaningless thought arising from the ignorance of the person.

"Like a dream, it appears through meditation upon that which is not the Self, by which both bondage and its opposite arise. Therefore, O Dhruva, may prosperity be yours; go to the Blessed Lord Adhokṣaja, who is the self of all beings and whose form is the self of all beings."
Worship his worshipful feet, which sever the cycle of worldly existence, for the sake of liberation;
he is joined with, yet remains detached from, his own *māyā* composed of the modes of nature, which acts as his power.
O King, son of Uttānapāda, choose freely from me whatever desire resides in your heart, without hesitation.
"O worthy one, we have heard that you are the most excellent recipient of boons from the feet of the Lotus-navelled Lord; therefore, O dear one, grant us this.
Maitreya said:
Thus urged for a boon by the king of kings, Dhruva, the great devotee of exalted intelligence, [proceeded].
He chose from Hari unwavering remembrance, by which one crosses over the darkness that is otherwise difficult to transcend with ease.
Having granted that to him with a pleased mind, Aiḍaviḍa then vanished while he was looking on; he, too, returned to his own city.

Then he worshipped the Lord of Sacrifice with rituals accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees; yet, while performing those rites— which involve materials, actions, and deities, and which bestow the fruits of action— he bore an intense current of devotion toward Acyuta, the Self of all, who is beyond all.
He beheld that all-pervading Lord established within himself and within all beings.
The subjects regarded him— who was thus endowed with such character, devoted to Brahman, compassionate toward the distressed, and the protector of the bridges of dharma— as their very father.

For thirty-six thousand years he ruled the circle of the earth, exhausting his merit through enjoyments and his demerit through non-enjoyment; thus did that high-souled one, whose senses were unshakable, spend a long time with many sacrifices.
Having passed on to his son the royal throne, which serves the three goals of human life,
he regarded this entire universe as a construction of *māyā* within the Self,
comparable to a dream or a city of the Gandharvas fashioned by ignorance.
Having considered his own self, wife, children, friends, military strength, prosperous treasury,
the inner apartments, the delightful pleasure gardens,
and the entire circle of the earth girdled by the oceans—
Thinking, "It has been sent by Time," he went to Viśālā. There,
with his senses purified, having plunged into the auspicious waters on a Monday,
he assumed a meditative posture, conquered his breath, and withdrew his senses into his mind.
In that gross form which was an image of the Blessed One, he placed [his mind];
meditating upon it without interruption, he released it into samādhi,
while continuously flowing with devotion toward Lord Hari.
Constantly overwhelmed by a stream of tears of bliss,
his heart melting away, and his limbs covered with horripilation,
he forgot himself; thus was he liberated from all limiting adjuncts.
Dhruva beheld an excellent celestial chariot descending from the sky,
illuminating the ten directions like the risen moon. Therein he saw two foremost gods with four arms.
The two dark-complexioned youths, with eyes like red lotuses, stood leaning upon their maces, well-dressed,
adorned with crowns, necklaces, armlets, and beautiful earrings.
Recognizing them as servants of the Supreme Singer, he rose up; forgetting his proper conduct out of awe, he bowed while chanting the names of the Enemy of Madhu.
"O foremost of the Pārṣatas," he said, with palms joined in reverence to Kṛṣṇa, whose mind was fixed upon Kṛṣṇa’s feet,
who stood with folded hands and a neck bowed in humility.
Approaching with smiles, Sunanda and Nanda,
who were highly esteemed by the Lotus-navelled Lord,
replied; Sunanda and Nanda said:
"O King, may it be well with you; listen attentively to our words.
We two are the sons of that wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the creator of the entire universe, whom you, though only five years old, satisfied through your ascetic penance."
The two attendants have arrived here to lead you to the abode of the Blessed One—
that most difficult-to-conquer station of Viṣṇu which the wise, though failing to reach it, gaze upon as supreme;
ascend that place where the moon, sun, and other planets, constellations, and stars revolve to the right.
"O dear one, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which is worthy of worship by all the worlds, has never before been occupied by your ancestors or by others; ascend it now.
This most excellent celestial chariot was [offered] by the crown of the Lord of Excellent Fame (Uttamaśloka).
"O long-lived one, you ought to mount this [palanquin] that has been brought here.
Maitreya said:
Having heard the honey-sweet speech of the two chief messengers of Vaikuṇṭha, he who is dear to Urukrama—
Having performed his ablutions and completed the daily auspicious rites, he bowed to the sages and received their blessings.
Having circumambulated and worshipped the preeminent sacrificial altar, and having saluted the two attendants,
he desired to occupy it, assuming a golden form.
Then the son of Uttānapāda beheld Death approaching;
placing his foot upon the head of Mṛtyu, he ascended to the wondrous abode.
Then the kettledrums resounded, as did the mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, and other instruments.
The chief Gandharvas sang and showers of flowers fell.
And Dhruva, as he was about to ascend to the heavenly realm, remembered his mother Sunīti, who had left the mountain behind;
"I am departing for heaven while she remains wretched."
When he had thus resolved, the two best of gods revealed themselves before him by means of a celestial chariot as they were proceeding ahead,
while gods traveling in their own aerial vehicles praised them here and there along the way.
Being showered with flowers, he gradually beheld the planets;
having traversed the three worlds by the path of the gods and even passed beyond the sages,
he finally reached the abode of Viṣṇu, where the movement of Dhruva is supreme.
That which shines by its own luster such that these three worlds indeed shine after it;
that which does not approach those beings who lack compassion, but who constantly perform auspicious deeds;
those who are peaceful, impartial in vision, pure, and pleasing to all living beings.

"Those who are dear friends of Acyuta go directly to the abode of Acyuta. Thus spoke Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, who was solely devoted to Kṛṣṇa and became like a stainless crest-jewel for the three worlds.
O descendant of Kuru, upon which [the wheel] the circle of luminaries is mounted and revolves with deep velocity like a herd of cows around a central post— that [wheel]—
the venerable sage Nārada beheld its majesty.
Striking his lute, he sang verses concerning the ancestors during the sacrificial session.
Nārada said:
"Surely, such is the destination of the son of Sunīti, who regarded her husband as a deity, through the power of his ascetic penance."

Even those who expound the Vedas, despite seeing the various means [of attainment], are not able to comprehend [the Lord], let alone kings. He who, at the age of five, having departed for the forest with a heart pierced and tormented by the word-arrows of his guru’s wife, obeying my command, conquered the unconquerable Lord— who was already defeated by the virtues of His devotees.
He who was a mere kṣatriya on earth might desire to ascend even after many series of years what he had already ascended;
yet, having propitiated Vaikuṇṭha at the age of fifteen, he attained that very abode in a few days.
Maitreya said:
All this that was asked of me here by you has been related to you—
the life story of Dhruva, whose fame is boundless, which is esteemed by the virtuous,
and which is auspicious, conducive to renown, long life, merit, and great well-being.
Having heard with faith these deeds of Acyuta, which lead to heaven, provide stability, bring about cheerfulness, are praiseworthy,
and destroy all sin, there arises devotion to the Lord by which the destruction of all afflictions occurs.
For those desiring greatness, this is the sacred ford; for those desiring to hear, it is the source of virtues such as good character;
for those desiring splendor, it is that wherein they find it; and for those who are high-minded, it is the source of honor.
One who is self-restrained should recite this in the morning in an assembly of the twice-born.

And in the evening, on the full moon day, on the Sinīvālī day, on the twelfth lunar day, or under the Śravaṇa asterism; or at the end of the day, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, at a solar transit, or even on a Sunday— one should hear the great life-story of Dhruva, whose fame is virtuous.

One who takes refuge at the feet of Him whose feet are the source of all holy places should cause those endowed with faith to hear [this teaching], not desiring anything for himself, being satisfied in his own self; thus he attains perfection. He who bestows the nectar of knowledge upon one who does not know the truth regarding the path of the virtuous—
The gods show favor to that compassionate Lord of the distressed. O best of the Kurus, I have related this account of Dhruva, whose deeds were renowned and pure—
he who, as a child, abandoned his toys, his mother, and his home to go for refuge to Viṣṇu.
Sūta said:
Having heard the description by Kauṣārava of Dhruva’s ascent to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha,
Vidura, his devotion for the Lord Adhokṣaja deeply rooted, proceeded once more to question him.
Vidura said:
O observer of noble vows, who were those known as the Pracetas, whose sons were they, in whose lineage were they renowned, and where did they perform their sacrificial session?
I consider Nārada to be a great devotee who has beheld the gods,

for he has proclaimed the yoga of action (*kriyā-yoga*), the method of worshiping Hari, [to be performed] by men whose character is rooted in their own duty (*svadharma*). By such men, the Blessed Lord, the Person of Sacrifice (*yajña-pūruṣa*), [is to be worshipped].

O Brahmana, you were indeed praised by the devoted Nārada while being worshipped; you ought to relate in their entirety to me, who am eager to hear them, those narrations of the Lord which were described there by the celestial sage.
Maitreya said:
When his father had departed for the forest, Dhruva’s son, Utkala,
did not desire the imperial sovereignty nor the throne of his father.
From birth, his mind was serene, free from attachment, and possessed equal vision;
he beheld the Self pervading the world and the world within the Self—
the Self as Brahman, the state of liberation, in whom all forms have subsided.

Having his heart's core of latent impressions— the impurities of karma— burned away by the fire of uninterrupted yoga, he attained the continuous bliss that is identical in essence with the rasa of awakening;
while abiding in his own true nature, he perceived nothing other than himself.
With the appearance of one who is dull-witted, blind, deaf, insane, or mute, and lacking intelligence,
he was observed on the road by the children like a fire whose flames have been extinguished.
Thinking him to be a fool or a madman, the elders of the clan along with the ministers—
They made Vatsara, the younger son of Bhr̥mi, the king for one year. Svarvīthi, the beloved wife of Vatsara, gave birth to six sons:
Puṣpārṇa, Tigmaketu, Iṣa, Ūrja, Vasu, and Jaya.
Puṣpārṇa had two wives, Prabhā and Doṣā. Prabhā’s sons were Prātaḥ (Morning), Madhyandina (Midday), and Sāyaṃ (Evening).
Doṣā’s sons were the three: Pradoṣa (Twilight), Niśitha (Midnight), and Vyuṣṭa (Dawn).
Vyushita placed his son Sarvatejas in the Puṣkariṇī pond. He, in turn, obtained a son named Cakṣu through his wife Ākūti, who was Manu.
Manu’s queen Naḍvalā gave birth to the sons known as the Virajas.
Ulmuka begot six excellent sons by Puṣkariṇī: Puru, Kutsa, Trita, Dyumna, Satyavān, and Ṛtavrata; as well as Agniṣṭoma, Atīrātra, Pradyumna, Śibi, and Ulmuka himself.
Aṅga begot Sumanas, Khyāti, Kratu, Aṅgiras, and Gaya. Sunīthā was the wife of Aṅga, and she gave birth to the formidable Vena.
Because of his wicked character, that royal sage became despondent and departed from the city.
O dear one, when the sages, enraged, had indeed cursed him with the thunderbolt of their speech,
they churned the right hand of that deceased man once more.
At that time, as the world was without a king, the subjects were oppressed by bandits.
The first lord of the earth, Pṛthu, was born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
Vidura said:
Of that high-souled, virtuous sage, a treasure-house of good character and devoted to Brahman—
How did the subjects of the king become so wicked that he departed with a troubled mind?
Or what sin did they commit against Vena that the sages, who were experts in dharma and observers of the vow of punishment, inflicted the rod of Brahmā upon the king?
"A protector of subjects is not to be disregarded by his subjects even if he is sinful, because by his own splendor he sustains the power of the world-protectors.
O Brāhmaṇa, tell me this: what were the deeds of the son of Sunīthā?"
To one who is faithful and devoted, you are the best knower of the higher and the lower.
Maitreya said:
The royal sage Aṅga performed the great sacrifice of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
The deities did not appear when they were summoned by those who discourse on the Veda.
Thereupon, the officiating priests, filled with wonder, said to the sacrificer:
"The deities do not accept the oblations being offered."
O King, your sacrificial offerings are pure, having been prepared with faith; the Vedic hymns have been applied by those firm in their vows without any lapse.
We do not perceive even the slightest offense against the gods here.
"That they do not accept their own shares, those gods who are witnesses to one's actions.
Maitreya said:
Having heard the words of the twice-born, the sacrificer Aṅga became deeply dejected in mind.
By his permission, he sent forth a voice from within the assembly to ask this:
"The gods do not come when summoned, nor do they accept their sacrificial cups here;
O lords of the assembly, tell me, what fault have I committed?"
The lords of the assembly said:
"O king, not even the slightest sin remains in you here;
however, there is one former sin because of which you are thus childless in this life."
"Likewise, may you accomplish your purpose; may it be well with you, O King.
May the enjoyer of sacrifices grant a son to you who desire a son. "In that way, the dwellers of heaven will accept their respective portions."
Since Hari, the Person of Sacrifice, was directly chosen as the offspring,
Hari shall grant whatever various desires that person may wish for;
for the attainment of results for men occurs exactly according to how He has been propitiated.

Having thus resolved, the brāhmaṇas offered a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) to Śipiviṣṭa Viṣṇu for the sake of that king’s progeny; from that offering, a man arose, adorned with golden garlands and wearing spotless garments.
Having taken the prepared milk-rice from a golden vessel with his joined palms, that king of noble intellect, permitted by the brahmins,
smelled it with joy and gave it to his wife.

Having consumed that *puṃsavana* (fertilizing substance), the queen conceived a child for her husband; and when the time had come, she who was previously childless gave birth to a boy. Even as a mere infant, that man remained devoted to his maternal grandfather.
From a portion of unrighteousness, Death was born; because of him, he became unrighteous.
Raising his bow, that hunter who roamed the forest killed miserable deer; people cried out, "This is Vena, the wicked one! and were filled with fear.

While his children were playing in the playground with their companions, that most cruel and merciless man forcibly killed them like animals. Seeing that wicked son, the king [restrained him] with various punishments.
When he was no longer capable of governing and became deeply dejected,
the gods were generally worshipped by those householders who were childless and who did not experience the unbearable suffering of maintaining wicked offspring.
Since it brings about ill repute and great unrighteousness for men,
since it causes opposition with everyone and results in endless mental anguish— who indeed would choose that which is called "progeny," for it is but a bond of delusion for the self?
A wise man should consider that for whose sake houses are a source of suffering;
I consider a bad son better than a good son who is a locus of grief. A mortal should become disenchanted with the household, for houses are a multitude of afflictions.
Thus, with a despondent mind, the king rose from his palace at midnight due to the dawning of great enlightenment;
finding no sleep and unnoticed by men, he abandoned and departed from his sleeping queen Vena-suvā.
Having realized that their lord had departed in disillusionment, the subjects, priests, ministers, friends, and their attendants [were overcome].

Distraught with excessive grief, they searched the earth like unsuccessful yogis searching for a hidden man; failing to find any trace of Prajāpati’s path, their efforts frustrated, they returned to the city,
saluted the assembled sages with tears, and reported the disappearance of their lord, the descendant of Puru.
Maitreya said:
Those sages, headed by Bhṛgu, who were observers of the welfare of the worlds,
perceived that in the absence of a protector for men, they had fallen into a state of equality with cattle.
The teachers of the Veda summoned Sunīthā, the mother of Vīra,
and consecrated Vena— whom she had naturally disapproved of— as the lord of the earth.
Hearing that Vena, whose commands were most fierce, had ascended the royal throne, [the sages approached him].

The Dasyus immediately hid away like rats terrified by a snake. Having ascended the position of king, intoxicated by the eightfold opulences, arrogant and self-conceited, he held those highly fortunate ones in contempt.
Thus blinded by intoxication, like an elephant in rut unrestrained and rampant, he traveled about mounted on his chariot as if shaking heaven and earth.
"O twice-born ones, no sacrifice is to be performed, no gift is to be given, and no oblation is to be offered anywhere! he proclaimed.

Thus, observing the conduct of the wicked Vena, the sages performing the sacrificial session (satrin), reflecting upon the calamity of the world, and out of compassion, obstructed the [unrighteous] dharma of Vena on all sides with the sound of their drums. They spoke as follows:

"Alas! A great calamity has befallen the world from both sides, like being between a thief and a king, both of whom are fiercely blazing. Out of fear of anarchy, this man—who is unworthy of kingship—has been made king."
Even from him there was fear; how then can there be well-being for embodied beings today?
Like milk nourishing a snake, it brings only harm to its own nourisher.
Vena was wicked by his very nature, though born from the womb of Sunīthā.
"Although he has been appointed as the protector of the subjects, he indeed wishes to destroy them;
nevertheless, let us conciliate him so that his sin may not touch us.
Knowing this, we have made the wicked Vena our king."

"If this unrighteous man does not accept our words even after being conciliated, we shall burn him with our own splendor, for he is already consumed by the world's reproach. Having thus resolved, the sages concealed their anger within themselves.
Having approached Vena and conciliated him with gentle words,
the sages spoke:
"O best of kings, O sir, please attend to this which we have to inform you."
O dear one, the practice of dharma by men through speech, mind, body, and intellect increases their lifespan, prosperity, strength,
and fame; it bestows worlds free from sorrow, and for those who are unattached, it grants infinity.
O hero, may that which is the hallmark of security for your subjects not perish;
for when that is destroyed, the king falls from his sovereignty.
O King, the ruler [must protect] the subjects from wicked ministers, thieves, and the like.
Just as one who protects and collects taxes rejoices both in this world and after death, so too does he rejoice whose kingdom and city the Blessed Lord, the Person of Sacrifice,
is worshipped according to His own dharma by people belonging to the various classes and stages of life.

O highly fortunate one, the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings and the soul of the universe, is well-pleased with that king who abides by his own command; when He, the Lord of the lords of the worlds, is satisfied, what is there that cannot be attained?
Indeed, the worlds along with their guardians respectfully offer tribute to him.

O King, you ought to protect your own realm by performing various sacrifices for his sake— he who is the embodiment of the three Vedas, the collection of all sacrifices to the gods of all worlds, consisting of ritual materials and austerity.

"O gods, you are portions of Lord Hari; when sacrifices are performed by the twice-born within your domain, you, being well-pleased and highly satisfied, bestow whatever is desired. Therefore, O hero, you ought not to act in such a way as to offend them.
Vena said:

"Alas, you fools! You consider yourselves righteous while actually practicing unrighteousness, for you have abandoned your husband who provides your livelihood and instead worship a paramour as your husband. These deluded women despise the Lord who has assumed the form of a king."
They do not find what is auspicious in this world or in the next. Who is this so-called Yajña-puruṣa, for whom you have such devotion— as if,
for example, unchaste women feel toward a paramour, being far removed from affection for their own husbands?
Viṣṇu, Viriñca, Giriśa, Indra, Vāyu, Yama, Ravi,
Parjanya, Dhanada, Soma, Kṣiti, Agni, and Apāmpati—
these and other deities are the source of boons and curses.
O King, all the gods reside within the body of the monarch;
therefore, O Brahmins, free from envy, worship me through your ritual acts. Bring offerings to me, for what other person is entitled to the first portion of the sacrifice?
Maitreya said:
Thus, with his intellect perverted, that most wicked man had gone astray; though being entreated, he did not grant their request, his auspicious fortune having fallen away.
Thus those twice-born ones were treated with disrespect by him who considered himself a scholar; when their noble request was frustrated, Vidura became enraged at him, saying:
"Let this wicked man, so naturally cruel, be slain! Let him be slain!"
While living, he will surely and swiftly reduce the world to ashes.
This man of wicked conduct does not deserve the excellent throne of a king,
he who shamelessly reviles Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice.
"Who indeed would despise this one, were it not for his inauspiciousness,
since he has attained such sovereignty as a recipient of [the Lord's] grace?
Thus resolved, the sages, their anger fully aroused, set out to kill him.

The sages struck Vena with their "huṃ" sounds because he had reviled Acyuta; once he was slain, they returned to their own hermitage sites. Sunīthā, grieving, protected her son’s body by means of her mystical power (vidyā-yoga).

Once, those sages, having bathed in the waters of the Sarasvatī and offered oblations into the fires, were seated on the riverbank engaged in sacred discourse when they observed portents that had arisen, which cause terror to the world. They spoke thus:

"May no misfortune from bandits befall this earth, which is now without a protector. While the sages were thus reflecting, a vast cloud of dust arose from all directions as the thieves ran about plundering.

Perceiving that the world was being plundered by those who seized the wealth of others, and that the people were intent on killing one another after their protector had passed away, the land became kingless, filled mostly with thieves, and devoid of strength.
Even though they were capable, those who perceived the faults of that [king] did not restrain him from his ways. Even for a Brahmin who is impartial, peaceful, and indifferent toward the wretched,
the Brahman flows away like water from a broken vessel.
"The lineage of this royal sage Aṅga does not deserve to come to an end;
for the kings in this dynasty, who take refuge in Keśava, possess unfailing potency.
Having thus resolved regarding the deceased monarch, the sages—
They churned his thigh with force, and from it there appeared a man named Bāhuka,
who was as black as a crow, with very short limbs, short arms, and large jaws;
he had short feet, a depressed tip of the nose, blood-red eyes, and copper-colored hair.
To him, who was bowed down in distress and saying, "What shall I do?", they said, "Sit down, my son"; thus he became a Niṣāda. His descendants, the Naiṣādas, dwell in the mountains and forests.
By whom, upon being born, the formidable impurity of Vena was removed.
Maitreya said:
Then, O Brahmins, for that king who remained childless, [the sages performed a sacrifice].
As his two arms were being churned, a pair was produced.
Seeing that a pair had been born, the sages who discourse on Brahman,
having recognized them as portions of the Blessed Lord, spoke with great satisfaction.
The sages said:
"This is a portion of the Blessed Viṣṇu who protects the world; and she is the manifestation of Lakṣmī, inseparable from the Supreme Person."
But this first among kings, a man who will spread his fame,
shall become the great king named Pṛthu of wide renown;
and this queen Sudatī, adorned with the ornaments of virtue, shall be his consort.
The beautiful Arci, who was devoted to Pṛthu, became his wife;
he was born as a direct portion of Hari for the sake of protecting the world,
and this Śrī, ever inseparable from him, was born as his devoted companion.
Maitreya said:
The brahmins offered him praise, the foremost of the Gandharvas sang,
the Siddhas showered streams of flowers, and the celestial women danced.
In the heavens, conchs, trumpets, drums, and other instruments resounded;
there, all the hosts of celestial sages and ancestors arrived. Brahmā, the preceptor of the world, having approached together with the gods and the lords of the immortals, [proceeded].
Seeing the mark of the wielder of the mace on the right hand of the son of Vena,
and the lotus on his feet, he indeed considered him to be a portion of Hari;
for he whose discus is irresistible is a partial incarnation of the Supreme Lord.
The consecration ceremony for him was commenced by Brahmins who were exponents of the Veda;
people from all directions brought for him the materials required for the royal inauguration.
Rivers, oceans, mountains, serpents, cows, birds, and wild animals [all brought their offerings].
The heavens, the earth, and all living beings brought gifts as offerings. Consecrated as the great king, well-dressed and beautifully adorned,
he shone like a second fire accompanied by his wife Arciṣmatī, who was likewise adorned.
To him, Dhanada presented a golden hero-throne;
Varuṇa gave an umbrella that shed water and possessed the luster of the moon;
Vāyu gave two fly-whisks made of hair; and Dharma gave a garland composed of his own fame.
Indra gave him his excellent crown; Yama, his staff of restraint;
Brahmā, armor made of the Veda; Sarasvatī, her most excellent necklace;
Hari, the Sudarśana discus; and his wife, the unassailable Śrī.

Rudra gave him a bow with ten moons, and Ambikā likewise a quiver with a hundred moons; Soma gave horses made of nectar, Tvaṣṭṛ a chariot that was the very seat of beauty, Agni a bow made of goat-skin, and Sūrya arrows consisting of rays of light.
The earth offered him sandals made of yoga; heaven daily presented a garland of flowers;
the celestial beings provided dance, song, instrumental music, and the power of invisibility;
the sages offered truthful blessings; and the ocean gave him his own son as a conch shell.
The oceans, mountains, and rivers served as the chariot tracks for that Great-Souled One;
then the herald, the panegyrist, and the bard approached to offer praise to him.
Having perceived those panegyrists, the powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena, [addressed them].
With a voice resonant like a thundercloud, he spoke these words with a smile.
Pṛthu said:
"O Sūta, O Māgadha, O gentle Vandin, for me whose virtues are now unmanifest in this world, let there be..."

"To what object should this praise of mine be applied, lest your words regarding me prove futile? Therefore, O you of beautiful speech, when we are out of sight, you may sufficiently compose hymns based on what you have heard from us;
for in the truthful recounting of the qualities of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka), cultured men do not utter anything contemptible."

Who, being capable of bestowing great virtues upon himself, would have others praise him even for his non-existent qualities? Deceived by the thought that these qualities would belong to him, the fool does not realize he is inviting public derision;
for even those renowned as powerful loathe the praising of themselves.
Modest and supremely noble, we have never even heard of such a censurable act as this being committed by a man; for we remain unknown in this world even to the most excellent women.
How then shall we cause ourselves to be sung of like children through such deeds?
Maitreya said:
While the king was speaking thus, the singers, urged by the sage,
praised him with joyful hearts, having partaken of the nectar of his words.
We are not capable of fully describing Your greatness, O Supreme Lord, who descended by Your own illusory power (māyā);
for even the intellects of the masters of speech falter when contemplating Your heroic deeds performed as the son of Vena.
Nevertheless, we remain devoted to the nectar of the stories concerning Pṛthu, the incarnation of a portion of Hari, whose fame is sublime.
"Urged by the sages according to their instruction, we shall perform praiseworthy deeds; for he is the best among those who uphold dharma, leading the world in accordance with dharma,
the protector of the bridges of dharma, and the punisher of those who oppose it."
He alone, indeed, sustains within His own body the bodies of the guardians of the worlds,
for the benefit of both worlds, according to their respective portions at the appropriate times.
He takes up wealth at the proper time and releases it again at the proper time.
Impartial toward all beings, the all-pervading Vainya blazed like the sun; though others might step upon him, he patiently endured their transgressions,
for he was ever compassionate toward distressed creatures and lived according to the duties of a protector of the earth.
When that god does not send rain, Hari, assuming the form of a king,
will easily protect the subjects whose lives are in peril, just like Indra. He nourishes the world with the nectar-like form of his speech.
With a glance full of passion and a beautiful, pure smile, he—
whose path is unmanifest, whose purpose is hidden, who is a profound creator, whose wealth is well-guarded,
and who is the sole abode of infinite majesty and virtues— is like Pracetās, though his self is concealed.
Difficult to approach and difficult to withstand, though near he is as if far away;
like a fire arising from the forest of Vena, he cannot be overcome.
Perceiving the actions of all beings both within and without by means of his spies, he remains ever vigilant.
Like a neutral supervisor or like the wind among embodied beings,

he who stands firm on the path of dharma does not punish one who is not deserving of punishment— even his own son— yet he punishes even his own son if he is deserving of punishment, regardless of whether he hates his own self.
The unimpeded wheel of this [king] Pṛthu revolves from the Āmānasā mountain as long as the divine sun shines with its rays of light;
for he will delight the world with his own deeds.
Then the subjects addressed this king with words that delighted the mind:
"He is firm in his vows, true to his promise, devoted to the Brahmanas, a servant of the elders,
a refuge for all beings, respectful, and compassionate toward the distressed."
He showed devotion toward the wives of others as he did toward his own mother;
he was as affectionate toward his children as a father, and served those who discourse on Brahman.
He cherished all embodied beings as his own self and increased the joy of his friends.
This one, though free from attachment, is engaged in the punishment of the wicked;
yet he is the Lord himself, the sovereign of the three worlds, the immutable Self descended by his own power (kalā),
in whom they perceive even that perceived diversity created by ignorance to be purposeless.
This sole hero, the protector of the earth’s circle from the mountain of sunrise, the lord of kings,
having mounted his victorious chariot and taken up his bow, moves about to the south like the sun; indeed,
the rulers of men along with the guardians of the worlds shall bring tribute to him in various places.
The women of those lands, extolling his glory, will consider him the first king, whose weapon was the discus.
This sovereign lord of the earth, the protector of subjects, milked the cow of the world to provide for their livelihood;
he who, like Indra, effortlessly leveled the earth by shattering mountains with the tip of his bow.
When he himself brandished the *āja-gava* bow and traversed the earth in battle, which was otherwise unbearable,
the wicked fled in every direction like a lion raising its tail.
He performed a hundred horse-sacrifices at the place where the Sarasvatī river appeared.
In the final age of the hundred sacrifices (*śata-kratu*), Purandara stole his horse;
having approached the blessed Sanat-kumāra alone in the grove of his own abode and worshipped him with devotion, he obtained that stainless knowledge by which one knows the supreme Brahman.

In various places, Pṛthu, whose prowess is renowned and whose valor is vast, will hear those various songs concerning himself; having conquered all directions with his unimpeded wheel, he has uprooted the thorns of the world by means of his own splendor.
"His majesty shall become the lord of the earth, his great power being celebrated in song by the lords of both gods and asuras.
Maitreya said:
"Thus was the Blessed Lord Vainya glorified through his qualities and deeds."
Having honored and greeted them with joy,
he gratified the social orders headed by the Brahmins, as well as his servants, ministers, domestic priests, citizens, country folk, guilds, and the constituent elements of the state.
Vidura said:
Why did the Earth, who possesses many forms, assume the shape of a cow? Who was the calf there, and what was the milking vessel that Pṛthu milked from her?
How was the Goddess Prakṛti, who is by nature uneven, made even by him? For what reason did the Lord seize his sacrificial horse?
O Brahman, [this was heard] from the blessed Sanat-kumāra, the supreme knower of Brahman.

Having attained knowledge along with realized wisdom, what destination did that royal sage reach? And whatever other sacred account there may be concerning the blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa— the source of good renown— relating to his previous incarnations, [please tell me].
"You ought to tell me, your devoted follower, as well as to Adhokṣaja, about him who, in the form of Vainya, milked this earth.
Sūta said:
Thus urged by Vidura regarding the topics of Vāsudeva,
Maitreya, his mind filled with joy, praised him and replied.
Maitreya said:
O dear one, when Pṛthu had been consecrated by the brāhmaṇas as the protector of the people,
the subjects— having approached the surface of the earth while their bodies were emaciated by hunger during a time of foodlessness— addressed their lord:
"O King, we are scorched by internal hunger just as trees are consumed by fire situated within their hollows."

Today we have come for refuge to you, the worthy protector who has been established as our sustainer and husband. O God of gods among men, may you strive to grant food to us who are tormented by hunger; for until we perish, deprived of our strength, you are indeed the Lord of livelihood and the guardian of the world.
Maitreya said:
O best of the Kurus, having heard the piteous lamentation of his subjects, Pṛthu meditated for a long time and discerned its cause.
Having thus resolved with his intellect, he grasped his bow and fixed an arrow upon it,
like the enraged destroyer of Tripura against the earth;
and the trembling earth beheld him with his weapon raised.
The cow, terrified, fled like a doe pursued by a hunter; Vainya,
enraged with eyes bloodshot red, ran after her,
fixing an arrow to his bow wherever she fled.
Running through the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the space between heaven and earth, that goddess beheld him here and there with his weapons raised;
she found no protector in the world from him, just as living beings find no refuge from death at the hands of Vainya’s son.
Terrified, she then turned back with a grieving heart and said to the illustrious one, who knows the dharma and is affectionate toward those who have sought refuge:
"Protect me as well; you are established in the protection of all living beings."
Why do you wish to kill me, who am helpless and innocent?
How could one who is considered a knower of dharma kill a woman? Indeed, living beings do not strike women, even when they have committed an offense.
O King, how much more so for those like you, who are compassionate and affectionate toward the distressed?
Having split me open— me, the undecaying boat upon which the universe, yourself, and these creatures are established— how will you sustain them all within the waters?
Pṛthu said:
"O Earth, I shall destroy you, who have turned your back on my command—
you who claim a share of the sacrificial grass yet do not bestow wealth upon us."
Having eaten grass every day, she no longer yields milk from her udder;
indeed, when she has become thus corrupted, punishment is not unmerited in this case.
For you, O Earth, were created by the Self-Existent One as the source of medicinal herbs and seeds.
"O dull-witted one, out of contempt for me, you do not release these [creatures] whom you have obstructed;
yet I shall silence the lamentations of these distressed ones, who are overcome by hunger, with my arrows, using the fat of your pierced body."
Whether he be a man, a woman, or even a eunuch, that lowest of beings who is self-conceited and devoid of compassion for all creatures— his execution by kings is no execution at all.
Having reduced you, who are arrogant, intoxicated with pride, and a cow of illusion, to pieces as small as sesame seeds with my arrows, [I shall punish you].
"I shall sustain these creatures by the power of my own yoga. To him,
who thus bore a form composed of fury like the God of Death himself,
the Earth, trembling with fear, spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Dhara said:
"Obeisances to the Supreme Person, who by His illusory power (*māyā*) manifests various bodies as the self of the modes;
obeisances to Him whose waves of delusion regarding substance, action, and agency have been washed away by the experience of His own true nature."

By whom I was fashioned as the abode of the Self, and from whom this collection of the creation of the modes [of nature] proceeds—that very Lord of Heaven stands before me with weapon raised to slay me; to what other refuge shall I resort?
He who, in the beginning, created this world of moving and non-moving beings by His own inconceivable power which rests within Himself.
"By her alone was he indeed intent upon protecting me; how then can he, who is devoted to righteousness, seek to kill me? Alas!

The purpose of the Lord is surely not perceived by people whose minds are unrefined by His invincible *māyā*. He is the one who acts and causes others to act, who is the manifold yet the one, and the Supreme Lord."

Omnipresent Lord, obeisances to You, the Supreme Person, the Creator, who by Your powers—consisting of substance, action, agency, and consciousness—sustain the creation and other processes of this universe; to You whose powers are both fully manifest and withdrawn. Indeed, O All-pervading One, this world composed of the elements, the senses, and the internal organ was fashioned by You from Yourself.

O Unborn One, desiring to establish me, the Primeval Boar raised me up from the waters of the netherworld (rasātala). Today, wishing indeed to protect the subjects situated upon me—the very lap of the waters—on a boat, you have become that bearer of the earth in the form of a hero; yet you, with fierce arrows, seek to slay me who am in the water.

"Surely, the activities of the lords cannot be understood by people like us, whose mental paths are deluded by the *māyā* of their creative qualities; let there be obeisances to those who bring glory to heroes.
Maitreya said:
Having thus praised Pṛthu, the Earth, her lips quivering with rage, spoke again;
having steadied herself by her own effort, she said:
"O Lord, restrain your anger and listen to what I have to say."
Just as a wise bee gathers the essence from all directions,
so too have the sages who perceive reality observed and employed various yogic paths in this world or the next for the sake of achieving the ultimate welfare of men.

He who properly follows those means previously shown, even if he is inferior, being endowed with faith, attains the goals directly. But the ignorant man who, disregarding them, undertakes matters on his own—
His undertakings and purposes repeatedly fail;
for those herbs which were created by Brahmā in the past, O Lord of the People,
I have seen them being consumed by the wicked who do not observe their vows.

"O guardians of the world, because you failed to protect and disregard me while the world was being plundered by thieves, I consumed the medicinal herbs for the sake of the sacrifice. Surely those plants have now been exhausted within me over the course of much time."
"Therefore, O hero, you ought to accept [the cow] by means of the yoga you have perceived; provide for me a calf, O brave one, so that I, being affectionate toward my offspring,
may milk from her desires consisting of milk and a suitable milking vessel."
O mighty-armed one, O source of all beings,
if the Blessed One desires the desired, nourishing food for all creatures,
then, O King, make me level so that the rain of the gods may flow like milk.
"O Lord, may you return to me even when we are separated; may it be well with you.
Having spoken these pleasant and beneficial words, the king took Manu by the hand as his calf and milked all the medicinal herbs from the earth.
Likewise, other wise men everywhere took the essence from her;
others, moreover, milked her—who was expanded by Pṛthu—according to their own desires. Then, O best of men, the sages milked the goddess for their sense faculties.
Having made Bṛhaspati the calf and the pure milk consisting of the Vedic meters,
the hosts of gods made Indra the calf and milked out the Soma;
with a golden vessel, they milked out vigor, energy, strength, and nourishment.
The Daityas and Dānavas, having made Prahlāda— the bull among the Asuras— their calf,
milked the milk of wine-liquor into an iron vessel;
the Gandharvas and Apsarases milked the milk [of celestial beauty] into a lotus-made vessel.

Having made Viśvāvasu, the celestial musician, the calf, they milked the honey of auspiciousness from the Gāndharva cow. With him as the calf, the highly fortunate ancestral deities of the Śrāddha ceremony, through their faith, milked the Kavya essence— the milk— into an unbaked earthen vessel.
The perfected ones (siddhas) fashioned Kapila as their calf; those such as the Vidyādharas and others produced their supernatural powers (siddhi) and knowledge in the sky through mere volition;
and other masters of illusion (māyin) created their illusory power (māyā), characterized by invisibility and wonders.
Having fashioned me as their calf,
the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas who feed on flesh milked from me the milk of their meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).
The lords of the Bhūtas, using me as their calf, milked the wine of blood into a skull-bowl.
Likewise, the biting serpents, snakes,
and *nāgas* made Takṣaka their calf and milked poison as their milk into the vessel of a cave;
and the beasts, making a bull their calf, milked grass as their milk.
In the forest, they milked the wild beasts with the lion as the vessel;
and the carnivorous creatures milked their own flesh from their own bodies.
With the eagle as the calf, they milked the birds, as well as all that is moving and unmoving.
The trees, with the banyan tree as their calf, produced milk consisting of various essences; the mountains, with the Himalayas as their calf, produced various minerals upon their own ridges.
All of them, each with its own principal calf, separately poured milk into their respective vessels.

They milked the earth, which had been made ready by Pṛthu and which yields all desires. Thus, O best of the Kurus, those beginning with Pṛthu— being consumers of food— milked the earth for their own food, producing different kinds of milk through the distinctions of the milking vessels, calves, and so forth.
Then King Pṛthu, the lord of the earth, being pleased and affectionate toward his daughter, out of love accepted her as his own daughter— she who was the cow that milks all desires.
The king of kings, crushing the mountain peaks with the tip of his bow, [proceeded].
The powerful Vainya generally made this circle of the earth level. Then, in this world, the blessed Vainya, the father and provider of livelihood for his subjects,
established dwellings here and there as was appropriate.
Villages, cities, towns, and various types of fortresses; cowherd settlements, cattle pens, military camps, mines, and market towns—
before the time of Pṛthu, such arrangements of cities and villages did not exist here at all.
They dwelt here and there at their ease, free from fear from any quarter.
Maitreya said:
Then the king consecrated himself for a hundred horse sacrifices.
In Brahmāvarta, the field of Manu, where the Sarasvatī flows toward the east,
the Lord Śatakratu (Indra), considering his own superior ritual merit,
could not endure the great sacrificial festival of Pṛthu.
There, the Lord Hari himself— the Sovereign,
the Soul of all, the Teacher of all worlds, and the Master— was experienced as the presiding lord of the sacrifice,
accompanied by Brahmā and Śiva, as well as the world-protectors along with their followers.
He was being celebrated in song by Gandharvas, sages, and throngs of Apsarases;
and by Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Daityas, Dānavas, Guhyakas, and others,
as well as the foremost attendants of Hari, headed by Sunanda and Nanda.
Kapila, Nārada, Datta, the masters of yoga such as Sanaka and others,
and those devotees eager for his service followed him; there,
the earth was a cow of plenty that yielded righteousness and fulfilled all desires.
O descendant of Bharata, she milked for the sacrificer all his desired objects; the rivers carried all kinds of juices— milk, curds, rice, and cow-products—
and the trees of massive stature produced honey as they blossomed.
The rivers brought heaps of jewels, the mountains four kinds of food, and all the worlds, together with their guardians, presented these as offerings;
such was the supreme prosperity of Pṛthu, the Lord Adhokṣaja.
Becoming envious, the lord Indra sought to obstruct the sacrifice;
while the son of Vena was performing his final horse-sacrifice for the Lord of the Yajus, Indra,
competing with him, carried away the sacrificial animal while remaining invisible.
The venerable Atri beheld him hurrying through the sky,
appearing like a heretic who has mistaken unrighteousness for dharma.
Urged by Atri, the great chariot-warrior, the son of Pṛthu, set out to slay him.
Enraged, he pursued him, crying out, "Stay! Stay!
Seeing him with such a form—matted-haired and covered in ashes—he considered him to be Dharma incarnate and did not discharge an arrow at him.
When he had desisted from the slaughter, Atri urged him once more to kill:
"O dear son, slay Mahendra, the lowest of the gods, who destroys the sacrifice. Thus addressed by the son of Vainya, he [Naraka] rushed through the sky with great speed.

Enraged, he pursued him like the king of vultures pursuing Rāvaṇa. Abandoning that horse-form and his own body, the self-ruling lord vanished from there; the hero, taking back his animal, returned to his father’s sacrifice.
O Lord, having witnessed that wonderful deed of his, the supreme sages gave him the name Vijitāśva. Then Hari, having unleashed a thick darkness, carried off the horse once again.
Concealed by the sacrificial post and its top-ring,
the omnipresent Lord Atri revealed himself as he hurried through the sky;
though the hero [Śiva] carried a skull and a skull-topped staff, he did not harm him.

Urged by Atri, he angrily aimed an arrow at him; the self-ruling king, abandoning both his horse and his form, stood there invisible. Then the hero, taking the horse, proceeded to the sacrifice for the ancestors.
Those of weak understanding took up that contemptible form of Hari.
Whatever forms Indra assumed out of a desire to seize the horse, those were fragments of sin; here, a "fragment" (khaṇḍa) is said to mean a "mark" (liṅga).

While Indra was thus carrying off the horse with the intent to destroy the sacrifice of Vainya, the minds of men became fixed upon heretics— those clad in nakedness, red robes, and so forth— who had been released after being seized by him, regarding their false doctrines as true dharma.
Generally, people become attached through delusion to those who are charming and eloquent. Perceiving this, the Lord Pṛthu, of vast prowess,
became enraged with Indra and took up an arrow as his bow was raised.
Seeing him intent on the slaughter of Śakra—himself difficult to behold and possessed of unbearable speed—the priests restrained him, saying:
"O high-minded one, it is not fitting here to kill another who has been impelled [by fate].
We shall summon Indra here, the destroyer of your purpose, whose splendor has been eclipsed by your own fame."
"O King, with our offerings that have not lost their potency, we shall forcibly sacrifice your ill-fortune immediately thereafter.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Sacrifice with wrath, Vidura and the other priests were about to offer oblations when the Self-born Brahmā approached and forbade them.
"Indra is not to be slain by you, for he is the sacrifice, the very body of the Lord.
You seek to kill him with a sacrifice, yet he is the one whose bodies the gods worship. O twice-born ones, behold this great transgression of dharma!"

This act was performed by Indra, desiring to destroy King Pṛthu of far-reaching fame; at that time, he had already completed ninety-nine sacrifices. "Enough of your well-performed sacrifices, since you are a knower of the dharma of liberation."
"You ought not to harbor anger toward either yourself or Mahendra;
indeed, may you be blessed, for both are the very embodiments of the One of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka). O Great King, do not entertain such anxiety; listen with a respectful mind to our words."
When one who meditates is struck by fate, his mind becomes excessively agitated and enters into blinding darkness; this sacrifice,
which is difficult to restrain among the gods,
is a transgression of dharma wherein there are heretics created by Indra.
Behold this people being carried away by these alluring heretics who are instigated by Indra; you, who are the destroyer of those who steal the sacrificial horse,
have descended here to protect the dharma of humanity according to the requirements of the age.

O son of Vena, by his transgression, that [power] has been snatched away today from his body; you are a portion of Viṣṇu, O Vainya. Therefore, having reflected upon the nature of this lord of creatures, fulfill the intention of the world-creators.
And destroy, O Lord, the illusion of Indra—the mother of false dharma—which leads the path of fierce heresy.
Maitreya said:
Thus instructed by the Teacher of the World, the lord of the people (Yayāti) acted accordingly and established a bond of affection even with Maghavan (Indra).
To Pṛthu, who had performed the purificatory ablution after his many great deeds,
those givers of boons who had been gratified at that sacrificial altar granted their boons;
for the brāhmaṇas, having received their sacrificial fees with faith, were satisfied and their blessings were fulfilled.
O steward,

having been honored by you, O mighty-armed one, all those invited— fathers, gods, sages, and men— have assembled and offered their blessings to the first king, who was duly honored with gifts and respect.
Maitreya said:
The all-pervading Lord Vaikuṇṭha,
the master of sacrifice and enjoyer of the sacrifice, being pleased by the sacrifices along with Indra, addressed him.
The Blessed Lord said:
"He has indeed brought about the failure of your hundred horse-sacrifices;
you ought to forgive him, for he is seeking your forgiveness."
O King, the wise and virtuous in this world are the best of men;
they do not harbor malice toward living beings because they do not identify the self with the body.
If even persons such as you are deluded by the illusory power of the Divine, how much more so are others?
Through long service to the elders, he has attained nothing but supreme weariness;
therefore, knowing this body to have been begun by ignorance, desire, and karma,
the awakened man does not become attached to it.
Unattached to this body produced by that [Supreme Being], and likewise to the home,
offspring, or wealth, what wise man would harbor a sense of "mine-ness"?
He is solitary, pure, self-luminous, devoid of qualities, yet the substratum of the qualities.

The Self is all-pervading, unobstructed, the witness, devoid of ego, and the supreme over the individual soul. That person who knows the Self as it truly is—abiding within the self—is not tainted by the qualities of material nature even while situated therein; such a one is established in Me.
O King, the mind of one who constantly worships Me through their own prescribed duty, endowed with faith and free from desire, gradually becomes serene;
such a person has completely renounced the modes of nature, possesses perfect vision, and has a pure heart.

He who knows this Self— which is peaceful, established in equanimity, indifferent like a supervisor over the substances, cognitions, and activities of the self, and which is immutable— attains the auspicious state of absolute Brahman.
The flow of the qualities (guṇas) belonging to the divided subtle body—which consists of substance, action, agency, and consciousness—continues;
yet the wise, having bound their affection to Me, do not undergo transformation when faced with prosperity or adversity.
They remain equanimous toward the highest, middling, and lowest, and are equal in pleasure and pain, with their senses and inner mind conquered.
O Hero, accompanied by all the worlds prepared for you, perform the protection of the entire world;

for the protection of subjects is the very welfare of a king, since he takes a sixth part of their merit in the afterlife. Otherwise, failing to protect his subjects while collecting taxes, he consumes their sin and has his own merit taken away.

"Thus, with the approval of the foremost of the twice-born, you shall follow the preeminent dharma; as one devoted to her, you will, in a short time, behold the perfected ones (siddhas) who have come to your home, for you are beloved by the world. And choose some boon from me, O lord of men, for I am constrained by your virtues and character."
"I am not easily attained through sacrifices, nor indeed through austerities or yoga, as I abide with an even mind.
Maitreya said:
Thus addressed by Viṣvaksena, the teacher of the world, he who conquers the universe—
Having been thus instructed, he accepted the command of Hari with his head;
as Indra touched his feet out of love, feeling ashamed of his own deed,
he embraced the performer of a hundred sacrifices and cast away all enmity.
Then the Blessed Lord, the Soul of the Universe, having been offered worship by Pṛthu,
and having had his lotus feet grasped with rising devotion,
though intent on departing, delayed out of grace for him.
