Beholding him, the lotus-petal-eyed one—the friend of the virtuous—did not proceed further. That first king, with palms joined in reverence, was unable to look upon Hari;
his eyes filled with tears, he said nothing at all, and overwhelmed by weeping, he stood there holding Him close to his heart.

Then, wiping away his teardrops and gazing with eyes that could not sate their sight upon the Supreme Person, who was touching the earth with his foot while resting the tips of his hands upon the high shoulder of the enemy of serpents, Pṛthu said: Pṛthu said:
O All-pervading Lord, O Sovereign Giver of boons, how could a wise man choose from you the gifts of those whose nature is subject to the transformations of the *guṇas*?
O Lord, Master of liberation, I do not choose even those boons which are available even to embodied beings dwelling in hell.
O Protector, I do not desire even that place where the nectar of your lotus feet is not found.
"O Supreme One, let that which has issued from the mouth of the Great Soul within my heart enter my ten thousand ears; this is my boon.

O Lord of Excellent Renown, the breeze carrying the drops of nectar from Your lotus feet—which issues from the mouths of the Great Ones—bestows memory upon us, the wretched yogis who have forgotten the path of reality; it is enough with boons other than this."

If one hears even once by chance Your auspicious fame, which is so pleasant to hear when encountered in the company of noble souls, how could a knower of virtues cease from it—unless he were a beast? For even Śrī, desiring to gather all virtues, chose You as her own.
Therefore, O Supreme Person among all beings, I worship You with longing, like Lakṣmī with her lotus hand, for You are the abode of all virtues.

"O Lord of the Universe, even though we two strive for the same husband and are solely intent on Your feet, there may still arise a quarrel between us. Yet, O Mother of the World, a calamity would surely occur for the world if our desired action were to take place.
O You who are compassionate toward the wretched, You make even a trivial thing great; what need have You for that [wife], when You delight in Your own abode?"
Therefore, the virtuous worship You alone, from whom the arising of the delusions of the modes of nature has been cast away.
O Blessed One, we know of no other cause for the existence of the saintly than the constant remembrance of Your feet.
I consider Your speech—which bewilders the worlds—to be a delusion, since You say to one who worships You, "Choose a boon."

If people are bound by the cord of Your speech, how then, being deluded, do they perform further action? O Lord, alas, people are shattered by Your māyā, for the ignorant one desires that which is other than the Truth.
Just as a father himself acts for the benefit of his child, so indeed should You act for our welfare.
Maitreya said:
Thus praised by the primordial king, the All-seeing Lord said to him, "O King, let there be devotion unto Me;
by good fortune, such an intellect has been formed in you, by which one overcomes My illusory power that is so difficult to abandon."
"Therefore, O Lord of Creatures, carry out what I have commanded with vigilance;
for the world that obeys my command attains prosperity everywhere.
Maitreya said:
Having thus responded to the meaningful words of the royal sage Vainya,
Acyuta, being honored by him and having shown him favor, made up his mind to depart.
[The assembly included] the celestial sages, ancestors, gandharvas, siddhas, cāraṇas, and pannagas.

The *kinnaras*, *apsarases*, mortals, birds, and numerous other beings were honored by the king with words, gifts, joined palms, and devotion as if they were the Lord of Sacrifice himself; thereafter,
they all departed, following after Vaikuṇṭha.
The Lord Acyuta, as if stealing away the mind of the royal sage and his preceptor, returned to His own abode;
the king, having offered obeisances to the Unseen who had revealed Himself, [proceeded].
And having offered worship to the Unmanifest, the god of gods, he went to his own city.
Maitreya said:
With pearl ornaments, garlands of flowers, fine silken garments, and golden archways...
It was adorned here and there with most fragrant incenses, and its streets, squares, and pathways were moistened with sandalwood and aloe-wood water;
it was further honored with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, fruits, sprouts, parched grain, and radiant lights.
It was adorned with clusters of plantain trunks and young betel-nut trees,
and decorated on all sides with garlands of tree sprouts;
the subjects honored it with lamps and offerings, gathering every auspicious item.
Accompanied by beautifully adorned maidens wearing polished earrings,
and amidst the sounding of conchs and kettledrums and the chanting of the Vedas by the officiating priests,
the hero— free from pride and being praised— entered the palace.
Honored by them here and there, the one of great fame, being pleased and bestowing desired boons upon those citizens and country-folk,
performed such deeds; for he was a Great One, the Greatest of all, whose conduct was irreproachable.
While ruling the circle of the earth, he established widespread fame and ascended to the supreme abode.
Sūta said:
That expanded glory of the first king was honored by all virtuous men for its manifold qualities.
The highly devoted Vidura, the steward, honoring him as he spoke, addressed Kauṣāravi, the lord of the assembly.
Vidura said:
"O brāhmaṇas, having been consecrated by the sages, Pṛthu received all the worship due to the gods."

Bearing the splendor of Viṣṇu in his arms, with which he milked the earth-cow— who indeed, being wise, would not hear of his glory, since all kings even today live at their will upon the remnants of his prowess? Tell me that pure deed of his.
Maitreya said:
Dwell­ing between the two rivers, the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
he experienced only those enjoyments already begun, with the desire to exhaust his merit.
His commands were never thwarted anywhere as he held the single scepter over the seven continents,
except toward the families of the brāhmaṇas and except for those of the lineage of Acyuta.
Once, there was a great sacrificial initiation (dīkṣā) for the gods.
O best of beings, there was an assembly of both Brahman-sages and royal sages. When all those worthy guests had been honored according to their merit,
he rose from the midst of the assembly like the moon, the lord of stars, rising among the constellations.
Tall and broad-shouldered, with long, muscular arms, he was fair-complexioned with eyes as red as lotuses;

he had a fine nose and a beautiful face, was gentle, with broad shoulders, a radiant smile, and excellent teeth; his chest was wide, his hips were large, and his belly was beautiful with folds like the petals of a lotus.
With a navel like a whirlpool, powerful, with golden thighs and prominent feet,
with fine, curly, dark, and glossy hair, and a neck marked by three lines like a conch shell;
having put on two costly, finest silk garments as lower and upper wraps.
With the beauty of his entire body revealed, having set aside his ornaments for the sake of the vow,
wearing a black antelope skin, glorious, with *kuśa* grass in hand and properly prepared,
he gazed all around with eyes as cool and moist as stars.
The lord of the earth spoke these words, as if gladdening the assembly—
a speech that was beautiful, with varied and refined words, smooth, polished, profound,
and composed— as if repeating it for the benefit of everyone present.
The King said:
"O members of the assembly, may it be well with you; listen, O virtuous ones who have come here.
Those who desire to know the dharma should declare their own intended purpose before the wise."

"I am the king who wields the rod of punishment, appointed here for the sake of the subjects; I am their protector, the provider of their livelihood, and the establisher of each in their respective boundaries.
From the performance of those duties of mine, [the results] are what the exponents of the Veda call..."

The worlds, which are the fulfillment of all desires, belong to him whose eye of destiny is satisfied. But that king who raises his hand [to punish] without instructing the subjects in their duties eats the impurity of the people and abandons his own fortune.

O blameless ones, O ancestors, gods, and sages, you who are free from envy, perform that [sacrifice] for the sake of your progenitor’s funeral cake and for your own benefit, with your minds fixed on Adhokṣaja; by doing so, you will have shown me favor, and you should approve of it.
The fruit of an action after death is equal for the performer, the instructor, and the one who permits it.
O best of the worthy, there is a master of sacrifice by that name;
for some, lands as bright as moonlight are seen here and in the hereafter.
[This was told] concerning Manu, Uttānapāda, Dhruva the lord of the earth,
the royal sage Priyavrata, Aṅga— the father of our father—
and likewise concerning others such as Ajātaśatru and Bhava.
The wielder of the mace has a task for both Prahlāda and Bali;
apart from his grandsons and others who are pitiable and deluded regarding dharma by death,
[he acts] because they are generally the sole cause for attaining the goals of the four aims of life, heaven, and liberation.
The longing for service at His feet instantly destroys the impurity of the intellect accumulated over countless births; this desire, increasing day by day, is like the river flowing from His big toe.
A person whose mental impurities have been entirely shaken off becomes empowered by the extraordinary potency of unattached discernment.
He who has made his abode at the soles of His feet does not again enter the cycle of worldly existence, which brings only suffering;
therefore, you should worship Him alone with your own natural dispositions, through the qualities of mind, speech, and body, and by your own prescribed duties—
being free from deceit— toward His lotus feet that grant all desires, until you have achieved the perfection of your goals according to your respective qualifications.
This sacrifice here, though inherently devoid of qualities, possesses manifold attributes through various substances, qualities, actions, and verbal expressions;
it is accomplished by means of purposes, intentions, signs, and names, yet in its essential nature, it is a mass of pure consciousness.
Having assumed a body through the collection of the principles of primary matter (*pradhāna*), time, intention, and merit, this [sacrifice] attains sentience.

The omnipresent Lord is perceived as the fruit of ritual action, just as fire, which is of the nature of the qualities of wood, is manifested within pieces of wood. Ah! These people of mine on the surface of the earth, firm in their vows, worship Hari—the Guru and Supreme Lord of those who enjoy the sacrifices—by means of the yoga of their own duty, and thus they bestow grace upon me.

May you never arise through fiery power, great supernatural opulences, forbearance, austerity, or learning— though you yourself were born from a royal lineage into the family of the unconquerable gods, who shine brilliantly among the twice-born,
O Lord of Brahmanas, by whose constant salutation of his feet the ancient Person, Hari, is pleased.
The leader of the greatest souls attained imperishable fortune and fame that purifies the world;

for by serving him, the Lord—who dwells within the hearts of all, who is self-sovereign, dear to the brāhmaṇas, and the master—becomes fully satisfied. Therefore, let the community of brāhmaṇas be served with one's whole being by those who are humble and devoted to their duties.
A person may attain, without excess, the ultimate tranquility of the self from the self as it becomes gracious;
for what greater mouth could there be for the fire-eaters (gods) than that which is served by constant association with Him?
Indeed, Ananta eats that which is offered with faith into His mouth by those learned in the truth, under the names of the sacrificial deities.
Indeed, even when the sacrificial fire has been cast outside by means of conscious effort, those who have reached the ultimate goal of the paramahaṃsas do not perceive it in that way;

rather, through faith, austerity, auspiciousness, silence, self-restraint, and meditative absorption, they sustain that eternal, stainless, and primeval Brahman for the sake of perceiving the ultimate reality,
in which this world appears as if in a mirror.
May my noble mother bear upon her crown for the duration of her life the dust from the lotus feet of those [sages],

by constantly wearing which sin is swiftly destroyed and all virtues attend one. Prosperities embrace him who is a repository of virtues, whose wealth is his character, who is grateful, and who takes refuge with the elders.
"May the community of Brahmins, the cows, and Janārdana along with his followers be gracious toward me.
Maitreya said:
To the king who was speaking thus, the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born [responded].
The virtuous, with delighted minds, praised him with cries of "Excellent!
Excellent!", for the Vedic revelation is true: "Through a son, one conquers the worlds.
Indeed, the sinful Vena, though struck down by the staff of the Brahmanas, has transcended the darkness.
And Hiraṇyakaśipu, O Blessed One, who was about to enter into darkness due to his blasphemy of the Lord,
escaped it through the power of his son Prahlāda.
O best of heroes, O father of the earth, may you live for eternal years!
He who possesses such devotion to Acyuta, the sole sustainer of all the worlds—
oh, we indeed have today found Mukunda as our protector through you alone, O one of pure fame,
for you reveal the stories of Viṣṇu, the god most supreme in renown and the deity devoted to the Brahmanas.
"O Lord, this instruction for our livelihood is not at all surprising;
for affection toward one's subjects is the natural disposition of great souls who are compassionate by nature.
O Master, today you have brought us to the further shore of darkness."

Salutations to the Great Person of increased goodness, who, having entered the priestly and warrior classes, sustains this world by his own splendor for those wandering with lost vision due to their actions known as destiny.
Maitreya said:
While the people were thus praising Pṛthu of vast prowess,
four sages, radiant as the sun, arrived there.
The king, along with his followers, beheld those lords of perfected beings as they descended from the sky, making the worlds sinless by their radiance; observing them,
he rose up as if desiring to reclaim his own life-breaths that had departed at the sight of them.

Accompanied by his assembly and followers, Vainya— the lord of the senses— like one restrained by the qualities (guṇas) out of respect, being a member of the assembly, bowed with his neck inclined in humility and duly honored those who had accepted the guest-offerings and seats.
Having his hair-knot cleansed by the water used for washing the feet of those [sages],
he conducted himself there with the conduct of the virtuous, as if honoring them while they sat upon golden seats like fires in their own hearths.
Endowed with faith and self-restraint, and being pleased, Pṛthu spoke to the elder brothers of Bhava:
Pṛthu said:
"O you who are the refuge of all auspicious things, what auspicious deed have I performed?"
For one who has obtained the sight of you— who are difficult even for yogis to behold—
what in this world or the next could possibly be more difficult to attain?
For him, O brahmins, Śiva and Viṣṇu along with their followers are well-pleased.

The world does not even perceive those who wander through the worlds, just as all beings do not perceive the Self, the seer of all, who is the cause of them. Even those householders who possess no wealth are truly fortunate and virtuous.
For those houses where the water, grass, ground, masters,

and servants are all worthy of honor are like trees that are the abodes of serpents; yet in those houses where the water from the feet of the Lord whose feet are the source of all holy places is absent, all prosperity remains unfulfilled.
"Welcome to you, O best of the twice-born! You wise ones, though appearing as children yet being mature, perform your vows with faith while desiring liberation.
O protectors, is all well with us who are seekers of the objects of the senses?"
In this world, which is a vessel of calamities for those fallen by their own past actions,
inquiries regarding well-being are not appropriate toward you who delight in the Self; for in you,
there exist no mental fluctuations concerning what is auspicious or inauspicious.

Therefore, having gained confidence in you, my ascetic friends, I ask you: by what means may there be security in this worldly existence? It is evident that the Blessed Lord, the creator of the self, is the very Self of those who possess self-mastery.
The unborn Lord wanders in this world in the form of a perfected being (siddha) for the sake of favoring His own people.
Maitreya said:
Having heard that well-spoken, essential, and sweet discourse of Pṛthu, [the King was satisfied].
Smiling as it were with affection, the youth replied.
Sanat-kumāra said:
"Well asked, O Great King, by you whose soul is devoted to the welfare of all beings."
Even for you, who are wise, the minds of the saintly are such as this;
indeed, the company of the saintly is approved by both parties,
since conversation and inquiry with them bestow peace upon all.

O King, there certainly exists for you a devotion to the chanting of the qualities of the lotus feet of the Enemy of Madhu; that devotion, when perfected, shakes off the impurity of the inner self consisting of desire and passion. This alone is the well-ascertained cause of the ultimate welfare of men, when properly reflected upon within the scriptures.

That firm attachment to the Self— which is distinct from the non-self— and to the Brahman devoid of qualities, arises through faith, the practice of the Lord’s dharma, inquiry, steadfastness in spiritual yoga,
worship of the Lord of Yoga, and by constantly hearing the meritorious narrations of the holy ones.

By not thirsting for the company of those who delight in wealth and the objects of the senses, by not accepting those things approved by them, by finding delight in solitude, and by contentment within oneself even without drinking the nectar of Hari’s qualities;
by non-violence, by the conduct of a paramahaṃsa, and by the remembrance of the supreme wine of Mukunda’s deeds.
Through restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*) free from desire, through freedom from blame, through lack of worldly activity, and through endurance of the pairs of opposites;

and through devotion— which repeatedly expands by chanting the qualities of Hari, who is the ornament of the ears of those devoted to Him— one becomes unattached to the unreal self consisting of the existent and non-existent, and attains immediate delight in the qualityless Brahman.

When a person who possesses a teacher develops ultimate devotion to Brahman, he burns away the heart— the sheath of the individual soul composed of the five elements— by the force of knowledge and detachment, just as fire rising from its source consumes its own weak fuel.
With his latent desires burnt away and all those qualities liberated, he no longer perceives anything external or internal to the Self.
The separation between the Supreme Self and the individual self that existed previously— just as a man [sees objects] in a dream— is destroyed when that [ignorance] perishes; then,
while the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) remains real, the person perceives both the self and the objects of the senses as the Supreme, but not otherwise.
When there is a cause, even in water and other such things,
a person perceives the distinction between himself and another, but not otherwise. The minds of those who meditate are distracted by the senses drawn toward their objects.
As water from a lake is drawn up by a pillar, it carries away the consciousness of the intellect;

when memory is lost, the mind falls away, and the loss of knowledge follows the destruction of memory. The wise declare that the obstruction of this [consciousness] is the self-effacement of the Self.

There is no greater transgression of a man's own self-interest in this world than that by which he regards the welfare of another as more dear than his own; for such a transgression results in the neglect of one's own purpose,
the obsession with the objects of the senses, and the total loss of all true goals for human beings.

One who desires to cross over intense darkness should never form an association with that by which one is fallen from knowledge and realization and enters into the state of being a mere material being (mukhyatā),
for it is the absolute destroyer of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Even there, liberation alone is desired as the ultimate goal,
because the objects of the three aims of life are eternally accompanied by the fear of death. And whatever states exist, whether superior or inferior, follow from the interplay of the *guṇas*.
O Lord, there is no security for those whose blessings have been destroyed by You;
therefore, O King, [grant it] to those among the moving and stationary beings of the worlds who are enveloped by the body, senses, vital breaths, intellect, and false ego.
Know that I am He, the Blessed Lord, who, as the Knower of the Field, shines forth within the heart as the All-pervading One,
appearing inwardly as the Self of both the existent and the non-existent in this world.

I take refuge in Him whose true nature is eternally liberated, pure, and stainless, who has cast off the impurity of karma and material nature, and in whom the delusion of Maya is dispelled by discernment— like the perception of a snake in a garland.
By devotion to the playful grace of the petals of whose lotus feet the virtuous untie the tightly knotted accumulation of karma— even so, those ascetics of empty intellect remain bound.
O you who move within the currents of worldly existence, resort to that Vāsudeva, the refuge-free one; for those without a boat, this great ocean of worldly life is difficult to cross,
as it is infested with the crocodiles of the six internal enemies.
Therefore, making the worshipful feet of the Blessed Lord Hari your boat,
cross over the ocean of calamities that is difficult to traverse.
Maitreya said:
Having thus had the path of the Self revealed by the son of Brahmā, the prince Kumāra, who possessed self-knowledge, the king, having duly praised him, spoke to him. The king said:

"O Brahmin, a favor was previously granted to me by Hari, who is compassionate toward those in distress; it was to bring that about, O Blessed One, that you have all come here. And it has been fully accomplished by your compassionate selves."
"Indeed, everything that remains from the meal of the saintly, along with my very self— O Brahmin, my life-breaths, my wife, my sons, my home with all its furnishings,
my kingdom, my army, my land, and my treasury— all this has been offered to you."
One who is learned in the Vedic scriptures is worthy of the command of armies, sovereignty, the leadership of punishment, and even lordship over all the worlds;
for the Brāhmaṇa eats his own, wears his own, and gives away his own.
By His very grace, the Kṣatriyas and others eat their food—
those by whom such a state of the Blessed One has been exclusively expounded to us through the scriptures on the nature of the Self.
"May those of abundant compassion always be satisfied by their own deeds;
for who indeed can repay that which makes one an object of their grace?
Maitreya said:
Those masters of self-discipline, honored by the first king, remained in the sky while men looked on, praising his character;
for Vainya was the foremost among the great through his instruction in spiritual realization and his steadfastness.
Established within the Self, he regarded himself as one whose desires were fulfilled;
and he performed his duties according to the time, the place, his strength, his fitness, and his wealth, dedicating them entirely to Brahman.
Having surrendered the fruit of his actions to Brahman, free from attachment and composed in mind,
and regarding himself as the presiding witness over action and as transcendent to material nature—
even while dwelling in his home, he was endowed with the splendor of imperial sovereignty.
Free from the notion of "I," he did not become attached to the objects of the senses, like the sun;
thus, performing his duties through the yoga of the inner self,
he begot sons equal to himself upon Pañcārcis.

Alone, Pṛthu, whose self is Acyuta, assumed at their respective times the qualities of all the world-protectors— Vijitāśva, Dhūmrakeśa, Haryakṣa, Draviṇa, and Vṛka— for the protection of the creation of the world.
Delighting the subjects with his gentle mental and vocal activities and virtuous qualities,
he assumed the title "King," like another Soma-rāja;
like the sun, he distributed and collected the wealth of the earth while shining upon it.
Ineffable in his splendor like fire, as invincible as Mahendra,
he was like the earth in forbearance and like the heavens in granting the desires of men; he rained down blessings according to their wishes, satisfying them like a rain-cloud.
He was as difficult to fathom as the ocean; like the king of mountains in his steadfastness;
like the King of Dharma in his instruction; like the Himalayas in his wondrous nature;
like Kubera in the abundance of his treasury; and like Varuṇa in the secrecy of his purpose.
Like Mātariśvan (the Wind-god), the Lord is the Self of all by virtue of His strength, majesty, and splendor;
like the King of Beasts, He is invincible.
Like Kandarpa (the God of Love), He is peerless in beauty, and like the King of Deer, He is wise.
In affection toward his children, he is like Manu among men; in sovereignty, he is the unborn Lord;
in the discourse on sacred knowledge, he is Bṛhaspati; and in self-mastery, he is Hari himself—[all these qualities being found] in devotion toward cows, gurus, and brāhmaṇas who follow Viṣvaksena.

Through modesty, humility, and virtuous character, Rāma entered the ear-cavities of women here and there throughout the three worlds— just as he had entered the hearts of the virtuous— by means of his fame, which was sung upward by men who were equal to him in their efforts.
Maitreya said:
Once, having seen that he was advanced in years, the self-possessed Vainya,
the lord of creatures, whose entire creation had been increased by himself, [reflected].
The sustainer of the world and all that is stationary, the upholder of dharma for the virtuous, he whose purpose for being born here had been accomplished by the command of the Lord,
entrusted his daughter to his sons as she seemed to weep from the pain of separation.
When his subjects were disheartened, he, accompanied by his wife, went alone to the forest of asceticism.
There, adhering to inviolable vows in accordance with the well-esteemed rules of the Vaikhānasas,
he undertook fierce austerities just as he had previously done for the sake of his own victory.

For some time he subsisted on bulbs, roots, and fruits; at other times he ate only dried leaves; for several fortnights he lived on water, and after that, he subsisted on air alone. In the summer the hero practiced the austerity of the five fires, and during the rains, the sage endured the downpour.
Submerged up to his neck in cold water, sleeping on the bare ground,
patient, restrained in speech, self-controlled, with vital energy drawn upward and his breath conquered,
he performed supreme austerity, desiring to worship Kṛṣṇa.
By that [practice] perfected in due order, the impurity of his latent tendencies and karma was destroyed;
with the sixfold group of vices restrained through breath-control, his bonds were severed.
Then the venerable Sanat-kumāra spoke that supreme spiritual truth.
By that very yoga, that bull among men worshipped the Supreme Person. For that virtuous man, who followed the path of the Lord and always strove with faith,
devotion toward the Brahman-like Lord became focused on no other object.

Through this [practice], his soul was purified by the service of the Blessed One; and by means of the sequential recollection of Him, there arose in him a knowledge accompanied by detachment, by which [knowledge] he became sharpened.

He cut through the sheath of his own individual soul, which was the locus of doubt; with his intellect severed from other objects and having attained the realization of the Self, he became free from desire.
By that same wisdom, he abandoned and cut asunder this world.
A disciplined ascetic remains vigilant through the paths of yoga only so long as he does not take delight in the narrations of the elder brother of Gada (Kṛṣṇa).
Thus, that foremost of heroes, having united his self with the Self, [attained liberation].
Having become firmly established in Brahman, at the appointed time he cast off his body:
pressing his anus with his heels, he gradually drew up the vital air (vāyu),
fixing it in the navel, the abdominal cavities, the heart, the chest, the throat, and the head.
Raising that [life-force] to his head and gradually withdrawing it, he— free from desire—

dissolved the wind into the wind, the body into the earth, and the fire into the fire; he dissolved the sense-organs into space and the liquid elements into water, each according to its place and in due order.

Having withdrawn the earth into water, that [water] into fire, that [fire] into air, and that [air] into ether; then having withdrawn the ether into the senses, the senses into the mind, those [senses and mind] into their respective subtle elements (tanmātras), and those [subtle elements] into the source of the elements (bhūtādi); he then merged them into the Great Self (mahat).

He deposited that arrangement of all qualities within the individual soul (jīva), which is composed of Māyā; and that person, the Lord who possesses latent tendencies, remained with those tendencies situated within himself,
yet by means of his various powers of detachment and vigor, he remained established in his own essential nature and cast them off.
The great queen named Arci, his wife, followed him into the forest; she was exceedingly delicate and undeserving of such a fate, for even the touch of her feet caused pain to the earth.
She remained devoted to her husband through her firm adherence to vows and dharma, and by her service that sustained the body of the sage.
Though she was emaciated by her ordeal, she found no distress, for she was filled with the bliss of the touch and honor of her beloved;

observing that her body’s consciousness and all its functions had failed, and seeing the corpse of her husband— the beloved of the Earth and of herself— she lamented briefly and then placed it upon a funeral pyre on a mountain ridge.
Having performed her duties and bathed in the waters of the river, she offered water for the funeral libations of her husband of noble deeds;
then, having bowed to the gods stationed in heaven and circumambulated them three times, she entered the fire while meditating on her husband’s feet.
Seeing that the virtuous woman had followed after Pṛthu, the best of heroes and her husband, [the people were struck with wonder].
The thousands of divine consorts, the bestowers of boons, along with the gods, offered praise upon that ridge of Mount Mandara as they showered down a rain of flowers;
while the celestial trumpets resounded, they spoke to one another.
The goddesses said:
"Oh, blessed is this bride who,
like the goddess Śrī, has with her whole being served as a wife the Lord of Sacrifice, the husband of the rulers of the earth!"
Surely this virtuous woman is now ascending after her husband, the son of Vena; look, she passes us by on a radiant path through her inconceivable deeds.
For what else is difficult for mortals to attain than the state of the Blessed Lord?
Those on earth whose lives are fickle who nevertheless strive for liberation from action—
alas, they are deceived and are betrayers of their own selves; having obtained a human birth that leads to final liberation, they become attached to sense objects with great difficulty on this earth.

Maitreya said: While the celestial women were thus offering praise, the bride went to the world of her husband— that destination which Vainya, the foremost among the knowers of the Self and a refuge of Acyuta, attained.

Such was the power of that most venerable Pṛthu; his exploits, which were of transcendent character, have been narrated to you. Whoever should read this most meritorious account with faith and concentration—
Whoever causes this to be heard or listens to it shall follow the path of Pṛthu.
A brāhmaṇa who recites it becomes endowed with spiritual luster; a kṣatriya becomes a lord of the earth;
a vaiśya becomes a master of merchants; and a śūdra attains the state of being most virtuous.
Having heard this three times, whether a man or a woman, even one who is untruthful, becomes most blessed with offspring if childless, most wealthy if destitute,
and if his fame is obscure, he becomes highly renowned; and if he is a fool, he becomes a scholar.
This [narrative] is a blessing for men, warding off inauspiciousness;
it bestows wealth, fame, long life, and heaven, and removes the impurities of the Kali age.
It should be heard by those who desire the complete attainment of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.

This supreme cause of the four [goals of life] should be proclaimed with faith. Having heard this, a king setting out for victory approaches those whom other kings first pay tribute to him, just as they did to Pṛthu.
Free from attachment to other things and bearing pure devotion for the Blessed Lord,
one should hear, cause others to hear, or recite this meritorious account of the son of Vena, as told by the son of Vicitravīrya, which reveals his great majesty.
By performing this most superhuman act in this world, one shall attain the earthly destination of Pṛthu;
and by listening daily with reverence to this account of Pṛthu’s deeds and spreading it about, that man— freed from attachment—
attains profound devotion for the Blessed One, whose feet are the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
Maitreya said:
Vijitāśva, the son of Pṛthu, was a sovereign king of great renown;
being affectionate toward his brothers, he gave the quarters of the earth to his younger brothers.
The Lord assigned the eastern quarter to Haryakṣa, the southern to Dhūmrakeśa,
the western to the one named Vṛka, and the fourth to Draviṇas. Having obtained the power of invisibility from Śakra, he became known as Antardhāna.
He begot three highly esteemed sons upon Śikhaṇḍinī:
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci— these who were formerly the fires,
but having been born again due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha, they subsequently attained the state of Yoga.
Antardhāna begot Havirdhāna by Nabhasvatī;
though he knew him to be the stealer of Indra’s horse, he did not slay him.
[Havirdhāna] practiced the cruel livelihood of kings, consisting of the collection of taxes, fines, tolls, and the like.
Thinking thus, under the pretext of a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*), he dismissed him;
there too, perceiving the Supreme Self as the Swan and the Person,
he worshipped Him and attained that world through his skillful meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
From Havirdhāna, Havirdhānī gave birth to six sons:
Barhiṣad, Gaya, Śukla, Kṛṣṇa, Satya, and Jitavrata.
Barhiṣad was highly fortunate, and Havirdhāni was a Prajāpati.
O best of the Kurus, he was proficient in the ritualistic sections of the Vedas as well as in yogic practices;
while he was performing sacrifices, this sacrificial ground of the gods was strewn with kusha grass whose tips pointed toward the east.
He married Śatadruti, the daughter of the ocean, as directed by the God of gods;
seeing her, whose every limb was beautiful, who was youthful and well-adorned,
moving about at her wedding, Agni desired her just as he had once desired Śukī.
The gods, asuras, gandharvas, sages, perfected beings (siddhas), humans,
and serpents were all conquered by Sūryā with the mere tinkling of her anklets in every direction.
Prācīnabarhis had ten sons by Śatadruti.
All of them, bearing the same name and observing the same vows, purified by their religious duties and possessed of great wisdom,
were commanded by their father to procreate; they entered the ocean for ascetic penance and,
for ten thousand years, worshipped the Lord of Penance through austerity.
"Reflecting upon, chanting, and worshiping that which was spoken by the gracious Giriśa when he was seen on the path, we remain self-controlled. Vidura said:
O brāhmaṇa, please tell us the meaningful account of how the meeting between the Pracetas and Śiva occurred on the road, and why Hara was so pleased with them. Indeed,
O brahminical sage, for embodied beings in this world, a meeting with Śiva is a rare and auspicious occurrence.

O sages, even those who delight in the Self meditate with detachment upon Him who is so difficult to attain and is their desired goal; yet the Lord Bhava, though endowed with that power, wanders about for the sake of the welfare of this world.
Maitreya said:
Taking their father’s words upon their heads,
those saintly Pracetās set out for the western direction, their minds intent on performing austerities.
He beheld a vast lake extending as far as the ocean,
as immense as the great mind itself, with its depths of water clear and serene,
filled with blue and red lotuses, *ambhojas*, *kahlāras*, and *indīvaras*.

Resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, ruddy geese, and ducks; where the trees, their hair-like creepers bristling with joy, were filled with the sweet humming of intoxicated bees; and where the breeze was a festival that scattered the pollen from the hearts of lotuses in every direction.

There, having heard the celestial music of the Gandharvas, which was enchanting to the ear, those princes were filled with wonder; and at that very moment, they beheld him emerging from that lake accompanied by his followers, amidst the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, and other instruments.
Seeing that foremost of immortals being praised by the followers of the gods,
who resembled molten gold, possessed a dark throat and three eyes,
and had a face gracious with favor, they bowed down, filled with wonder.

The Blessed Lord, who removes the suffering of those who have sought refuge and is affectionately devoted to dharma, being pleased with them— themselves pleased and endowed with virtue and knowledge— spoke to them. Śrī Rudra said:
O sons who sit upon the sacrificial altar, your intended purpose is known to me. For the sake of bestowing grace upon you—may it be auspicious for you—I have granted this vision.
He who is manifest as the Supreme beyond the three modes of nature and beyond that which is designated as the individual soul (jīva)—[that Lord has appeared before you].
He who has taken refuge in the Blessed Vāsudeva is indeed dear to me.

A person devoted to his own duty (*svadharma*) attains the state of Viriñca (Brahmā) after a hundred births; thereafter, he attains Me, the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*), the station of the devotees of the Lord (*bhāgavata*) and Viṣṇu (*vaiṣṇava*). O gods, it is just as I am at the end of the cosmic cycle (*kalātyaye*).
"Now, you are devotees of the Lord and as dear to Me as the Lord Himself;
indeed, there is never anyone else more dear to Me than My devotees.
This secluded place is sacred, auspicious, and supremely conducive for chanting."
"Listen also to that which brings about the highest good; I shall speak it to you.
Maitreya said:
Thus the Lord, whose heart was filled with compassion, spoke auspiciously to them.
To the princes who stood with palms joined in reverence, Śrī Rudra, who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa, spoke these words:
"Victory to you, O best among the knowers of the Self! May there be well-being for my welfare."
Obeisances to You, who have been attained through Your own grace; obeisances to the Self of all.
Obeisances to the one whose navel is a lotus, the self of the subtle elements and the senses; to Vāsudeva, the peaceful, the immovable, and the self-luminous.
Salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa, the subtle one, the endless one, and the bringer of the end; salutations to Pradyumna, the inner self who awakens the universe.
Salutations again and again to Aniruddha, the lord of the senses and the self of the faculties.
Obeisances to the Supreme Swan, the Perfect One, whose self is composed;
obeisances eternally to Him who dwells in purity, the gateway to heaven and liberation. Obeisances to Him of golden potency, the thread of the fourfold sacrificial ritual.
Obeisances to the one who is nourishment and food, the Lord of the three Vedas, whose seed is the sacrifice; obeisances to the giver of satisfaction to living beings, the self of all flavors.
Obeisances to the one who is the body of the souls of all beings, the most excellent, and the most massive.
Obeisances to the protector of the three worlds, who possesses energy and strength; obeisances to the sky, whose mark is the sun, and who is the self both within and without;
obeisances to that holy world of immense splendor.

Salutations to the one who impels toward worldly activity and the one who leads toward cessation; to the deity of the ancestors and of ritual action; to Death, the ripening of unrighteousness and the giver of suffering.
Salutations to You, O Lord of blessings, the progenitor and the causal Self.
Obeisances to the great Dharma, to Kṛṣṇa of unimpeded intelligence,
to the Puruṣa, the ancient one, and the Lord of Sāṅkhya and Yoga; obeisances to Him who is endowed with the three potencies, the bountiful giver, and the self of the ego.
Obeisances to You, whose form is the intention of the mind and who are the source of the manifestation of speech. Grant us, who long to behold You, that vision which is honored by the devotees—
a form most dear to Your own kin and the collyrium for the eyes of all the senses.
Dark as a glossy rain-cloud in the monsoon, the embodiment of all beauty,
with four long and handsome arms, a well-formed and radiant face,
eyes like the petals of a lotus bud, beautiful eyebrows, and a fine nose.

With beautiful teeth and lovely cheeks, his face was adorned with symmetrical ears and ornaments; his eyes were upturned with a smile of affection, and he was graced by curls of hair that enhanced his beauty; he wore a fine silk garment like the filaments of a blooming lotus, and polished earrings.
He bore a shimmering crown, bracelets, necklaces, anklets, and a girdle;
He possessed the conch, discus, mace, lotus, garland, and the supreme jewel; He had the luster of a lion’s shoulders and the Kaustubha gem upon His auspicious neck.

With His navel-whorl, deep and resonant, which casts out the very touchstone for the luster of eternal Śrī, He causes the entire universe to enter within, as its folds— beautifully curved and agitated by the flow of His exhalation and inhalation— contract and expand.
He wore a dark-blue lower garment and a glistening golden belt; his feet, calves, and thighs were symmetrical and beautiful, with well-formed, slightly sunken knees.
With His foot, which possessed the luster of an autumn lotus petal and dispelled our inner sins with the radiance of His toenails, [He touched her].
O Guru, show us Your own state, which dispels all fear for those who take refuge in You; for You are the guide on the path for those immersed in darkness.
This form of Yours is to be meditated upon by those desiring self-purification, for it is the yoga of devotion that grants fearlessness to those who perform their own prescribed duties.

You are attainable by one who possesses devotion, yet you are difficult for all embodied beings to reach; you are the desired goal even of sovereign kingship, and you are the ultimate destination for those who know the Self.
Having propitiated You—who are difficult to propitiate even by the virtuous—through that which is hard for them to obtain...
Who, indeed, would desire anything external with exclusive devotion, other than the soles of Your feet,
where all fear has been cast away and even Death does not dare to look upon it,
while destroying the entire universe with his eyebrows flashing in prowess and heroism?

I do not value even heaven or liberation from rebirth for half a moment as much as the company of those who are attached to the Blessed One; what need is there to mention the worldly boons sought by mortals?
Furthermore, for those whose sins have been washed away by bathing internally and externally in the sacred waters of Your fame, O Lord of sinless feet—

For those whose character is marked by compassion for all beings and a virtuous nature, association with you would be a source of grace; yet this is not so for us. For your path cannot be perceived even by a sage whose mind has entered the cave of darkness—the delusion of external objects—and who, though purified, has not been graced by the yoga of devotion to You, through which one truly perceives Your state.
That in which this universe is manifested, and that which shines forth within the universe—

that you are, the Supreme Brahman, the supreme light, expansive like the ether. You, who by your illusory power (*māyā*) of manifold forms create this world, sustain it, and again dissolve it, yet remain changeless.
O Blessed One, because of our own miserable state, we perceive You—who are independent of all else—as if You were distinct from us, as though You were a mere "existent" object.
Yet it is You alone whom the yogis, endowed with faith, worship through various ritual acts for the sake of perfection;
they alone are truly wise in both the Veda and the Tantra, perceiving You as that which is indicated by the elements, the senses, and the internal organ.
You alone are the primordial Puruṣa; when Your power is dormant, it is divided by that [power] into the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas.
From this [Puruṣa] arise the Mahat, the ego, ether, air, fire, water, earth, the celestial sages, and the hosts of beings—from which all this proceeds.
Having created this universe by Your own power, You have entered this fourfold city [of the body] as a portion of Yourself.
Moreover, he who, while being a person of realization, consumes the honey of the senses within himself—

he is indeed you, O Time, whose vehicle is the end of all things, who drags away the worlds with exceedingly fierce speed; your true nature is inferred by the beings you consume, and you are as irresistible as a wind that sweeps away rows of clouds.
While he is heedless due to his constant brooding over what ought to be done, his greed increased and his longing for sense objects intensified,
you, remaining vigilant, suddenly seize him— just as the serpent Antaka, licking its lips, seizes a mouse.
What wise man would abandon your lotus feet, he by whom the banner of pride has been utterly destroyed?
Out of apprehension, our preceptor as well as the fourteen Manus performed worship even without logical justification;
therefore, O Brahman, you are for us the Supreme Soul and the refuge of the wise,
whose protection from the fear of Rudra has destroyed the universe, and who are yourself free from all fear.
"Recite this, O princes; may it be auspicious for you. Being purified, perform your own duty with your intentions offered to the Blessed Lord.
[Meditate] upon Him alone—the Self abiding within the self and situated in all beings."
Worship Hari, chanting His names and meditating upon Him repeatedly; having approached the instructions of yoga and maintaining the vows of sages, all of you,
with concentrated minds, should practice this with devotion.

Long ago, the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Creator of the Universe, spoke these words to us, his sons headed by Bhṛgu, as he desired to create while we ourselves were desiring to create: "Impelled by me, all of you shall become lords of progeny for the sake of creating offspring."
By this [mantra], his darkness destroyed, he desires to create various progeny;
moreover, a person who is constantly engaged, reciting this with focused attention and devoted to Vāsudeva, attains the highest good before long.
Among all things that lead to welfare in this world, knowledge is the supreme means to the highest good.
The boat of knowledge carries one across the ocean of calamities, which is otherwise difficult to cross.
This applies to whoever, endowed with faith, recites this hymn to the Blessed One sung by me.
By studying this, one worships Hari, who is otherwise difficult to propitiate; from Him—
who is well-pleased by this song sung by me and who is the sole beloved of all that is auspicious— the person obtains whatever he desires without delay.

O sons of the king of men, this hymn of praise to the Supreme Person, the Supreme Self, has been sung by me; the mortal who, having risen at dawn, listens to it with joined palms and endowed with faith, or causes others to hear it, is liberated from the bonds of karma.
"Chanting with one-pointed minds, practice great austerity; at its conclusion, you shall obtain your desired goal.
Maitreya said:
Having thus instructed them, the Blessed One was worshipped by the followers of Bṛhaspati.
While the princes were looking on, Hara vanished right there.
All the Pracetasas, chanting that hymn to the Blessed One sung by Rudra,
performed austerities in the water for ten thousand years.
O Vidura, Nārada, who knows the truth of the supreme self and is compassionate, awakened Prācīnabarhiṣ, whose mind was attached to ritual activities, saying:
"O King, which among the various forms of action do you seek for your own ultimate good?"
"The cessation of suffering and the attainment of happiness—that is the highest good; that is not sought here [in this world].
The King said:
"O highly fortunate one, my intellect being cast away by ritual action, I do not know the Supreme."
"Tell me that pure knowledge by which I may be liberated from karmic bonds;
for the fool whose mind is fixed on children, wife, wealth, and property within houses of deceptive dharma finds no higher goal, wandering instead upon the paths of saṃsāra."
Nārada said:
O King, Lord of Creatures, behold these thousands of multitudes of living beings who have been slaughtered by you, merciless as you are, for the sake of the sacrifice.
"These people are waiting for you, remembering your slaughter; once you have passed away, they will rise up in fury and cut you to pieces with iron mallets.
In this regard, I shall relate to you this ancient history."
Listen as I relate the life-story of Purañjana.
O King, there was once a king named Purañjana of great renown. He had a friend whose name was unknown and whose activities were likewise unknown.
Seeking refuge, that lord wandered the earth;
when he found nothing suitable, he became as if dejected.
He did not consider any of the cities on the surface of the earth to be good enough.
Desiring various objects of desire for their respective attainment,
he once beheld upon the southern ridges of the Himalayas a city distinguished by the marks of excellence and possessing nine gates.
It was crowded everywhere with houses featuring walls, groves, watchtowers, moats, axles, and gateways, and with turrets made of gold, silver,
and iron; it was adorned with blue sapphire, crystal, lapis lazuli, pearl, emerald, and ruby.
It was like the city of Bhogavatī, radiant with splendor and adorned with well-constructed mansions;
it was provided with assembly halls, courtyards, and thoroughfares, as well as pleasure gardens, marketplaces,
sacred shrines, banners, and flags, and featured altars made of coral.
Outside the city, in a grove filled with divine trees and creepers, where the water-bodies resounded with the clamor of flocks of warbling birds,
and which was cooled by breezes from the flower-bearing season carrying droplets from snowy waterfalls;

In that place, where the abundance of lotus ponds with branches of swaying sprouts provides a refuge undisturbed by herds of various wild animals who observe the vows of sages, a traveler feels as if he were being summoned by the warbling of cuckoos.
There he beheld that most excellent woman who had arrived by chance,
coming with ten servants, each leading a hundred attendants,
and protected on all sides by a gatekeeper in the form of a serpent with an upraised hood.
Seeking her bull, she was a young woman of unripe youth who could assume any form at will; she possessed a beautiful nose, lovely teeth, and a fine face with shapely cheeks,
while her well-placed ears bore the beauty of earrings.
She was dark-complexioned with a beautiful waist, wearing a saffron-colored lower garment and a golden girdle; moving along with her tinkling feet adorned with anklets, she appeared like a goddess.
Her breasts, which had manifested their youthful fullness, were symmetrical, well-rounded, and closely set.
As she, walking with the grace of an elephant, was hiding her body with the hem of her garment out of modesty,
the hero spoke charmingly to her, who was beautiful with a bashful smile; he was touched by her affectionate side-glances, which were like arrows, and by her eyebrows dancing with love.
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one? Whose are you, and from where have you come here, O virtuous lady?
O timid one, why do you approach this city? Tell me what you intend to do. And who are these eleven great warriors who follow in your path?"
"O fair-browed one, are these women yours? And who is this serpent walking before you?
Are you Hrī, Bhavānī, Vāk, or Ramā, searching for your husband in this secluded forest like a sage?
Where has the lotus bud fallen from the tip of your hand—she who grants all desires through the longing for your feet?"

O lady of shapely thighs, none among these women touches the earth; you ought to adorn this city together with that most excellent of heroes of wondrous deeds, just as Śrī adorns the Supreme Person at the sacrifice.
For he has shattered my senses with his sidelong glances, while his eyebrows playfully quiver amidst a bashful smile.
"O blessed one, the god of love, incited by you, torments me; therefore, O beautiful lady, show favor to me.

O fair-browed one with lovely eyes, lift up your face—which is covered by a mass of long, dark curls and possesses sweet speech—and show it to me, O girl of pure smiles, for it is not turned toward me out of modesty."
Nārada said:
Thus, O hero, the woman, being deluded, laughed and welcomed that Purañjana as he entreated her like one who is not firm.
"O bull among men, we do not fully know our own creator,
nor our lineage and the name by which he was made;
today, we know ourselves only as being present here, and nothing beyond that."
"O hero, by whom this city was fashioned as a refuge for himself;
these are my friends and companions, both men and women, O giver of honor.
While I sleep, this serpent remains awake, protecting the city."
"By good fortune you have arrived; may prosperity be yours! O subduer of enemies, if you desire the pleasures of the village life, I shall provide them for you along with my own kinsmen.
O Lord, please take up residence in this city of nine gates."
Accepting sensual enjoyments brought to me by my own hand for a hundred years—
who else but you could I have delighted? For you were one who knew no discontent, lacked discernment, was not intent on the hereafter, and was a beast ignorant of even tomorrow's needs.
For here indeed are dharma, wealth, and pleasure; progeny, bliss, immortality, and fame;
as well as those sorrowless and stainless worlds which even the liberated ones do not know—[all these belong] to the ancestors, gods, sages, mortals, all beings, and the self.

They say that in this worldly existence, the householder’s life is the secure refuge. O hero, what woman like me would not choose as her husband one such as you— renowned, generous, pleasant to behold, and beloved?

O mighty-armed one, whose mind would not be captivated by the arms of that woman, which possess the coils of serpents upon this earth— arms that move about to dispel the distress of the multitude of the helpless with a glance of a smile raised by compassion? Nārada said:
O King, having thus made a mutual agreement there, that couple entered the city and rejoiced for a hundred years,
while being serenaded here and there with charming songs by singers.
While sporting, surrounded by women, he entered a lake during the summer heat.
That city had seven gates above and two below;
within it, there was a certain Lord for the purpose of experiencing various sense objects.
There are five gates: three to the east, one to the south, one to the north, and two to the west;
O King, I shall describe their names to you. Khadyotā and Āvirmukhī are the two eastern gates, constructed together in one place.
Accompanied by Dyumant, he travels through the countryside made radiant by those two;
Nalinī and Nālinī are the two eastern gates constructed together,
and accompanied by Avadhūta, he goes through the fragrant region by way of them.

To the east is the gate named Mukhyā; through it, the king of the city, accompanied by the merchant Rasajña, goes to the two marketplaces of Āpaṇa and Bahūdana. O King, to the south of the city is the gate named Pitṛhū, through which Purañjana passes.
Accompanied by Śrutadharā, Purañjana went to the kingdom of Dakṣiṇa-pañcāla from the city named Devahū, via its northern gate; accompanied by Śrutadharā, he went to the kingdom of Uttara-pañcāla.

Behind him was a gatekeeper named Āsurī; accompanied by her and filled with intoxication, Purañjana went to the region called Grāmaka. Behind him was another gatekeeper named Nirṛti; accompanied by her, Purañjana went forth.
Accompanied by a hunter, he went to the region named Vaiśasa;
there, both Andha and Nirvāk-Peśaskṛt were among those ancient inhabitants,
and the lord of the sighted proceeded with them and acted through them.
Whenever he enters the inner apartments accompanied by Viṣūcī,
he experiences delusion, serenity, or joy arising from his wife and children;
thus, attached to such activities, the ignorant man, whose soul is consumed by desire, is deceived.
Whatever the queen desired, he followed that very thing.
Sometimes, while she was drinking wine, he drank it too, overwhelmed by intoxication;
sometimes, while she was eating, he ate; and when she was chewing, he chewed along with her.
In some places he sang when she was singing, and in others he wept when she was weeping; in some places he laughed when she was laughing, and in others he chattered after her as she chattered;
in some places he ran when she was running, and he stood when she stood.
He lies down when she lies down; he sits beside her when she is sitting; sometimes he hears when she hears, and he looks when she looks;
sometimes he smells when she smells, and he touches when she touches.
Sometimes he grieves like a wretched man when his wife grieves;
he rejoices when she rejoices, and he delights when she is delighted. Thus deceived by the queen, he was deluded by all the primary elements of nature.
Though unwilling, the ignorant man imitates [the Lord] out of weakness, like a toy deer.
Nārada said:
Once that great archer mounted his swift chariot drawn by five horses.
It has two enemies, two wheels, one axle, three poles, five joints;
it has one rein, one driver, one nest, and two shafts;
it possesses five weapons, seven guards, and five strides.
Mounting a chariot with golden trappings, clad in golden armor, and equipped with inexhaustible quivers, the commander of eleven armies set out for the forest five *prasthas* away;
there, arrogant and having taken up his bow and arrows, he went hunting.

Abandoning his wife, who did not deserve such treatment, he— eager for the sport of hunting, having adopted a demonic disposition, cruel-minded and merciless— slaughtered those dwelling in the forests with sharpened arrows in the woods.

When sacrificial sites are seen, a king who is excessively greedy might slaughter animals in the forest for his own purposes; therefore, he is restrained by the rule that one should kill only as many as are required.
A wise man should perform such obligatory duties in this manner.
O Indra among kings, by that action he is not tainted, provided it is performed with knowledge;
otherwise, performing action while mounted on pride, one is bound.
Fallen into the flow of the material modes and deprived of wisdom, he goes downward.
There, for those whose limbs were pierced by arrows with variegated feathers,
a distressing and unbearable calamity befell the suffering ones who were compassionate by nature;
[he struck] hares, boars, buffaloes, gavayas, ruru deer, and porcupines.
Slaying various other sacrificial animals, he experienced great exhaustion;
then, weary from hunger and thirst, he returned home,
and having bathed and taken his accustomed meal, he lay down once his fatigue had subsided.
He honored himself with incense, unguents, garlands, and other offerings;
with all his limbs beautifully adorned, he fixed his mind upon the queen.
Satiated, joyful, and exceedingly proud, his heart was drawn away by the god of love.
He did not look upon his beautiful wife, the mistress of the household; instead, like one dejected, he questioned the women of the inner apartments as if he were a stranger:
"O lovely ladies, is all well with you and your lord, as it was before?"
Nowadays, the riches of the household no longer please me as they once did;
for if there were not a mother or a wife in the home who regards her husband as a deity, what wise man would remain there like a wretched person in a broken chariot?
"Where is that woman who, illuminating my wisdom at every step, rescued me as I was sinking in the ocean of calamity?
The women said:
"O Lord of Men, we do not know what your beloved intends;
behold her, O slayer of enemies, lying upon the bare ground with no bedding.
Nārada said:
Seeing his queen fallen and shaken upon the ground, Purañjana—
his wisdom destroyed by attachment to her— fell into a state of extreme despondency; he consoled her with gentle words while his heart burned with grief.
He did not perceive within himself any sign of the intensity of affection for his beloved;
then the hero, skilled in conciliation, slowly sought to appease her,
touched her two feet, and spoke to her as she was cherished upon his lap.
Purañjana said:
"O auspicious lady, surely those servants who have not performed meritorious deeds are such that their masters,
even when they have committed offenses against them, do not apply the rod of punishment by bringing them under their own control."
"O slender one, the punishment inflicted by a master upon his servants is the highest favor;
yet this child, being impatient, does not understand that act of a kinsman.
Therefore, O lady with beautiful teeth and lovely brows, show me your face—your face graced by smiles and glances lingering with the weight of affection and bashfulness."
"O wise lady, show us your face adorned with rows of dark locks and a prominent nose, speaking sweet words to your own people.
O wife of a hero, I shall impose punishment upon that man who has committed an offense against anyone other than a family of Brahmins;
I shall not look upon him without fear unless he is exultant in the three worlds as a servant of the enemy of Mura (Kṛṣṇa)."

Your face is without its tilaka, soiled, joyless, fierce with agitation, unadorned, and devoid of its natural luster; even Your noble breasts are marred by grief, and Your bimba-like lips have lost the hue of their saffron paste. Be gracious to me, Your friend, who has committed an offense by going out at will for the hunt, overcome as I am by this addiction.
"What woman, desiring her own welfare, would not devote herself to her husband when he has fallen under her control, his manhood dissolved by the force of the flower-arrowed god?
Nārada said:
"Having thus brought Purañjana under her influence through her charms..."

O great king, Purañjanī took delight in pleasing her husband; O King, that monarch welcomed his queen as she approached him— well-bathed, with a radiant countenance, having performed auspicious rites, and fully satisfied.

Embraced by her and his neck encircled by her arms, his consciousness drawn away by secret mantras, he— possessing a great mind and intoxicated with pride— rested upon a costly couch supported by the arms of his queen; thus absorbed in the company of that woman, he did not perceive the irresistible force of time passing day and night.
Overwhelmed by darkness, that hero considers her alone to be the Supreme, not his own self nor the Supreme Being.
O King of kings, as he thus took delight with her, his mind defiled by lust, his youth passed away like half a moment.
Upon Purañjanī, Purañjana begot one thousand and eleven sons; the Virāṭ then passed half of his life away. He also had one hundred and ten daughters who brought glory to their father and mother.
O Lord of Creatures, those citizens of Paurañjaya were endowed with the virtues of good character and nobility.
That lord of Pañcāla united his sons, who increased the lineage of their fathers,
with wives, and his daughters with suitable husbands.
Each of his sons had one hundred sons,
by whom the Paurañjana lineage was greatly increased among the Pañcālas;
while they were the heirs to that inheritance, they lived off the household treasury and its attendants.
Bound by a deep-seated sense of possessiveness toward sense objects,
he performed terrible sacrifices involving the slaughter of animals after being initiated,
seeking various desires just as you do for the gods, the ancestors, and the lords of spirits.
While he was thus engaged and his mind was distracted by attachment to his family,
O King, that time which is so unpleasant to beloved women arrived;
it was the lord of the Gandharvas, known as Caṇḍavega.
Three hundred and sixty powerful Gandharvas,
and an equal number of Gandharvīs— both white and dark— who engage in sexual union,
plunder by turns that city fashioned to provide every desire.
When those followers of Caṇḍavega began to seize the city of Purañjana,
Prajāgara resisted them there for one hundred years with seven hundred and twenty men.
The powerful Purañjana, the lord of the city, fought with the Gandharvas;
as his own forces were being depleted by many in that battle,
he became distressed and fell into deep anxiety, along with his kingdom, city, and kinsmen.

That very same king, a consumer of honey, while ruling in the city of Pañcāla with his own attendants, accepted the tribute brought before him; being conquered by women, he did not perceive the danger. A certain daughter of Time (Kāla) desired a husband from within the three worlds.
As she wandered about, O Barhiṣmat, no one greeted her with joy;
due to her misfortune, she was renowned in the world as "Durbhagā" (the Unfortunate).
Yet, she who had been pleased by the royal sage granted a boon to Pūru, who had offered her his own conduct.
Once, while wandering through the worlds of Brahmā,
she, deluded by lust though knowing me to be one of great vows, approached me on earth and,
becoming enraged, cast upon me an unbearable and vast curse.

"O sage, you ought not to remain in one place while turning away from my request. Then, her resolve frustrated, the maiden approached the lord of the Yavanas whom I had instructed and chose him as her husband by the name of Bhaya.
"O Ṛṣabha, I choose you, the hero desired by all, as my husband;
for the resolve of living beings directed toward you indeed never fails.
"These two types of fools grieve over their lack of success: those who are ignorant and those who are obstinately attached to what is unreal."
That which is offered according to worldly custom and scripture he neither gives nor desires;
therefore, O gentle one, accept me who am devoted to you, and show compassion to me. Such is the duty of a man: that he shows mercy to those who are distressed.
Having heard the words spoken by Kālakanyā, the Lord of the Yavanas,
desiring to perform a secret act of the gods, spoke to her with a smile:
"I have already chosen a husband for you through my own meditative concentration."
"This world does not welcome you, for you are inauspicious and disapproved of.
Since your course is obscure, enjoy this world fashioned by karma;
for you, joined with my army, shall bring about the destruction of all creatures."
"This Prajvāra is my brother; you, too, become my sister. Together with us both, I shall move through this world unmanifested, accompanied by a formidable army.
Nārada said:
O Barhiṣman, those soldiers of the one named Fear, who carry out his commands,
roamed this earth accompanied by Fever and the Daughter of Time.
Once, O King, they impetuously entered the city of Purañjana.
They besieged the city, which was rich in earthly enjoyments and guarded by an aged serpent;
meanwhile, the daughter of Time (Kālakanyā) forcibly devoured the city of Purañjana,
overwhelmed by whom a person immediately becomes devoid of essence.
While she was being enjoyed by him, the Yavanas entered from all directions through the gates and violently oppressed the entire city. As that city was being tormented, the conceited Purañjana—

As a householder, agitated by the sense of "mine," embraced by his daughters, his prosperity lost, wretched, and devoted to sense objects, he experienced manifold miseries; his wisdom destroyed and his sovereignty stolen by force by the Gandharvas and Yavanas.
Seeing his own city in ruins, his sons, grandsons, followers, and ministers indifferent and hostile, his wife devoid of affection,
himself seized by his daughter, and the Pañcālas corrupted by the enemy;
Fallen into endless anxiety, he found no remedy for it;
wretched and longing for pleasures with his daughter, his time had passed away, and his affection for his own self, wife, and children had vanished as he fondled them.
The king set out to abandon that city— which was overrun by Gandharvas and Yavanas and oppressed by the Maiden of Time— even though he had no desire to do so; meanwhile,
his elder brother named Bhaya appeared as a raging fever.

Out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his brother, he burned that entire city down. As it was being consumed by fire, the head of the household, along with his wife, his attendants, his citizens, and his kin, was filled with intense distress.
When his city was besieged by the Yavanas and seized by the Maiden of Time (Kālakanyā),
and it was consumed by a raging fire, the city guardian lamented;
trembling violently and in great distress, he was unable to protect it there.

Then, O King, when his limbs had grown weak and his manliness had been snatched away by the Gandharvas, he was besieged by the Yavana enemies; like a bird from the hollow of a tree filled with fire, he desired to depart and wept aloud.
The foolish householder, identifying with his daughters, sons, grandsons, sisters, brothers-in-law, and attendants,
as well as whatever remains of his own property— the household, treasury, and furnishings—
clings to them with the thought, "This is mine," while dwelling in his homes.
Distressed by his infatuation when their separation had arrived, he brooded:
"Now that I have gone to another world, how will this wife of mine, left without a protector,
survive while grieving for her young children?"
Devoted to me, she does not eat when I have not eaten, nor does she bathe when I have not bathed;
when I am angry, she is greatly terrified, and when I rebuke her, she remains silent out of fear. When I am asleep, she, emaciated by grief, awakens me.

Even a hero, though he be a father of sons, will not follow this path of householdership. How indeed will these wretched boys and helpless girls survive when I have gone, like those on a shattered boat in the ocean?
While he was thus grieving with such a wretched intellect— though he did not deserve it— the one named Bhaya (Fear) approached him, having resolved to seize him,
as he was being led like an animal by the Yavanas toward his own abode.
The followers, running after him in great distress and lamenting,
abandoned the city; for when the serpent had departed,
the city, being besieged, fell apart and returned to its original state of nature.
Being violently dragged by the powerful Yavana,
he was overcome by darkness and could not find his friend or companion before him;
those sacrificial animals had been slaughtered by that merciless man.

Remembering his past offense, they angrily hacked him with axes. Having been defiled by attachment to women, he remained for eternal years in a shoreless darkness, experiencing suffering while his memory was lost.
Mentally grasping her alone, he became that most excellent woman;
thereafter, in the palace of the lion among kings, the ruler of Vidarbha,
Malayadhvaja married the princess of Vidarbha, for whom valor was the bride-price.
Having conquered the kṣatriyas in battle, Pāṇḍya, the conqueror of enemy cities,
begot upon her a daughter with dark eyes;
he also begot seven younger sons, who became the seven Draviḍa kings.
O King, each one of them had a hundred million sons,
and the earth will be enjoyed by the descendants of their lineages for another manvantara.
Formerly, Agastya married a daughter who was firm in her vows.
In that [dynasty] was born the sage Dṛḍhacyuta, the son of Idhmavāha;
and the royal seer Malayadhvaja, having divided the earth among his sons,
went to the Kulācala mountain, desiring to worship Kṛṣṇa.
Leaving her home, children, and enjoyments, the daughter of Vidarbha, with eyes as intoxicating as wine,
followed the Lord of Pāṇḍya, just as moonlight follows the moon.
There, she [saw] the rivers named Candravasā, Tāmraparṇī, and Vaṭodakā.
Constantly purifying himself in both places with the holy waters thereof, he subsisted on bulbs,
stalks, roots, fruits, flowers, leaves, grass, and water; thus,
gradually emaciating his body, he engaged in ascetic penance.
With equal vision, he conquered the pairs of opposites: cold and heat, wind and rain, hunger and thirst, the pleasant and the unpleasant, and happiness and suffering;
for he had purified his impurities through austerity, knowledge, and the observances of *niyama* and *yama*.
Having conquered his senses, breath, and mind, he yoked his self to the Brahman;
remaining steady for a hundred divine years, he sat motionless like a pillar in one place,
bearing the Vedas and finding no pleasure in anything other than the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.

O King, having realized through direct instruction from his guru Hari— the Blessed One himself— that the Self is all-pervading and yet distinct within the self, he desisted from further inquiry, like one who has awakened from a dream.

With the flickering lamp of pure knowledge, he beheld the Self within the Supreme Brahman— which faces all directions— and likewise the Supreme Brahman within the Self; thus, having abandoned all other perception, he indeed desisted from this world.
The princess of Vidarbha, who regarded her husband as her deity, abandoned all worldly enjoyments and served with love her husband Malayadhvaja, the knower of the highest dharma;
she was clothed in rags, emaciated by her vows, and her hair was matted into a single braid.
When that woman did not know her beloved had passed away, she appeared like a flame extinguished upon its master; nevertheless,
having assumed a perfectly steady posture, she continued to attend to him just as before.
When, while worshipping her husband’s feet, she no longer felt warmth there,
her heart became agitated like that of a doe strayed from its herd; grieving for herself as one wretched and friendless, she was overwhelmed by tears of distress.
Having wetted her breasts in the forest, she wept aloud:
"Arise, arise, O royal sage! You ought to protect this earth, girt by the oceans, which is terrified of the bandits and their kinsmen."
Thus lamenting, the young woman followed her husband into the forest;
falling at her husband's feet, she wept and shed tears.
Having piled a funeral pyre made of wood, she placed her husband’s body upon it.

Having set fire [to herself] and lamenting, she resolved to follow him in death. At that moment, O Lord, a certain self-controlled Brahmin friend who had been there previously spoke to her as she wept, consoling her with gentle words.
The brāhmaṇa said:
Who are you? To whom do you belong? And who is this person lying here for whose sake you grieve?
Do you know me, your friend, with whom you used to wander in the past?
Do you not remember yourself, O friend, as one whose companion was unknown?
Having abandoned me while seeking my abode, you have gone away, intent on earthly enjoyments.
O noble one, both I and you were once companions, swans dwelling in Lake Mānasa.
For a thousand years, there was no one else in between;
yet you, O friend, having abandoned me and fallen to the worldly mind, went to the earth and,
while wandering about, beheld a footstep fashioned by some woman.
The body has five gardens, nine gates, one guardian, three storehouses, six families, five markets, and five primary elements; it has women as its masters.
O Lord, the objects of the five senses are the gardens, and the vital breaths are the nine gates.
Fire, water, and food are its storehouses; the family is the collection of the senses.
Trade is the power of action, and the unchanging material nature of the elements is the capital.
The Person, the master of this power, having entered therein, does not perceive it.
There, touched by Rāmā and sporting with her, you lost all memory of your former state;
O Lord, through that association you have reached such a wretched condition. You are not the daughter of Vidarbha, nor is this hero your friend.
"You are not the husband of Purañjanī by whom you were imprisoned in the nine-gated city;
for this is an illusion created by me, because of which you consider yourself a man when you are actually a woman, or both, when you are neither. Behold us as two swans and see our true nature."
"I am you, and you are not other than me; you are indeed I—consider this, O friend!
Wise men never perceive even the slightest difference between us two, just as a person perceives his own single self in both a mirror and his own eyes."
"One should perceive our two internal states as having become twofold in that very same way.
Thus enlightened by the swan, that mental swan became established in its own nature; through that non-deviation, it regained the consciousness it had lost.
"O Barhiṣmat, this spiritual truth has been shown through indirect description,
for the Blessed Lord, the creator of the universe, is fond of the indirect.
Thus spoke Prācīnabarhis.
"O Blessed One, your words are not fully understood by us;
the wise understand them, but we do not, being deluded by our own actions.
Nārada said:
One should know Puruṣa as Purañjana, who manifests his own city—
whether it has one, two, three, four, or many feet, or is footless.
O friend, he who is unperceived is the Lord of that Puruṣa.
That which cannot be fully known by men through names, actions,
or qualities— when the Puruṣa desired to grasp the modes of nature in their entirety, he conceived of that [body] as excellent, possessing nine gates, two hands, and two feet.
One should know that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the woman, by whom the notions of "I" and "mine" are produced;
