presiding over which in this body, the person experiences the qualities through the senses.
The group of senses are his companions, as are knowledge and action, which are brought about by her.

One should know that his friends are the five functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is like a serpent with five coils; his great strength is the mind (*manas*), the leader of both types of sense organs;
and the Pañcālas are the five sense objects, within which lies the city of nine gates.
The two eyes, the two nostrils, the two ears, the mouth, and the organs of generation and excretion—
these are the pairs of gates through which one goes outward, joined with the senses. The five [gates] consisting of the two eyes, the two nostrils, and the mouth are situated in the front.
The right ear is known as Dakṣiṇā and the left as Uttarā;
the two western doors are said here to be the anus and the genitals.
The two eyes are fashioned together here as Khadyotā and Āvirmukhī.
The Lord perceives with His eye that form which is brilliantly illuminated by those two [eyes].
The nose is called Nalinī and Nālinī; fragrance is called Saurabha.
The sense of smell is Avadhūta; the mouth is Mukhya; speech is Vipaṇa; and taste is Rasavid.
The marketplace here is commerce; the "wonderful" is the blind man's abundant food.

The right ear is known as the invoker of the ancestors (*pitṛhū*), and the left ear is remembered as the invoker of the gods (*devahū*). The scripture consisting of both the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛtta*) and the path of renunciation (*nivṛtta*) is designated as Pañcāla.

The path of the ancestors (pitṛ-yāna) and the path of the gods (deva-yāna) proceed from the ears of one who retains what he has heard. The vulva is the gate leading downward; it is the sexual union that constitutes the pleasure of village-dwellers.
The generative organ is called "intoxication," and the anus is said to be "destruction" (nirṛti).
The anus is the hell Vaiśasa and the genitals are the hunter; now hear from me about the two blind ones.
The hands and feet are the person (puruṣa), joined with which one moves and acts.
The heart is the inner apartment, and the mind is called Viṣūci.

Therein, one experiences delusion, clarity, or joy through the qualities [of the mind]. To whatever extent the one affected by the qualities undergoes modification or causes modification, to that same extent the witnessing Self is made to conform to those fluctuations.

The body is a chariot with the senses as its horses, the year as its speed, and no other path; it has two wheels of action, the three qualities as its banner, and the five breaths as its seat. It has the mind as its reins, the intellect as its driver, the heart as its interior, and the pairs of opposites as its pole.
With the objects of the five senses as its projectiles and the seven constituent elements as its armor,
the external army of the eleven senses— driven by intention and prowess— rushes toward the mirage of worldly existence, finding diversion in the five slaughter-houses.
The year, characterized by its fierce velocity, is Time (Kāla). The days of that year are known here as the Gandharvas, and the nights as the Gandharvīs.
By their revolving, they carry away the three hundred and sixty years of one's lifespan.
Old age is Time’s maiden, Jarā herself; the world does not welcome her. Yet Mṛtyu, the lord of the Yavanas, took his sister for the sake of destruction.
Mental agonies and physical ailments are his soldiers, and the Yavanas are his wandering spies.

Afflicted by various kinds of sufferings arising from the divine, the elemental, and the personal— such as possession by spirits, sudden onset of disease, fever, and the two types of burning sensations—
the embodied soul, shrouded in darkness, remains within the body for a hundred years.

Having superimposed the attributes of the vital breath, the senses, and the mind upon the Self, the one devoid of qualities (the *nirguṇa*) lies down meditating on fragments of desire, performing actions with the thought "I am [this]" and "this is mine.
This occurs when, failing to recognize the Supreme Lord as the ultimate teacher, one fails to know the Self.
But the person who perceives his own self becomes attached to the qualities of material nature;
then, identifying with those qualities, he performs actions helplessly—
whether white, black, or red— and is born again according to his karma.

From the mode of goodness (sattva), one occasionally attains worlds abounding in light; yet at other times, through the exertions of ritual action, one reaches realms where suffering is the ultimate result and where darkness and grief predominate.
In some cases a man attains them, in others a woman, and in still others, one whose intellect is blinded attains neither.
Whether one is a god, a human, or an animal, existence occurs according to the qualities of one's past actions.
Just as a wretched dog, overcome by hunger, wanders from house to house and finds whatever is destined for it— be it a stick or a morsel of rice— so too does one find their lot.
In the same way, the individual soul (jīva), whose nature is desire, wandering by various paths, experiences what is ordained as pleasant or unpleasant— whether high, low,
or in between— through even one of the three types of suffering caused by destiny, other beings, or the self.
If there were no distinction for the individual soul (jīva), then each and every action would be its own remedy;
for just as a man carrying a heavy burden on his head shifts it to his shoulder, so too are all remedial actions.
Remedies for karmic actions are not absolute;
indeed, O sinless one, both action and its remedy are merely products of ignorance, like a dream within a dream.
For even when the object [of desire] does not exist, the cycle of worldly existence does not cease.

Just as one wanders in a dream by means of the mind in its subtle form (*liṅga-rūpa*), so too does this succession of misfortunes— the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*)— arise for the self which has become an object of experience; its cessation occurs through supreme devotion toward the Guru.

O royal sage, when devotional yoga is properly concentrated upon the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, it will produce both detachment and knowledge; and by taking refuge in the narrations of Acyuta, that state will be attained very soon.
O King, for one who constantly hears, believes, and studies this [account] where the pure-hearted devotees (*bhāgavatas*) are present,
their minds remain ever intent upon hearing and recounting the qualities of the Blessed Lord.
In that place, the great rivers—the remnants of the nectar of the deeds of Madhubhid—resound and flow everywhere;
O King, those who drink from them with their ears fixed intently remain unthirsting, for hunger, thirst, fear, grief, and delusion do not touch them.
By these natural afflictions, the world of living beings is constantly oppressed.

Indeed, neither Prajāpati, nor the Lord Giriśa himself, nor Manu, nor the lords of creatures such as Dakṣa and others, nor the lifelong celibates such as Sanaka and his brothers, take delight in the nectar-ocean of Hari’s narrations.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Bhṛgu, and Vasiṣṭha— these exponents of Brahman, who culminate with me,
remain even today masters of speech through their asceticism, knowledge, and meditative concentration.
Even while seeing, they do not see the Supreme Lord who sees all;
wandering in the vast expanse of the difficult-to-traverse Śabdabrahman,
they worship Him as delimited by the characteristics of mantras and thus do not know the Supreme.
The intelligence of all living beings is constantly engaged in nourishing the body; what, then, is the distinction of human beings at that time?
Having attained the state of humanity here, one should abandon the false attachment to the body and other such things.
By departing from this world through the path of the Self, that individual soul becomes distinguished;
when the Lord, who is absorbed in the Self, bestows His grace upon someone,
that person abandons the intellect fixed upon worldly affairs and the Vedas.
Therefore, O Barhiṣman, do not fix your vision on the goal in ritual acts that merely appear to yield results through ignorance— acts which are heard of but whose true nature remains untouched;
for they do not know their own world, wherein the Lord Janārdana resides.
Those of smoky intellect, who do not know the Truth, say that the Veda is accompanied by ritual action;
having strewn the entire circle of the earth with Darbha grass pointing eastward,
they remain rigid and proud, performing great slaughter— yet you do not recognize that action which is supreme.
That action is which pleases Hari; that is knowledge by which the mind is fixed upon Him.
Hari is the Self of all embodied beings, the Lord who is Himself the material cause.
The root of His feet is the refuge, from which security for men in this world arises.
"He indeed is the most beloved Self, from whom there is not even the slightest fear"—he who knows this is truly wise; he who is wise is the Guru, Hari.
Nārada said:
O bull among men, your question has indeed been thus resolved. Now listen to me as I explain this profound and well-determined secret.
Having entered into a conflict with a small, moving creature within the refuge of the flowers—
O hunter, look at that deer— its ears captivated by the *sāman* chants of the six-legged bees— and now pierced by your arrow, fleeing while disregarding the life-devouring wolves ahead.

The meaning of this is as follows: In the hermitage that serves as a refuge for women who possess qualities equal to flowers, he— who, like a swarm of bees, gathers the most insignificant fragments of sensual pleasure born from the ripening of desire-driven karma, such as the pleasures of the tongue and the genitals— having coupled with them, has his mind fixed upon them amidst the exceedingly captivating conversations of women and others, which are like the songs of six-legged bees.

"O King, you ought to behold this very self of yours with its heart pierced— this one whom the hunter Death has followed secretly from behind while it sported in the house, disregarding those specific fragments of time (the days and nights) that steal away its life like a pack of wolves snatching at prey whose ears have been excessively enticed."
Having observed the behavior of the deer within yourself,
restrain your mind in the heart and the river of the ears in the mind; abandon this forest-dwelling of women, which is the song of the assembly of the most wicked.
"Delight the refuge of the swans (the liberated souls) and gradually cease [from worldly activity].
The King said:
"O Brahmin, I have heard and reflected upon that which the Blessed One has spoken."

"The teachers do not know this; what would they say if they knew? O Brahmin, my great doubt regarding this matter has been severed by you—for even the sages are bewildered where the functions of the senses do not reach."
"Whatever actions a person undertakes here, having abandoned them, he experiences their results in the next world with another body"—
this is the teaching of those who know the Vedas, heard here and there.
"Action that is performed in secret, not revealed, is said to be [meritorious].
Nārada said:
"By the very same means by which a person undertakes an action, by that same means he experiences its result in the hereafter."
For he himself experiences [the results] through the unobstructed medium of the subtle body (liṅga) and the mind;
just as a person leaves behind this sleeping, breathing body,
so does he experience the karma deposited within himself, whether by means of that same [subtle body] or another.
Whatever this person grasps with his mind while saying "I am this," that man performs a successful action by which there is rebirth;
for the mind is inferred by both types of sense-perceptions.
In this way, the karma born of previous bodies is perceived through the fluctuations of the mind;
for what has not been experienced, nor seen or heard by this present body,
could ever be apprehended in its form or nature within the self?
Therefore, have faith in such a manifestation of the body of this one who bears the marks of royalty; an object not previously experienced cannot touch the mind.
It is the mind alone that foretells the signs of a person's future form.

Blessings to you; likewise, that which is yet to come and that which will not come to pass are both seen here within the mind, though unseen and unheard elsewhere. Just so, one should infer [the nature of things] based on their dependence upon place, time, and action.
All objects of the senses come repeatedly and pass away many times into the mind according to the sequence of time; yet for all people who possess a mind,
when that mind is fixed solely on pure being and remains by the side of the Blessed Lord, [the senses do not prevail].
Just as the moon shines while being eclipsed by Rāhu,
so too this notion of "I" and "mine" appears in the person;
for as long as the beginningless array of intellect, mind, senses, objects, and the modes of nature persists, this state remains obscured.
Due to the obstruction of the movement of the vital breaths during sleep, fainting, or affliction,
the knowledge that "I am not here" does not arise even in death or intense fever;
likewise, in the womb or in childhood, because of physical immaturity, that elevenfold knowledge is absent at those times.
The subtle body (liṅga) of the youth is no longer visible, just like the moon on the new-moon day;
yet, even though its object no longer exists, transmigratory existence does not cease,
for one who meditates upon sense-objects experiences the arrival of misfortune, just as in a dream.

Thus, this fivefold subtle body (liṅga), which is threefold and sixteen-fold in its expansion, when joined with consciousness, is designated as the "jīva. By means of this, the person (puruṣa) assumes and abandons bodies.
Through this [body], one experiences joy, sorrow, fear, suffering, and happiness.
If there should arise devotion to Kṛṣṇa, compassion for living beings, and unimpeded knowledge of the Self,
then liberation from the cycle of worldly existence would surely come to that person.
Just as this grass-leech does not leave and yet leaves [its former blade], so too a person,
even when dying, cannot abandon their identification with the previous body;
otherwise, having seen the unseen, they would perish like a being in a dream.

O lord of men, the mind alone is the creator of the existence of all beings; it encompasses the past, the present, and the future, as well as the secret of all secrets while they sleep, until one finds another through the intervention of karmic actions.
When one repeatedly accumulates actions by meditating on those performed with the senses,
bondage arises for the non-Self in the presence of action and ignorance;
therefore, to counteract that, worship Hari with your whole being.
"Beholding the universe as being of that nature, since its maintenance, origin, and dissolution proceed from Him.
Maitreya said:
"The venerable Nārada, the foremost of the devotees of the Lord, [described] the path of the two swans."
Having shown him this and taken leave of him, he departed for the realm of the Siddhas;
then the royal sage Prācīnabarhi, having instructed his sons in the protection and propagation of his subjects, went to the hermitage of Kapila to practice austerities.
There, with one-pointed mind and steady intellect, the wise one, free from attachment, worshipped the lotus feet of Govinda with devotion and attained identity with Him.
O sinless one, this transcendental knowledge regarding the Self was sung by the celestial sage.
Whoever causes this to be heard or whoever hears it is liberated from the marks of conditioned existence.
This [narrative], which purifies the world through the glory of Mukunda,
has issued from the mouth of the best of divine sages and is the purification of the self.

He who attains this supreme state being thus glorified does not wander in this worldly existence, being liberated from all bonds. This wonderful mystery concerning the supreme self has been attained by me.
"Thus, for the man, the state of being a woman is severed, and there is no longer any doubt regarding the hereafter.
Vidura said:
"O Brahmin, those sons of Prācīnabarhis who were mentioned by you—"

Having propitiated Hari with the song of Rudra, what perfection did they attain? Was it in this world or the next? Or rather, since they were attendants at the side of the beloved Lord of Kaivalya, having by chance approached the divine Giriśa, the Pracetās surely attained the Supreme.
Maitreya said:
Within the ocean, the Pracetasas, carrying out their father’s command,
gratified Purañjana through austerity and by means of non-sacrificial offerings.
At the end of ten thousand years, the eternal Person appeared before them, pacifying their suffering with his tranquil luster;
he was mounted upon the shoulders of Garuḍa like a cloud upon the peak of Mount Meru.
Clad in yellow garments, with a jeweled neck-ornament, he made the quarters of the sky free from darkness;
his face was radiant with cheeks illuminated by shimmering golden ornaments, and his crown gleamed brightly.
Attended by his eight weapons, his attendants, sages, and the lords of the gods,
his glory was sung by Garuḍa and the Kinnaras;
he possessed the splendor of the central circle of his eight stout and long arms.
Surrounded by a forest garland whose splendor rivaled that of Śrī herself,
the Supreme Person spoke to his surrendered sons with a voice like the roar of rain-clouds and a compassionate glance.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Choose a boon—may it be well with you—you who are my sons, O princes.
Because of your affection, you whose duties are not separate from mine, I am pleased by your friendship."
The man who daily remembers you during the twilight prayers attains a sense of equality toward his brothers as well as friendship toward all living beings.
Furthermore, those who, with concentrated minds, [chant] my hymn sung by Rudra in the evening and the morning—
They praised him, saying: "I shall grant you boons of every desire and excellent wisdom, since you have joyfully accepted your father’s command;
thus, your radiant fame shall endure throughout the worlds."
A son, renowned and not inferior to Brahmā in his qualities, shall be born, who by his own prowess will fill these three worlds. Kaṇḍu obtained a lotus-eyed daughter from Pramlocā.
The princes gathered that [lotus] which had been cast away;
and King Soma, filled with compassion, placed his forefinger, which showered nectar, into the mouth of her who was emaciated by hunger and weeping.
"Commanded by our father to create progeny, follow my instructions in this matter:
marry that maiden of exquisite form without delay. She shall be the common wife of you all, for you are all of one mind in dharma and conduct."
"May this wife, her mind fully surrendered, share in the same dharma and conduct as you;
for a thousand times a thousand divine years,
may she enjoy earthly pleasures and celestial blessings from me, her vital energy never failing."
Then, through unswerving devotion to Me, when the latent impressions of the material qualities have been ripened,
you shall depart from this hellish existence and attain My abode—
even for those men who enter household life while performing virtuous deeds.
For those whose lives have been filled with news of Me, home is no longer considered a bond.
Since they have attained this Brahman— which the exponents of the Veda declare to be ever-new within the heart—
they are neither deluded, nor do they grieve, nor do they rejoice.
Maitreya said: As Janārdana, the vessel of all human goals, was speaking thus, the Pracetasas, with palms joined in reverence,
their darkness, passion, and impurities destroyed by the sight of him, praised their dearest friend with voices faltering with emotion.
The Pracetās said:
"Obeisances, obeisances unto the destroyer of afflictions, whose sublime qualities and names have been fully described;
obeisances unto Him who precedes the speed of mind and speech, and whose path cannot be traversed by the paths of all the senses."
Salutations to the pure and peaceful one, who, through his own steadfastness, shines as the non-dual within the mind;
salutations to him who assumes forms through the qualities of *māyā* during the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe;
salutations to Hari, the embodiment of pure goodness, whose intellect is like that of a horse.
Salutations to Vāsudeva, to Kṛṣṇa, the source of all the Sātvatas; salutations to the one with a lotus-navel, salutations to the one garlanded with lotuses;
salutations to the one with lotus-feet, salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one.
"Obeisances to Him whose pure garment is the reddish-yellow hue of the filaments of a lotus;
obeisances, we offer, to the Witness, the abode of all beings.
This form has been shown by the Blessed One for the total destruction of all afflictions."
What else could be more compassionate than this shown to us who are so afflicted?
For this indeed is what must be done by all-pervading lords who are affectionate toward the distressed: that you are remembered at the proper time through your own wisdom, O destroyer of misfortune.
O Lord of the universe, that by which even the smallest beings here find peace— why does he, who is hidden within our hearts, not grant us his blessings? This alone is the boon we desire.

The Blessed One, who is the liberation, the guru, and the ultimate goal for those in whom he is pleased— O Lord, even though you are higher than the highest, we choose a boon from you; for there is no end to your manifestations, and thus you are sung as Ananta (the Infinite).
When the *pārijāta* tree was easily obtained, the deer did not resort to anything else;
having reached the very root of Your feet, what more could we possibly choose?
Only so long as we are touched by Your *māyā* do we wander here through the results of our past actions.

May we have association with those who are attached to you in birth after birth; we do not weigh even a fraction of such association against heaven or liberation from rebirth— how much less, O Blessed One, could we value the worldly boons sought by mortals?
Where refined stories are celebrated, from which the cessation of thirst arises;
where there is enmity toward no living being and where there is no agitation whatsoever; where Nārāyaṇa, the Lord himself, the goal of those who have renounced, resides.

He is praised again and again in the assemblies of the saintly by those free from attachment; for one who fears the world, would not the meeting with Your devotees— who wander on foot with the desire to purify sacred fords— be pleasing?
O Blessed One, we have today attained You as our refuge— the best of physicians for the incurable disease of worldly existence and death— through a moment’s union with Your dear friend Bhava himself.
For we have studied the Vedas, and we have gratified our gurus, brahmins, and elders through constant service.

O Lord, our noble kinsmen, friends, brothers, and all living beings have indeed been free from malice toward us. Whatever austerity we have performed for such a long time while deprived of food within the waters—
all this we offer unto You, the Infinite Being, for Your complete satisfaction.

Manu, the self-born, the Blessed One, and Bhava, as well as others whose natures are purified by austerity and knowledge—even they, though unable to see the further shore of His majesty, offer praise; yet we, moreover, extol Him as being equal to our own selves.
Obeisances to the Equal One, the Pure One, the Supreme Person.
"Obeisances to You, Vāsudeva, the pure essence, the Blessed Lord.
Maitreya said:
Thus praised by the Pracetās, Hari, who is affectionate toward those who seek refuge, was pleased and said, "So be it."

To those who did not wish for his departure and whose eyes were never satiated with beholding him, he whose prowess is beyond cessation returned to his own abode. Then, emerging from the waters of the ocean,
the Pracetasas saw the earth covered by trees that stood as high as if to obstruct the very sky, and they became enraged.
Then, O King, Agni and Māruta, out of wrath, emitted from their mouths a fire like the *saṃvartaka* at the end of an eon, in order to strip the earth of its vegetation;
seeing those trees being reduced to ashes, the Grandfather (Brahmā) [intervened].
Upon his arrival, he pacified the sons of Barhiṣmat through various means.
At that time, those trees which remained there, being afraid, rescued their daughter;
they were then instructed by the Self-born (Brahmā) regarding the Pracetas.

And they, by the command of Brahmā, married Māriṣā, from whom, due to his great contempt for her, Aja was born, though he was not born from a womb. Then, when the Cākṣuṣa interval arrived, the previous creation was swept away by Time.
He who, impelled by the gods, created the desired progeny was Dakṣa;
and because he, upon being born, seized with his own luster the splendor of all luminous beings,
and because of his skill (*dākṣya*) in performing ritual acts, they called him Dakṣa.
Having consecrated him in the creation and protection of progeny, the Anādi (the Beginningless One) appointed him and likewise appointed all the other Prajāpatis.
Maitreya said:
Then, having attained wisdom and remembering what Lord Adhokṣaja had spoken, they abandoned their wife and son and departed from their home.
Having been initiated for the sacrificial session of Brahman (*brahma-satra*), they offered as the oblation the very self of all living beings.

In the western direction, on the shore where Jājali had attained perfection, Nārada—worthy of worship by gods and asuras—beheld those who had conquered their vital breaths, mind, speech, and sight; who were masters of their postures; whose bodies were tranquil and composed; and who had fixed their selves upon the supreme, stainless Brahman.
When he had arrived, they rose, prostrated themselves, and greeted him;
having honored him and offered him a seat as was appropriate, they sat comfortably and then spoke.
The Pracetases said:
"Welcome to you, O celestial sage! By good fortune, you have come into our sight today.
O Brahmin, your wandering is for the sake of granting fearlessness, just like that of the sun.
Whatever has been commanded by the Blessed One, by Śiva, and by Adhokṣaja—"
O Lord, for us who have been mostly wasted away by attachment to household life,
please illuminate that knowledge of the self which reveals the true nature of reality,
by which we may easily cross over the difficult-to-traverse ocean of worldly existence.
Maitreya said:
Thus questioned by the Pracetasas, the venerable sage Nārada,
whose soul was absorbed in the Blessed One of excellent renown, spoke to the kings.
Nārada said: That birth, those actions, that lifespan, and those thoughts and words of men are indeed meaningful by which Hari, the Lord and Soul of the Universe, is served.
What is the use here of the three births— those pertaining to Śukra, Savitṛ, and Yajña—
or of the activities prescribed by the three Vedas, even if one possesses the lifespan of a god?
What is the use of sacred learning, austerity, words, or the fluctuations of the mind?
Of what use is subtle intelligence, or strength consisting of the power of the senses; or what use is yoga, Sāṅkhya, renunciation, or Vedic study;
or what use are other auspicious things, if they do not lead one to Hari, the giver of the self?
For in reality, the Self is the ultimate limit of all that is auspicious;
indeed, Hari is the Self, the giver of the Self, and the beloved of all living beings.
Just as by watering the root of a tree, its trunk, branches, and twigs are all satisfied.
Just as the offering of the vital breath constitutes the worship of all the senses, so too does the worship of Acyuta constitute the worship of all things.
Just as the waters originate from the sun and enter back into it at the proper time,
so do all beings— both stationary and moving— originate from the earth and likewise, the flow of the material qualities (guṇas) proceeds from Hari alone.

This supreme state of the Self of the universe shines forth once and for all, like the radiance of the sun; it is the cessation of the delusion of distinctions between substance, action, and knowledge, wherein the vital breaths awaken from their dormant powers.
O King, just as clouds, darkness, and light appear and disappear in succession within the sky, so do these states come and go.
Thus, these powers— rajas, tamas, and sattva— are but the flow [of manifestations] within the Supreme Brahman.
Therefore, with single-minded devotion, truly worship Him who is the one Self of all embodied beings, the Time, the Pradhāna, the Puruṣa, and the Supreme Lord,
whose stream of qualities has been destroyed by His own splendor.
Janārdana is quickly pleased by compassion toward all beings, by contentment with whatever may come, and by the complete stilling of all the senses;
he is summoned by the constant cultivation of devotion within a soul that is stainless because all desires have been destroyed.
Because Hari has surrendered His own independence to His devotees, He does not deviate from them, for He is like an imperishable jewel that cannot pass through a hole [without being caught].
Indeed, Hari— who is dear to those who have no wealth other than the Self, who knows the essence of devotion, and who is the beloved of the wise— does not accept the worship of the evil-minded who,
intoxicated by their learning, wealth, lineage, and ritual acts, commit sins against the saintly who possess nothing.

Since He, being self-sufficient and dependent only on His own circle of servants, does not seek after Śrī who follows Him, nor after the lords of men or the gods who desire Her, how could a grateful person ever abandon Him? Maitreya said:
"O King, having thus related these and other stories of the Lord to the Pracetasas,
the sage Svāyambhuva departed for the world of Brahmā.
They, too, [heard] that fame issuing from his mouth, which removes the impurities of the world."

Having heard of that foot of Hari, they meditated upon it and attained His state. O Vidura, I have related to you this conversation between the Pracetas and Nārada, which glorifies Hari, concerning that which you asked of me.
Śrī Śuka said:
O best of kings, you have been described the lineage of Uttānapāda, the son of Manu; now learn also of the lineage of Priyavrata.

He who, having received the science of the Self from Nārada, enjoyed the earth and then divided it among his sons, attained the supreme abode of the Lord; and Kṣattṛ, having heard this excellent discourse on the teachings of the Unconquered (Kṛṣṇa) as described by Kauṣāravi.
With his emotion fully aroused and his eyes clouded with tears, he placed the foot of the sage upon his head and that of Hari within his heart.
Vidura said:
"O Great Yogin, today this very person has been [graced] by you, whose nature is compassion..."
There, Hari, who possesses nothing yet is the goal of all, showed them the further shore of darkness.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus bowed down and taken leave of him, Vidura went to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).

Desiring to see his own kinsmen, he set out with a heart full of joy. O King, whoever hears this account of those monarchs who had dedicated their souls to Hari shall obtain long life, wealth, fame, well-being, a favorable rebirth, and sovereignty.
